          "uuid": "e8dbd059-6b19-4acc-904a-d13f3a6df68e",
          "filename": "€(txt)_JSON Packaging for a Multi-Document “Pandora’s Box”",
          "content": "JSON Packaging for a Multi-Document “Pandora’s Box”\n\nModern JSON is a lightweight, text-based data format that is easy for humans to read and write and easy for machines to parse and generate.  Because JSON inherently represents data as nested objects and arrays, we can bundle multiple documents into one structured JSON “package.”  For example, each document can be represented as an object, and a top-level array or object can collect them.  (In fact, if you need to store several objects in one JSON file, you must put them in an array.)  This approach is analogous to a compound JSON document or “bundle.”  In the JSON Schema world, such a “compound schema document” explicitly contains multiple embedded resources.  Similarly, the JSON:API specification defines compound documents where related resources are included together in a single JSON payload (using a top-level included array).\n\nBy analogy, each thematic entity (e.g. “The Fecal Truth”, “Sticks, Stones and Marrowed Bones”, “The Monarch”) can be one object (one “Pandora box”) containing its related materials.  For example, a JSON package might look like:\n\n{\n  \"LibertyJusticeAgency\": {\n    \"description\": \"Collection of themed documents\",\n    \"entities\": [\n      {\n        \"name\": \"The Fecal Truth\",\n        \"theme\": \"Environmental commentary\",\n        \"documents\": [\n          {\n            \"title\": \"Fecal Truth Overview\",\n            \"format\": \"markdown\",\n            \"file\": \"fecal_truth.md\",\n            \"url\": \"http://example.com/fecal_truth.md\"\n          },\n          {\n            \"title\": \"Underlying Data\",\n            \"format\": \"pdf\",\n            \"file\": \"data_report.pdf\",\n            \"url\": \"http://example.com/data_report.pdf\"\n          }\n        ]\n      },\n      {\n        \"name\": \"Sticks, Stones and Marrowed Bones\",\n        \"theme\": \"Philosophical essay\",\n        \"documents\": [\n          {\n            \"title\": \"Essay Draft\",\n            \"format\": \"docx\",\n            \"file\": \"sticks_stones_essay.docx\",\n            \"url\": \"http://example.com/sticks_stones_essay.docx\"\n          },\n          {\n            \"title\": \"Historical Notes\",\n            \"format\": \"html\",\n            \"file\": \"historical_notes.html\",\n            \"url\": \"http://example.com/historical_notes.html\"\n          }\n        ]\n      },\n      {\n        \"name\": \"The Monarch\",\n        \"theme\": \"Political analysis\",\n        \"documents\": [\n          {\n            \"title\": \"Monarch Timeline\",\n            \"format\": \"pdf\",\n            \"file\": \"monarch_timeline.pdf\",\n            \"url\": \"http://example.com/monarch_timeline.pdf\"\n          },\n          {\n            \"title\": \"Charter Text\",\n            \"format\": \"markdown\",\n            \"file\": \"monarch_charter.md\",\n            \"url\": \"http://example.com/monarch_charter.md\"\n          }\n        ]\n      }\n    ]\n  }\n}\n\nIn this structure, each entity has its own documents array.  Each document entry can include metadata (title, format, etc.) and either the content itself or a link to it.  For diverse formats (DOCX, HTML, PDF, Markdown, etc.), the JSON can store either:\n\nExternal references (URLs or file paths) to the actual files, leaving the JSON lightweight, or\n\nEmbedded content (e.g. as Base64-encoded strings inside JSON).\n\n\nNote that JSON cannot natively contain binary data; any binary (like a PDF or Word file) must be encoded as text (for example, Base64).  While Base64 is a common solution, it adds about 33% size overhead (3 bytes become 4 chars).  In practice, it’s often simpler to put the binary files (PDF, DOCX, etc.) in the same folder as the JSON and use a URL or relative path in the JSON entry.\n\nEach entity-object acts as a “Pandora box” of related materials.  The JSON schema for each box might include additional fields (tags, creation date, symbol markers, etc.).  For example, you might prefix certain documents with a symbol (like € or π) to indicate status (as your notes suggest).  These symbols can appear in the JSON as part of file names or metadata fields.  Using a structured JSON object means all these pieces – the text, the themes, the file pointers, the metadata – live together in a coherent package.\n\nConnecting Documents and Interactions: This JSON package can also be designed for interactivity.  For instance, one can serve it via a web API (e.g. using a JSON:API or REST endpoint) so that reader applications can fetch and display the document collection. Readers could interact by, say, submitting feedback or annotations. Those interactions could update the JSON (e.g. adding comments or new links), effectively making it “self-updating.” For example, a web front-end might display the JSON contents and allow readers to append notes; those notes would get written back into the JSON (server-side) – similar to how a CMS lets users contribute content via structured JSON APIs.  The key is that JSON’s plain-text nature and nested structure make it easy to programmatically read, modify, and extend.  In fact, JSON:API explicitly supports updating compound documents and relationships via its standard (using HTTP PATCH/POST).\n\nImplementation Tips:\n\nTop-level structure: Use one top-level JSON object (or array) as the “container.”  Inside it, have an \"entities\" array or similar to hold each themed box.  This follows JSON’s hierarchical pattern.\n\nArrays for multiple items: Whenever you have multiple documents, place them in an array.  JSON arrays ([...]) can hold any number of objects, ensuring valid JSON.\n\nDescriptive metadata: Include fields like name, description, theme, and custom symbols (e.g. \"status\": \"prime\").  This makes the JSON “rich” and self-describing.\n\nLinking content: For HTML/Markdown docs, you could even include the raw text (as a string) inside JSON; for large files (PDF, DOCX) it’s best to link by filename or URL.  In JSON Schema and OpenAPI, the idea of “bundling” separate files into one JSON file is well-established.  Likewise, JSON:API’s compound document shows how to list all related resources in one JSON payload.\n\nVersioning and updates: Because JSON is text, you can version it (e.g. with a timestamp or revision field).  New documents can be added by appending objects to arrays, and a consuming application can fetch updates as needed.\n\nSelf-updating mechanics: To allow reader interactions (comments, edits), you could deploy a lightweight server or use a static site with forms that modify the JSON.  For example, reading/writing the JSON through a small backend (Node, Python, etc.) would let others “interact” with it.  Even without a full server, platforms like GitHub allow JSON changes via pull requests.\n\n\nBy organizing your series of documents into this “layered” JSON package, you essentially create a living collection. Each entity’s JSON object is like a sealed Pandora’s box: it contains all the related files and lore. As new files are added or readers contribute insights, you update the JSON (unsealing and resealing the box) so the structure stays coherent. This approach leverages JSON’s flexibility (easy nesting and arrays) and is informed by real-world practices (JSON Schema bundling, compound documents). The result is a single, manageable JSON file (or set of files) that holds your entire narrative package across formats, ready for parsing, display, and even reader engagement.\n\nSources: JSON’s flexibility for data interchange, the need for arrays to hold multiple objects, and the concept of “bundling” many files in one JSON are all documented in authoritative JSON guides and specs. (Embedding binary is not native to JSON, so external links or base64 are necessary.) These principles ensure the JSON “Pandora boxes” are robust, extensible, and interactive.\n\n",

Logic Gates Layer\n```python\nclass LogicGate:\n    def __init__(self, type):\n        self.type = type  # AND, OR, NOT, etc.\n        self.inputs = []\n        self.output = None\n        self.complexity_score = self.calculate_complexity()\n    \n    def calculate_complexity(self):\n        # Base complexity for different gate types\n        complexity_map = {\n            'NOT': 1,\n            'AND': 2,\n            'OR': 2,\n            'NAND': 3,\n            'NOR': 3,\n            'XOR': 4\n        }\n        return complexity_map.get(self.type, 1)\n```\n\n### 3. Metrics\n```python\ndef calculate_system_complexity(components):\n    total_complexity = 0\n    for component in components:\n        # Base complexity\n        base = component.complexity_score\n        \n        # Connection complexity\n        connections = len(component.inputs) + 1  # +1 for output\n        \n        # State complexity\n        states = component.possible_states if hasattr(component, 'possible_states') else 2\n        \n        # Combined complexity\n        component_complexity = base * connections * math.log2(states)\n        total_complexity += component_complexity\n        \n    return total_complexity\n```\n\n### 2. \\n\\n\\n3\\n\\nINTRODUCTION\\n\\n\\nIntroduction\\nThis is the DUNGEONS & DRAGONS\\u00ae Roleplaying Game the game\\nthat defines the genre and has set the standard for fantasy role-\\nplaying for more than 30 years.\\nSpecifically this is the Dungeon Master\\u2019s Guide. This book con-\\ntains information that every Dungeon Master (DM) needs to set\\nup adventures narrate the action run the monsters and referee\\nthe DUNGEONS &DRAGONS game. This book the Player\\u2019s Handbook\\nand the Monster Manual comprise the core rules for the D&D\\u00ae\\ngame. \\n\\n\\nTHE DUNGEON MASTER\\nWe\\u2019ve distilled our knowledge of the D&D\\u00ae game into the mate-\\nrial that follows. Whether you need to know how to design an\\nadventure a campaign or an entire game world the material in\\nthis book can and will help you.\\nYou\\u2019re a member of a select group. Truly not everyone has the cre-\\nativity and the dedication to be a DM. Dungeon Mastering (DMing)\\ncan be challenging but it\\u2019s not a chore. You\\u2019re the lucky one out of\\nyour entire circle of friends who play the game. The real fun is in\\nyour hands. As you flip through the Monster Manual or look at pub-\\nlished adventures on a store shelf you get to decide what the player\\ncharacters (PCs) take on next. You get to build a whole world as well\\nas design and play all its nonplayer characters (NPCs).\\nIt\\u2019s good to be the DM.\\nThe DM defines the game. A good DM results in a good game.\\nSince you control the pacing and the types of adventures and\\nencounters the whole tenor of the game is in your hands. It\\u2019s fun\\nbut it\\u2019s a big responsibility. If you\\u2019re the sort of person who likes to\\nprovide the fun for your friends or to come up with new ideas\\nthen you\\u2019re an ideal candidate for DM.\\nOnce your group has a Dungeon Master however that doesn\\u2019t\\nmean that you can\\u2019t switch around. This book contains a battle\\ngrid and other tools to help you visualize the action.\\nThe poster-sized sheet in the back of the book has a 1-inch grid\\non one side and a collection of rooms that can be used to repre-\\nsent areas in a dungeon on the other side.\\nThe last 12 pages of this book (just ahead of the index) present a\\nvariety of visual aids that you can use to set up and play out\\nencounters and adventures on the grid:\\n\\u2014Six pages of diagrams that show the squares contained\\nwithin areas of different sizes and shapes and graphic depictions\\nof space and reach for creatures of varying sizes.\\n\\u2014Six pages of illustrations that represent various dungeon\\nfeatures sized to fit the 1-inch grid that you can photocopy cut\\nout and place on the grid\\u2014enabling players to actually see\\nwhat lies before their characters as they make their way through\\nthe dungeon. \\n\\n\\nFINAL NOTE\\nThe power of creating worlds controlling deities and dragons and\\nleading entire nations is in your hands. Character growth happens in the midst of such interactions.\\n   - **Monologues or soliloquies** offer insight into a character\\u2019s internal motivations, which may reveal personal struggles or shifts in their values.\\n   - **Group decisions and ethical dilemmas** can be tracked to assess how group dynamics evolve and how individual characters influence decisions.\\n\\n2. **Conversation Transcript Collection**\\n   - In a tabletop setting, the **Dungeon Master (DM)** can summarize these conversations or record significant moments to review after sessions. You can also ask players to write down their thoughts between sessions, which would serve as mini-reflections for their characters.\\n\\n### II. Conversation Analysis\\n\\n1. **Identify Key Themes**\\n   - **Character motivations and goals**: Use the conversations to trace the **personal growth** of characters. This can be through **changing goals, alliances, or ethical shifts** over time.\\n   - **Ethical dilemmas and decision-making**: Keep track of difficult choices that force characters to re-evaluate their beliefs. **How do their responses change over time?** This could reveal growth, internal conflict, or new priorities.\\n   - **Power dynamics**: Look at how relationships between characters evolve based on **who leads, who follows, and who challenges the norms** within the group.\\n   - **Cultural and societal influences**: Introduce these elements through NPCs or quests. How do the characters\\u2019 backgrounds shape their worldview, and how are those views challenged?\\n\\n2. **Character Development**\\n   - Assess **changes in belief systems**: As players interact, their characters might change from selfish to selfless, vengeful to forgiving, etc.\\n   - **Behavioral shifts**: Look for signs of evolving behavior patterns, such as a typically peaceful character resorting to violence or a greedy character showing generosity.\\n   - **Relationships**: Track the evolution of friendships, rivalries, and mentor-student dynamics to see how these affect decision-making and loyalty.\\n\\n3. **Identify Ethical Dilemmas**\\n   - Explore **the nature of dilemmas** by categorizing decisions into moral choices (e.g., sacrifice one for many or save a loved one).\\n   - Track **choices made** and their **consequences**, both immediate and long-term.\\n   - Use these dilemmas to **challenge the characters' ethical boundaries**, ensuring they must revisit or redefine their values.\\n\\n4. **Analyze Decision-Making**\\n   - Record **how characters justify their decisions**\\u2014are they driven by emotion, logic, or social expectations?\\n   - Consider what **external factors** influence decisions, such as loyalty to party members, fear of the unknown, or moral codes.\\n\\n### III. Application to Essence Document\\n\\n1. **Character Profiles**\\n   - Add details to the **Essence document** about how characters change based on their conversations. Include newly learned information about their motivations, beliefs, and shifts in behavior.\\n   - Introduce or update **character traits**, such as fear of failure or newfound confidence, based on narrative development.\\n   - Enhance **backstories** to reflect these changes, adding new layers of complexity that inform future decisions.\\n\\n2. **Ethical Dilemmas**\\n   - Expand on existing dilemmas, incorporating **conversations as precursors** to larger story arcs. This could involve teasing out moral themes slowly over multiple sessions.\\n   - Introduce more **nuanced dilemmas** as characters become more ethically complex. For example, a paladin might struggle with upholding justice versus personal revenge.\\n\\n3. **Decision-Making**\\n   - Introduce more **grey-area decisions** as the campaign progresses, forcing the characters to weigh pros and cons in more sophisticated ways.\\n   - Tailor **future encounters** based on characters' past decisions, showing the ripple effects of their choices (e.g., NPCs reacting differently to the group based on earlier conversations).\\n\\n4. **Depth in Relationships**\\n   - Develop **in-game mechanics** that enhance relationships: bond points, rivalries, or trust levels based on in-character interactions.\\n   - Introduce challenges that force the characters to confront or solidify relationships, using conversation-driven moments to foster loyalty or betrayal.\\n\\n### Integration with D&D Mechanics\\n- Use tools such as **Proficiency Bonuses**, **Ability Checks**, and **Skill Rolls** (outlined in the basic D&D cheat sheet\\u301011\\u2020source\\u3011) to introduce gameplay mechanics for conversations:\\n  - \\n\\n\\n3\\n\\nINTRODUCTION\\n\\n\\nIntroduction\\nThis is the DUNGEONS & DRAGONS\\u00ae Roleplaying Game the game\\nthat defines the genre and has set the standard for fantasy role-\\nplaying for more than 30 years.\\nSpecifically this is the Dungeon Master\\u2019s Guide. This book con-\\ntains information that every Dungeon Master (DM) needs to set\\nup adventures narrate the action run the monsters and referee\\nthe DUNGEONS &DRAGONS game. This book the Player\\u2019s Handbook\\nand the Monster Manual comprise the core rules for the D&D\\u00ae\\ngame. \\n\\n\\nTHE DUNGEON MASTER\\nWe\\u2019ve distilled our knowledge of the D&D\\u00ae game into the mate-\\nrial that follows. Whether you need to know how to design an\\nadventure a campaign or an entire game world the material in\\nthis book can and will help you.\\nYou\\u2019re a member of a select group. Truly not everyone has the cre-\\nativity and the dedication to be a DM. Dungeon Mastering (DMing)\\ncan be challenging but it\\u2019s not a chore. You\\u2019re the lucky one out of\\nyour entire circle of friends who play the game. The real fun is in\\nyour hands. As you flip through the Monster Manual or look at pub-\\nlished adventures on a store shelf you get to decide what the player\\ncharacters (PCs) take on next. You get to build a whole world as well\\nas design and play all its nonplayer characters (NPCs).\\nIt\\u2019s good to be the DM.\\nThe DM defines the game. A good DM results in a good game.\\nSince you control the pacing and the types of adventures and\\nencounters the whole tenor of the game is in your hands. It\\u2019s fun\\nbut it\\u2019s a big responsibility. If you\\u2019re the sort of person who likes to\\nprovide the fun for your friends or to come up with new ideas\\nthen you\\u2019re an ideal candidate for DM.\\nOnce your group has a Dungeon Master however that doesn\\u2019t\\nmean that you can\\u2019t switch around. Some DMs like to take a turn\\nat being a player and many players eventually want to try their\\nhand at DMing.\\n\\n\\npqqrs \\n\\n\\nHOW TO USE THIS BOOK\\nNo one expects you to read this book cover to cover. It\\u2019s not a\\nnovel. Instead we arranged this book into topics that you can refer\\nto when you need them. Plus an extended glossary at the back of\\nthe book provides quick reference to DM-related topics. \\nBased on those portions of the game that you control you\\u2019ll find\\nchapters that deal with running the game adjudicating play writ-\\ning adventures building a campaign awarding experience and\\nfinding or creating the right magic items to stock your dungeons.\\nRefer to the table of contents and the index to locate the specific\\ntopic you need at any given time.\\n\\n\\nPLAYING ON THE BATTLE GRID\\nThe D&D game assumes the use of miniature figures and the\\nrules are written from that perspective. This book contains a battle\\ngrid and other tools to help you visualize the action.\\nThe poster-sized sheet in the back of the book has a 1-inch grid\\non one side and a collection of rooms that can be used to repre-\\nsent areas in a dungeon on the other side.\\nThe last 12 pages of this book (just ahead of the index) present a\\nvariety of visual aids that you can use to set up and play out\\nencounters and adventures on the grid:\\n\\u2014Six pages of diagrams that show the squares contained\\nwithin areas of different sizes and shapes and graphic depictions\\nof space and reach for creatures of varying sizes.\\n\\u2014Six pages of illustrations that represent various dungeon\\nfeatures sized to fit the 1-inch grid that you can photocopy cut\\nout and place on the grid\\u2014enabling players to actually see\\nwhat lies before their characters as they make their way through\\nthe dungeon. \\n\\n\\nFINAL NOTE\\nThe power of creating worlds controlling deities and dragons and\\nleading entire nations is in your hands. You are the master of the\\ngame\\u2014the rules the setting the action and ultimately the fun.\\nThis is a great deal of power and you must use it wisely. This book\\nshows you how.\\n\\n\\nWHY A REVISION?\\nThe new DUNGEONS & DRAGONS game debuted in 2000. In the three years\\nsince the d20 Game System energized the roleplaying game industry pqqrs\\nwe\\u2019ve gathered tons of data on how the game is being played. \"\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n\\nSynthetic biological circuit - Wikipedia\\n\\n\\nSynthetic biological circuit\\nSynthetic biological circuits are an application of synthetic biology where biological parts inside a\\n\\ncell are designed to perform logical functions mimicking those observed in electronic circuits.\\n\\nTypically, these circuits are categorized as either genetic circuits, RNA circuits, or protein circuits,\\n\\ndepending on the types of biomolecule that interact to create the circuit's behavior. The applications\\n\\nof all three types of circuit range from simply inducing production to adding a measurable element,\\n\\nlike green fluorescent protein, to an existing natural biological circuit, to implementing completely\\n\\nnew systems of many parts.[1]\\n\\nThe lac operon is a natural biological circuit on\\n\\nwhich many synthetic circuits are based. Top:\\n\\nRepressed, Bottom: Active.\\n\\n1: RNA polymerase, 2: Repressor, 3: Promoter,\\n\\n4: Operator, 5: Lactose, 6: lacZ, 7: lacY, 8: lacA.\\n\\nA ribosome is a biological machine.\\n\\nThe goal of synthetic biology is to generate an array of tunable and characterized parts, or modules,\\n\\nwith which any desirable synthetic biological circuit can be easily designed and implemented.[2]\\n\\nThese circuits can serve as a method to modify cellular functions, create cellular responses to\\n\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthetic_biology\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cell_(biology)\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_circuit\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biomolecule\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_fluorescent_protein\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_regulatory_network\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lac_Operon.svg\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lac_Operon.svg\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Protein_translation.gif\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Protein_translation.gif\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ribosome\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_machine\\n\\n\\nenvironmental conditions, or influence cellular development. By implementing rational, controllable\\n\\nlogic elements in cellular systems, researchers can use living systems as engineered \\\"biological\\n\\nmachines\\\" to perform a vast range of useful functions.[1]\\n\\nThe first natural gene circuit studied in detail was the lac operon. In studies of diauxic growth of E.\\n\\ncoli on two-sugar media, Jacques Monod and Francois Jacob discovered that E.coli preferentially\\n\\nconsumes the more easily processed glucose before switching to lactose metabolism. They\\n\\ndiscovered that the mechanism that controlled the metabolic \\\"switching\\\" function was a two-part\\n\\ncontrol mechanism on the lac operon. When lactose is present in the cell the enzyme \\u03b2-\\n\\ngalactosidase is produced to convert lactose into glucose or galactose. When lactose is absent in\\n\\nthe cell the lac repressor inhibits the production of the enzyme \\u03b2-galactosidase to prevent any\\n\\ninefficient processes within the cell.\\n\\nThe lac operon is used in the biotechnology industry for production of recombinant proteins for\\n\\ntherapeutic use. The gene or genes for producing an exogenous protein are placed on a plasmid\\n\\nunder the control of the lac promoter. Initially the cells are grown in a medium that does not contain\\n\\nlactose or other sugars, so the new genes are not expressed. Once the cells reach a certain point in\\n\\ntheir growth, isopropyl \\u03b2-D-1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG) is added. IPTG, a molecule similar to\\n\\nlactose, but with a sulfur bond that is not hydrolyzable so that E. coli does not digest it, is used to\\n\\nactivate or \\\"induce\\\" the production of the new protein. Once the cells are induced, it is difficult to\\n\\nremove IPTG from the cells and therefore it is difficult to stop expression.\\n\\nTwo early examples of synthetic biological circuits were published in Nature in 2000. One, by Tim\\n\\nGardner, Charles Cantor, and Jim Collins working at Boston University, demonstrated a \\\"bistable\\\"\\n\\nswitch in E. coli. The switch is turned on by heating the culture of bacteria and turned off by addition\\n\\nof IPTG. They used green fluorescent protein as a reporter for their system.[3] The second, by\\n\\nMichael Elowitz and Stanislas Leibler, showed that three repressor genes could be connected to\\n\\nform a negative feedback loop termed the Repressilator that produces self-sustaining oscillations\\n\\nof protein levels in E. coli.[4]\\n\\nCurrently, synthetic circuits are a burgeoning area of research in systems biology with more\\n\\npublications detailing synthetic biological circuits published every year.[5] There has been significant\\n\\ninterest in encouraging education and outreach as well: the International Genetically Engineered\\n\\nMachines Competition[6] manages the creation and standardization of BioBrick parts as a means to\\n\\nallow undergraduate and high school students to design their own synthetic biological circuits.\\n\\nHistory\\n\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_machine\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_machine\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lac_operon\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diauxie\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/E._coli\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/E._coli\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Monod\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francois_Jacob\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glucose\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lactose\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enzyme\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/%CE%92-galactosidase\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/%CE%92-galactosidase\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glucose\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galactose\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biotechnology\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recombinant_DNA\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proteins\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exogenous\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plasmid\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/IPTG\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regulation_of_gene_expression#Inducible_vs._repressible_systems\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature_(journal)\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Collins_(bioengineer)\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_University\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Elowitz\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanislas_Leibler\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negative_feedback\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repressilator\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systems_biology\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/BioBrick\\n\\n\\nBoth immediate and long term applications exist for the use of synthetic biological circuits,\\n\\nincluding different applications for metabolic engineering, and synthetic biology. Those\\n\\ndemonstrated successfully include pharmaceutical production,[7] and fuel production.[8] However,\\n\\nmethods involving direct genetic introduction are not inherently effective without invoking the basic\\n\\nprinciples of synthetic cellular circuits. For example, each of these successful systems employs a\\n\\nmethod to introduce all-or-none induction or expression. This is a biological circuit where a simple\\n\\nrepressor or promoter is introduced to facilitate creation of the product, or inhibition of a competing\\n\\npathway. However, with the limited understanding of cellular networks and natural circuitry,\\n\\nimplementation of more robust schemes with more precise control and feedback is hindered.\\n\\nTherein lies the immediate interest in synthetic cellular circuits.\\n\\nDevelopment in understanding cellular circuitry can lead to exciting new modifications, such as cells\\n\\nwhich can respond to environmental stimuli. For example, cells could be developed that signal toxic\\n\\nsurroundings and react by activating pathways used to degrade the perceived toxin.[9] To develop\\n\\nsuch a cell, it is necessary to create a complex synthetic cellular circuit which can respond\\n\\nappropriately to a given stimulus.\\n\\nGiven synthetic cellular circuits represent a form of control for cellular activities, it can be reasoned\\n\\nthat with complete understanding of cellular pathways, \\\"plug and play\\\"[1] cells with well defined\\n\\ngenetic circuitry can be engineered. It is widely believed that if a proper toolbox of parts is\\n\\ngenerated,[10] synthetic cells can be developed implementing only the pathways necessary for cell\\n\\nsurvival and reproduction. From this cell, to be thought of as a minimal genome cell, one can add\\n\\npieces from the toolbox to create a well defined pathway with appropriate synthetic circuitry for an\\n\\neffective feedback system. Because of the basic ground up construction method, and the proposed\\n\\ndatabase of mapped circuitry pieces, techniques mirroring those used to model computer or\\n\\nelectronic circuits can be used to redesign cells and model cells for easy troubleshooting and\\n\\npredictive behavior and yields.\\n\\nOscillators\\n\\n1. Repressilator\\n\\n2. Mammalian tunable synthetic oscillator\\n\\nInterest and goals\\n\\nExample circuits\\n\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metabolic_engineering\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthetic_biology\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repressor\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Promoter_(genetics)\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genome\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repressilator\\n\\n\\n3. Bacterial tunable synthetic oscillator\\n\\n4. Coupled bacterial oscillator\\n\\n5. Globally coupled bacterial oscillator\\n\\nElowitz et al. and Fung et al. created oscillatory circuits that use multiple self-regulating\\n\\nmechanisms to create a time-dependent oscillation of gene product expression.[11][12]\\n\\nBistable switches\\n\\n1. Toggle-switch\\n\\nGardner et al. used mutual repression between two control units to create an implementation of a\\n\\ntoggle switch capable of controlling cells in a bistable manner: transient stimuli resulting in\\n\\npersistent responses.[3]\\n\\nGene regulation is an essential part of developmental processes. During development, genes are\\n\\nturned on and off in different tissues, changes in regulatory mechanisms may result in genetic\\n\\nswitching in a bistable system, the gene switches serve as regulatory molecule binding sites. These\\n\\nare proteins that activate transcription when they land on a gene switch and thereby express the\\n\\ngene that was expected to operate as a memory device, allowing cell fate decisions to be chosen\\n\\nand maintained.[13]\\n\\nToggle switch which operates using two mutually inhibitory genes, each promoter is inhibited by the\\n\\nrepressor that is transcribed by the opposing promoter. Toggle switch design: Inducer 1 inactivates\\n\\nrepressor 1, which means repressor 2 is produced. Repressor 2, in turn, stops transcription of the\\n\\nrepressor 1 gene and the reporter gene.[14]\\n\\n\\n\\nLogical operators\\n\\nThe logical AND gate.[15][16] If Signal A AND Signal B are present, then the desired gene product will result. All promoters\\n\\nshown are inducible, activated by the displayed gene product. Each signal activates expression of a separate gene (shown\\n\\nin light blue). The expressed proteins then can either form a complete complex in cytosol, that is capable of activating\\n\\nexpression of the output (shown), or can act separately to induce expression, such as separately removing an inhibiting\\n\\nprotein and inducing activation of the uninhibited promoter.\\n\\nThe logical OR gate.[15][16] If Signal A OR Signal B are present, then the desired gene product will result. All promoters\\n\\nshown are inducible. Either signal is capable of activating the expression of the output gene product, and only the action of\\n\\na single promoter is required for gene expression. Post-transcriptional regulation mechanisms can prevent the presence of\\n\\nboth inputs producing a compounded high output, such as implementing a low binding affinity ribosome binding site.\\n\\nThe logical Negated AND gate.[15][16] If Signal A AND Signal B are present, then the desired gene product will NOT result. All\\n\\npromoters shown are inducible. The activating promoter for the output gene is constitutive, and thus not shown. The\\n\\nconstitutive promoter for the output gene keeps it \\\"on\\\" and is only deactivated when (similar to the AND gate) a complex as\\n\\na result of two input signal gene products blocks the expression of the output gene.\\n\\nAnalog tuners\\n\\nUsing negative feedback and identical promoters, linearizer gene circuits can impose uniform gene\\n\\nexpression that depends linearly on extracellular chemical inducer concentration.[17]\\n\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:SynBioCirc-AndLogicGate.jpg\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:SynBioCirc-AndLogicGate.jpg\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND_gate\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cytosol\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:SynBioCirc-OrLogicGate.jpg\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:SynBioCirc-OrLogicGate.jpg\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/OR_gate\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ribosome_binding_site\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:SynBioCirc-NandLogicGate.jpg\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:SynBioCirc-NandLogicGate.jpg\\nhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negated_AND_gate\\n\\n\\nControllers of gene expression heterogeneity\\n\\nSynthetic gene circuits can control gene expression heterogeneity can be controlled independently\\n\\nof the gene expression mean.[18]\\n\\nOther engineered systems\\n\\nEngineered systems are the result of implementation of combinations of different control\\n\\nmechanisms. A limited counting mechanism was implemented by a pulse-controlled gene\\n\\ncascade[19] and application of logic elements enables genetic \\\"programming\\\" of cells as in the\\n\\nresearch of Tabor et al., which synthesized a photosensitive bacterial edge detection program.[20]\\n\\nComputational design and evaluation\\n\\nof DNA circuits to achieve optimal\\n\\nperformance\\n\\nRecent developments in artificial gene synthesis and the corresponding increase in competition\\n\\nwithin the industry have led to a significant drop in price and wait time of gene synthesis and helped\\n\\nimprove methods used in circuit design.[21] At the moment, circuit design is improving at a slow\\n\\npace because of insufficient organization of known multiple gene interactions and mathematical\\n\\nmodels. This issue is being addressed by applying computer-aided design (CAD) software to\\n\\nprovide multimedia representations of circuits through images, text and programming language\\n\\napplied to biological circuits.[22] Some of the more well known CAD programs include GenoCAD,\\n\\nClotho framework and j5.[23][24][25] GenoCAD uses grammars, which are either opensource or user\\n\\ngenerated \\\"rules\\\" which include the available genes and known gene interactions for cloning\\n\\norganisms. We are also grateful to the authors and co-authors\nwho responded to our emails and in some cases managed to provide papers\nor further information on their studies: Kiyomi Chujo, Susan Conrad,\nAveril Coxhead, Ewa Donesch-Jezo, Laura Gavioli, Zeping Huang, Ali Akbar\nJafarpour,\n\nBetsy Kerr, Hsien-Chin Liou, Gillian Mansfield, Daehyeon Nam, Yasunori\nNishina, Kathryn Oghigian, Simon Smith, and Serge Verlinde (whether\ntheir papers could finally be included or not).\n\n# Abstract \n\nThis study applied systematic meta-analytic procedures to summarize\nfindings from experimental and quasi-experimental investigations into\nthe effectiveness of using the tools and techniques of corpus\nlinguistics for second language (L2) learning or use, here referred to\nas data-driven learning (DDL). Analysis of 64 separate studies\nrepresenting 88 unique samples reporting sufficient data indicated that\nDDL approaches result in large overall effects for both\ncontrol/experimental group comparisons (*d* = 0.95) and for pre/posttest\ndesigns (*d* = 1.50). Further investigation of moderator variables\nrevealed that small effect sizes were generally tied to small sample\nsizes. Research has barely begun in some key areas, and\ndurability/transfer of learning through delayed posttesting remains an\narea in need of further investigation. Although DDL research\ndemonstrably improved over the period investigated, further changes in\npractice and reporting are recommended.\n\n**Keywords** corpus-based language learning; data-driven learning; DDL;\nmeta-analysis; research synthesis\n\n# Introduction \n\nThe purpose of the present synthesis was to answer the question of\nwhether there are, on the whole, positive learning outcomes resulting\nfrom language learners' use of the tools and techniques of corpus\nlinguistics in what has come to be known as *data-driven learning* or\nDDL (Johns, 1990). This approach essentially involves getting foreign or\nsecond language (L2) learners to work with written or spoken corpus\ndata. Figure 1 shows a typical concordance output for the word *back*,\nthe learner's task being to identify idiomatic versus literal uses,\nassess their relative frequencies, verify these frequencies in 20 random\nlines from a different corpus, and then compare the concordance data\nwith the entry for this word in a range of dictionaries.^1^ Although the\napproach itself may seem rather time-consuming for a single word, it is\nthe processes that are important, and DDL may help learner development\nif it leads, for example, to increased language sensitivity, noticing,\ninduction, and ability to work with authentic data.\n\n![](media/image3.jpg){width=\"6.295833333333333in\"\nheight=\"3.078472222222222in\"}\n\n**Figure 1** Concordance output from the Brown corpus for the word\n*back* (http://www.lextutor.ca/conc).\n\n## The case in principle: Arguments for and against \n\nThe DDL approach is geared to making sense of language input but has\nseveral potential advantages that other input approaches do not. Core\namong these is that input assembly replaces input simplification, thus\nmaintaining authenticity of language. Another advantage lies in\nidentifying which forms and meanings in a language (whether words,\nstructures, pragmatic patterns, etc.) are most frequent and thus\nprobably most worth knowing. DDL consists in the consultation of\nlanguage data by learners themselves and thus incorporates the notions\nof learner autonomy, induction, exemplar-based learning, and\nconstructivism, in the sense of letting learners discover linguistic\npatterns for themselves (with varying degrees of guidance) rather than\nbeing spoon-fed predigested rules. In addition to these mainly\npedagogical principles that have been extensively discussed in the\nliterature, DDL has a number of potential theoretical advantages as a\nmethod of making input comprehensible.\n\n1.  DDL reflects current linguistic theory. Language is increasingly\n    seen as dynamic, complex, probabilistic, interactive, and patterned\n    rather than rule-governed, as highlighted by current usage-based\n    theories of language (e.g., Tomasello, 2003). Reflecting this,\n    linguistic knowledge can be conceived of as a mental corpus\n    (Taylor, 2012) of combined experiences of language use. Corpus\n    linguistics has given rise to many insights to this patterning,\n    including the idiom principle (Sinclair, 1991), lexical priming\n    (Hoey, 2005), and norms and expectations (Hanks, 2013). DDL helps\n    learners to recognise the fuzzy nature of authentic language use in\n    context, essential if they are to deal with it.\n\n2.  DDL reflects current learning theory. Rules are hard, patterns are\n    easy; or rather, rules are an artificial intellectual abstraction,\n    whereas the human brain is programmed to detect patterns in the\n    world around us (e.g., Barrett, Dunbar, & Lycett, 2002), including\n    while learning and using language. This coincides with\n    constructivist principles (Cobb, 1999a) and allows the learner to\n    proceed towards the target norm by progressive approximations\n    (Aston, 1998, p. 13). DDL arguably promotes such skills, which\n    should be transferable to new contexts and thus produce better\n    learning outside the classroom, increasing learner autonomy and\n    life-long learning for them.\n\n3.  DDL reflects current psycholinguistic theory. Because pattern\n    induction is a natural process, it reduces the cognitive load of\n    processing (Sweller, Ayers, & Kalyuga, 2011), freeing up resources\n    for the still considerable effort of meaning construction required\n    on the part of the learner---effort being the often missing\n    component in instructed language learning and a reliable predictor\n    of both depth and retention (Hulstijn & Laufer, 2001). DDL also\n    provides access to the massive amounts of authentic language needed\n    (input flood) but, crucially, it organizes it to make patterns\n    salient, as is necessary for noticing (Schmidt, 1990). There is also\n    increasing psycholinguistic evidence for the importance of chunking\n    (Millar, 2011), which DDL helps to highlight.\n\n4.  DDL reflects current second language acquisition (SLA) research\n    findings. A rebalancing of language instruction from overemphasis on\n    meaning and top-down processing to inclusion of form-focus and\n    bottom-up processes has been recommended for years (Doughty &\n    Williams, 1998), but in practice the result has often seemed to lead\n    back to vocabulary lists and grammar exercises. DDL offers a way\n    forward on this front.\n\n5.  DDL reflects and may inform existing learner practice. Learners are\n    already involved in using information and communication technology\n    (ICT) to search for answers to their language questions, especially\n    via the use of Google as a \"concordancer\" for the web as \"corpus\"\n    (Chinnery, 2008; Kilgarriff & Grefenstette, 2003). Properly\n    conceived DDL activities can build on these existing behaviours,\n    refining them and using them as a way in to corpus work (Boulton,\n    2015).\n\nAlthough advocates of DDL are quick to seize on such alleged advantages,\nothers are equally quick to point out potential counter-arguments. These\nare not articulated often in the DDL research literature, which is\ntypically cast from a positive or even enthusiastic perspective, and\nhence suffers from a version of publication bias. Among the most\nfrequently cited criticisms: many language teachers and students remain\nuncomfortable with computer work generally (even if they use ICT for\nother purposes on a daily basis); chopped-off concordance lines may help\nexpose patterns yet be off-putting to some and are not designed for\ngaining meaning as traditionally conceived via linear reading; most\ncorpora are composed of authentic native language well beyond the\ncomfort level of many learners; and DDL work requires substantial\ntraining, and the processes are time-consuming when learners could\nsimply be told or use pedagogically derived resources such as\ndictionaries. Even many of our colleagues who are provisionally\nsupportive of concordance work would nonetheless prefer to constrain its\nuse to specific situations such as teaching advanced learners only or\nrestrict the implementation to simplified corpora only, to paper\nconcordance lines only, to use as a reference tool rather than a\nlearning aid, or to vocabulary/collocation acquisition or awareness\nraising. These misgivings, although vaguely defined and forming an\ninformal, fugitive literature, definitely exist, deserve to be taken\nseriously, and may find either support or rebuttal in whatever we\nuncovered in this meta-analysis.\n\n## The need for evidence: From primary research to meta-analysis \n\nThe in-principle case for or against DDL might seem irresolvable. An\nalternative is to treat it as an empirical matter, and this is the\nmotivation for this effects-oriented meta-analysis. Our definition of\nthe field as the use of the tools and techniques of corpus linguistics\nfor L2 learning or use gives a deliberately broad remit. This is not an\noriginal definition, mirroring as it does that offered by Gilquin and\nGranger (2010, p. 359), though it clearly goes beyond the narrow view of\nDDL as entirely autonomous, serendipitous corpus browsing---a strawman\nview which has been seized upon perhaps more by critics than advocates\nbecause it is \"doubtful... whether this can be fruitfully put into\npractice in the reality of ELT classrooms\" (Mukherjee, 2006, p. 14). The\nbroader definition proposed here thus makes sense from a pedagogical and\ntheoretical perspective (cf. Boulton, 2011). It is also the goal of this\ntype of synthesis \"to make generalizations... across a range of\npopulations and scenarios\" (Plonsky & Ziegler, 2016, p. 19). For present\npurposes, this definition allowed us to cover studies which researchers\nhave offered as examples of DDL rather than inventing some arbitrary or\nsubjective cut-off point. For example, although most DDL has been\ninductive, it may include some deductive practices (e.g., Oghigian &\nChujo, 2010) which have thus been included here. Conversely, the vast\nmajority of inductive language work has made no use of corpus tools or\ntechniques and was thus excluded as it did not represent DDL in the\ncommonly accepted sense.\n\nThe studies have variously reported both hands-on concordancing and use\nof printed concordances or worksheets, large general corpora and small\ntailor-made ones, corpora as learning aids or reference resources, and\nso forth. A potential drawback to a broad collection of studies lies in\nthe possibility of comparing \"apples and oranges.\" A meta-analysis only\nworks insofar as the studies included can be treated as approximate\nreplications of the same phenomenon (Lipsey & Wilson, 2001) among the\nsame basic population. The sheer variety of research questions and\ndesigns in DDL initially led Boulton (2012) to wonder if a metaanalysis\nwas possible at all. In fact, the studies included in a meta-analysis\ncan rarely be considered identical (Borenstein, Hedges, Higgins, &\nRothstein, 2009), and studies that appear similar to one researcher may\nbe different to another (Lipsey & Wilson, 2001). In the end, it is a\nquestion of granularity because meta-analyses have been conducted on far\nwider bases, such as whether computer-assisted language learning (CALL)\nis effective (e.g., Grgurović, Chapelle, & Shelley, 2013; Felix, 2008),\nwhether language instruction makes a difference (Norris & Ortega, 2000,\n2001), or what factors affect educational achievement (Hattie, 2009). To\nlaunch this meta-analysis, we only needed studies that were \"similar\nenough\" (Norris & Ortega, 2006, p. 216). A broader domain for inclusion\nbetter reflects the diversity of practices in real-world contexts and\nincreases generalizability, and a larger dataset increases power and\naccuracy (Plonsky & Brown, 2014). In line with most metaanalyses,\nassuming a random-effects model then allowed us to proceed to the more\ninteresting part of the analysis: Whether variation in effect sizes can\nbe attributed to differences in study designs, populations, language\nfocus, implementation or other features, all of which can be treated as\nmoderator variables (Cumming, 2012). In other words, our meta-analysis\nbegan with a collection of \"fruit,\" with a view to separating apples and\noranges later on (Ortega, 2010).\n\nA meta-analysis synthesizes quantitative results in the form of effect\nsizes. These are simple to calculate and understand in terms of the\nbasic formulae used and can be averaged across studies. A meta-analysis\nnevertheless offers a daunting array of choice-points throughout its\nexecution. In preparing this study, we drew on a number of existing\nmeta-analyses in applied linguistics beginning with Norris and Ortega\n(2000), as well as various manuals and textbooks (e.g., Cumming, 2012;\nLipsey & Wilson, 2001) and notable articles examining good practice\n(e.g., Plonsky & Oswald, 2014; Plonsky & Ziegler, 2016). Due to its\nnature, a meta-analysis cannot accommodate qualitative studies. Their\nfindings may nonetheless help to inform and validate all types of\nstudies in future. For a comparison of meta-analyses and narrative\nsurveys, see Norris and Ortega (2006) and the special issue of *Applied\nLinguistics* edited by R. Ellis (2015).\n\nAn earlier attempt at meta-analyzing DDL research (Cobb & Boulton, 2015)\nreported effect sizes of *d* = 1.68 for within-groups (pre/posttests)\nand *d* = 1.04 for between-groups (control/experimental) designs. We\nstressed however that this was only a preliminary study and that the\nhigh *d* values were worth a second, critical look in a more principled\nmetaanalysis. The most obvious change is the increase from 21 to 88\nunique samples drawn from a wider, more exhaustive and up-to-date trawl\nof papers (e.g., PhD dissertations, use of more databases, more recent\ncut-off point). Other differences include more rigorous extraction of\neffect sizes (including values derived from *t* and *F* tests and\nmissing data solicited directly from the authors) as well as the\nformulae used and their interpretation (unbiased *d*, winsorizing),\ninclusion of a separate effect size for every unique sample in each\nstudy, and a detailed coding manual with calculation of subeffect sizes\nallowing a post hoc moderator analysis in an attempt to identify what\nmay be responsible for variation between studies (entirely absent in the\nprevious paper). Although there have been various other attempts at\nsynthesis of DDL (e.g., Boulton, 2017; Chambers, 2007), to our knowledge\nthe only other meta-analysis to date is by Mizumoto and Chujo (2015).\nTheir survey of 14 studies arrived at an overall effect size of *d* =\n0.97, and identified lexicogrammar as the most promising area for DDL\nwork (*d* = 2.93). It should be noted that their study drew only on\nwithin-groups designs in papers co-authored by Chujo and was exclusive\nto the Japanese context among lower-proficiency learners of English. The\npresent meta-analysis sought to broaden this scope.\n\nWe therefore sought to answer three main research questions:\n\n1.  How much DDL research is there?\n\n2.  How effective is DDL, and how efficient is it?\n\n3.  How can we best account for any variation observed?\n\n# Method \n\n## Data collection \n\nThe first stage in the data collection process was to assemble as many\nstudies as possible conforming to the definition given above. Ideally\nthe result would be an exhaustive collection, though practical\nconsiderations meant that a number of further criteria needed to be\napplied. In the present case, we included only full-text descriptions\nthat were publicly available and text types where we were relatively\nlikely to access the majority of the work. We did not institute start or\nfinish cut-off points, accepting any study up to and including the first\nsix months of 2014, though it is likely that some prior publications\nwill be referenced online at a later date.\n\nBecause our goal was to gain a comprehensive view of the entire field\n\"warts and all,\" the solution was to include all studies initially, then\nto compare factors possibly related to quality as moderator variables.\nThis allowed us to avoid quality judgements that are highly subjective\n(Lipsey & Wilson, 2001); for example, it is common for double-blind\nreviews of the same paper to come to quite opposite recommendations. It\nalso avoided indirect quality indicators such as restricting the\nperimeter to internationally recognized peer-reviewed journals, thus\nexcluding much that may be of value and introducing publication bias.\nBurston (2013) reported that nearly 60% of all MALL (mobile-assisted\nlanguage learning) studies would be excluded under such a criterion.\nNonetheless, publication bias is still likely insofar as studies which\ndo not produce significant differences or other desired outcomes are\nmore likely to remain unpublished altogether (N. Ellis, 2006), the\nfamous *file-drawer problem* (Rosenthal, 1979).\n\nExtending the trawl to fugitive or grey literature rather than\nattempting to judge the quality of the papers of course leaves a\nmeta-analysis open to charges of \"garbage in, garbage out.\" Our\nintention here was to begin inclusive and to let the analysis itself\nshow whether the different source types influenced the outcomes. In\nother words, quality can be treated as an empirical part of the\ninvestigation (Norris & Ortega, 2006, p. 18--19; Ortega, 2010, p. 121;\nPlonsky, 2014, p. 466) and may give rise to recommendations for future\nresearch. We therefore included studies from less well-known or regional\noutlets along with PhD dissertations and any other form of full-text\nwrite-up. Excluded from the study were MA theses, conference posters and\npresentations because collection would have been highly serendipitous\nand fragmentary and reporting partial.\n\nKeywords in all searches included various combinations of\n*corpus/corpora*, *data-driven*, *DDL*, *Johns*,\n*concordance/concordancer/concordancing*, with contextualizers\n*language*, *learning*. Some searches produced tens of thousands of\npotential hits; in such cases, either the query was narrowed by\nintroducing more search terms or the list was browsed until 100\nconsecutive entries yielded no new hits (cf. Plonsky, 2011). Once a\nseemingly relevant title was detected, the abstract was read and\ncandidate papers were downloaded or obtained from other sources in order\nto constitute as large an initial pool as possible.\n\nThe trawls began with a search of various online databases: *Linguistics\nand Language*\n\n## Behavior Abstracts, the Modern Language Association International Bibliography, ProQuest \n\n*Dissertations and Theses*, Education Resources Information Center,\nJSTOR, the *Directory of Open Access Journals* online, and Google\nScholar (with the additional filter of pdf files only to reduce vast\nnumbers of hits, often of slide presentations, websites, and notes). The\nbibliographies of all papers were then scoured for possible further\nleads. Next, Google was used to locate other papers that referred to\nthose already found by searching for exact-word titles (within quotation\nmarks). Though not common practice, *ancestry chasing* (Li, Shintani, &\nEllis, 2012) or *forward citations* (Plonsky, 2011) did produce some\npublications which otherwise would have slipped through the net. Further\nsearches were conducted on the websites of all sources that had more\nthan one paper on the list at this stage or that seemed particularly\npromising for other reasons. This included journals, publishers, and\nwebsites for conference proceedings or known series of publications.\nWhere a website did not have an adequate search engine built in, an\nadvanced Google search was conducted specifying the site.\n\nThe trawls thus conducted brought up a total of 205 publications that we\nboth agreed corresponded to our broad definition of empirical\nevaluations of DDL. The full list is provided in Appendix S1 in the\nSupporting Information online. Among those not pursued were seven papers\nin languages other than English. Because none were suitable for\nmeta-analysis, this justified the decision to limit our cull to English\nonly. However, we have inevitably missed out some relevant and\ninteresting data reported in other languages; for example, 5 of the 14\nDDL papers surveyed by Mizumoto and Chujo (2015) were in Japanese. Two\npapers were excluded for plagiarism, confirmed after consultation with\nthe original author. Twelve studies were reported in more than one paper\n(typically a paper derived from a PhD dissertation or expanding a short\npublication in conference proceedings). This is not uncommon (cf.\nBurston, 2015; Shintani, Li, & Ellis, 2013; Spada & Tomita, 2010), and\nthese cases were counted as a single study, based on one main\npublication backed up where necessary with extra information from the\nsecondary source(s). The pool of papers was further reduced for one of\nthree main reasons:\n\n1.  Some did not focus on outcomes but on some other aspect such as\n    learners' behavior or feedback on the treatment, often collected via\n    observations or logs, questionnaires or interviews.\n\n2.  Some used designs or instruments unsuitable for the current study,\n    such as posttests for two different experimental DDL groups but no\n    pretest or control group, description of error types, or relative\n    frequencies of target item use.\n\n3.  Some did not provide the data necessary to calculate effect sizes,\n    that is, the number of participants, the mean scores, and standard\n    deviations, or the raw scores or statistics from which these could\n    be derived. E-mails were sent to all authors of papers that fell\n    into this category, which allowed us to add several studies that\n    otherwise would have been excluded (see Author Note for all authors\n    who responded to such requests, whether fruitfully or not).\n\n## [**Table 1** Inclusion/exclusion criteria for studies in the meta-analy]{.underline}sis pool of 205 publications presenting empirical\nDDL studies was reduced to those that conformed to the criteria for\ninclusion in the meta-analysis (see Table\n\n1).^2^\n\n### Coding and data extraction \n\nOnce the papers had been selected for inclusion, a coding manual was\ndrawn up for descriptive and potential moderator variables. The various\ncategories were divided into the same sections used by many other\nmeta-analyses: publication, population, treatment, and design. To ensure\nharmonization, we applied our own criteria rather than adopting labels\nused in the original studies (cf. Jeon & Kaya, 2006), but still, like H.\nLin (2014, p. 135), we often had to rely on \"best guesses due to\ninsufficient information given in the primary studies.\" The complete\ncoding table can be found in Appendix S2 in the Supporting Information\nonline, with a brief description of the criteria applied. It should be\nnoted that the coding scheme refers to the study as a whole rather than\njust to the meta-analysis; in particular, the number of participants may\nvary where not all could be used for calculating effect sizes.\n\nOnce the coding manual had been agreed on, three papers were\nindependently coded and the results compared. A further set of 10 papers\nwas then randomly selected and again independently coded to check\ninterrater reliability. Given the complexity of the coding sheet, this\nwas assessed simply by counting the number of discrepancies between the\ntwo authors' coding rather than using calculations such as Cohen's\nkappa, following standard procedure in meta-analyses (e.g., Plonsky,\n2011). In each of the four sections, agreement was rated at 90% to 96%;\nall disagreements were satisfactorily resolved, and the coding sheet\nrefined where necessary. To complete the spreadsheet, the first author\ninput an initial coding which was then thoroughly checked by the second,\nand any further issues encountered were again resolved through\ndiscussion. Coding all papers by two separate, experienced researchers\nimproves reliability but is relatively exceptional. In many\nmetaanalyses, coding is performed by a single researcher or assistant.\n\nCollecting, selecting, and coding the studies were time-consuming but\nrelatively unproblematic procedures, with issues arising easily\nresolved. Far more complex in the end was extracting the data needed for\nthe meta-analysis and the calculation of the effect sizes themselves.\nSome studies had extremely convoluted designs with a plethora of\npossible comparisons. Though this is often glossed over in survey papers\nor treated as purely mechanical, it does present the meta-analyst with\nnumerous choices in extracting the essential data. The first author\nprovided a preliminary summary in a similar manner to the coding.\nBecause major issues had been resolved in advance, this was accepted by\nthe second author following minor revisions such that no interrater\nreliability calculation was deemed necessary. The main choices are\noutlined below. It must be remembered that the overall objective was to\nseek maximum granularity by extracting as many data-points as were\navailable while preserving data that might be used in understanding\nmoderators of the overall effects (Research Question 3). The full table\ncan again be found in the Supporting Information online.\n\nSome studies had two or more entirely independent experimental groups.\nThese were each treated separately and not combined. Following Norris\nand Ortega (2000), where two control or comparison groups were involved,\nthe one closest to the experimental design was chosen (e.g., traditional\ntreatment rather than no treatment, dictionaries rather than no\nreference tools). The result was consequently both more conservative and\nmore ecologically valid because most other between-groups studies have\ninvolved comparison groups rather than true no-treatment controls. A\nsmall number of studies were longitudinal in nature with several\nintermediary tests. Although these are interesting and to be encouraged\n(e.g., Larsen-Freeman, 2006), for present purposes we included only\npretest and posttest data.\n\nThe data for delayed test results are included in the supporting\ninformation online ([https://osf.io/jkktw]{.underline}) but not\ndiscussed further here. This is common in meta-analyses and simplifies\nwhat is already a complicated picture, especially where the delay period\nvaries substantially from one study to another. A small number of\nstudies used the same students in both experimental and control\ntreatments---either where the test included items that had been\nsubjected to different treatments (e.g., some via DDL, some via\ntraditional methods) or where students alternated between treatments in\ndifferent weeks or switched treatments part way through. In such cases,\nthe same participants functioned as both experimental and control\nsubjects, and were counted as such---an example of good practice\naccording to Felix (2008).\n\nMany studies provided results with quite a high degree of granularity\nderived from different instruments (e.g., multiple choice vs. cloze) or\nfor different language items (e.g., collocations vs. lexicogrammar),\nskills or functions (e.g., error correction vs. translation). These were\nrecorded individually, each with its own effect size, so that subsequent\nanalysis might identify relevant moderator variables (cf. Norris &\nOrtega, 2000). But for the main study, we followed standard practice by\naveraging the various elements to arrive at a single effect size for\neach unique sample---what Li et al. (2012, p. 9) called \"shifting units\nof analysis.\"\n\nIn most cases, the data needed for effect sizes could be collected from\nthe tables or text in the papers themselves. For the sake of\nconsistency, effect sizes were calculated for all papers, even where\nthey were originally given in the studies themselves. We repeatedly\nfound it necessary to take a step back from the data with a common-sense\neye on items that stood out as being statistically unlikely or\nimpossible (cf. Larson-Hall & Plonsky, 2015). Where the summary data\nwere incomplete for the main elements (*N*, *M*, *SD*), various options\nwere available. Some studies were reported in more than one paper and\nthe data could be completed from the sister publication. Where the\nprimary data were given in an appendix, these could be used to calculate\nmissing elements. In four cases, we were able to use data from *t* or\n*F* tests, but only to extract a single effect size in otherwise rich\nstudies. For the remaining 13 studies, we emailed the authors. Five\n(38%) responded with the appropriate data; three responded but were\nunable to help. For comparison, Plonsky, Egbert, and Laflair (2015) had\na positive return from 14% of authors contacted.\n\n### Effect sizes \n\nSome studies were conducted between groups (control vs. experimental,\nhenceforth C/E), others within groups (pretest vs. posttest, henceforth\nP/P); some featured both designs. The two were meta-analyzed here but\nkept separate for a number of reasons (Lipsey & Wilson, 2001). In\nparticular, one would expect the mean to be higher in P/P designs,\npartly as use of the same participants reduces extraneous variance\n(Plonsky & Oswald, 2014) but also because the only difference between\nthe two tests is an intervention: even poor teaching normally leads to\nsome improvement. In the C/E design, however, very few studies use true\ncontrols with no intervention whatsoever. Where medicine compares\ntreatment against a placebo, in SLA it is arguably more desirable to\ncompare against whatever instruction learners would otherwise have. The\ncomparison is thus between two interventions (i.e., experimental vs.\ntraditional), each of which will have some effect, and in theory either\ncould be more effective than the other. In other words, DDL versus no\nteaching should lead to a higher effect size than DDL versus traditional\nteaching.\n\nCohen's *d* (Cohen, 1988; see Figure 2) is the most common formula in\nmeta-analyses in language teaching. Adopting familiar statistics\nincreases transparency, comparability, and replicability (Plonsky,\n2014), and we were anxious to avoid \"technicism, or the overemphasis on\nmanipulating data via novel meta-analytic techniques to the detriment of\ntheoretical and conceptual depth\" (Norris & Ortega, 2007, p. 810).\nEssentially, this measure compares the difference between the mean\nscores (pre/posttests for within-groups, or control/experimental\nposttests for between-groups), divided by the pooled standard deviation\nof both groups (more highly dispersed scores reduce the reliability and\npower of the results) and measured in *SD* units. Because the component\ndata are simply descriptive statistics, they can be extracted from *t*\nor *F* tests using equations given in Lipsey and Wilson (2001, p.\n198--199; see Figures 3 and 4).\n\n𝑑 = 𝑀\\$ − 𝑀&\n\n> '[𝑆𝐷\\$]{.underline}& [+ 𝑆𝐷&]{.underline}&\n>\n> 2\n\n**Figure 2** Formula for calculating Cohen's *d* from *M* and *SD*.\n\n𝑑 = ,𝐹(𝑁~\\$~ + 𝑁𝑛~&~)\n\n> 𝑁\\$𝑁&\n\n**Figure 3** Formula for calculating *d* from *F-*test information.\n\n𝑑 = 𝑡,𝑁\\$ + 𝑁&\n\n> 𝑁\\$𝑁&\n\n**Figure 4** Formula for calculating *d* from *t*-test information.\n\nA further consideration involved effect-size weighting in the case of\nsmall samples (of which there were many in this analysis) which may have\nhigh sampling error (Lipsey & Wilson, 2001). Weighting is a\ncontroversial issue. A common method used in meta-analyses is the\nformula for \"unbiased *d*\" (Hedges, 1981), which Cumming (2012, p. 294)\ncalled a \"very good approximation adjustment\" (see Figure 5). All values\nfor *d* given in these analyses were calculated using the unbiased *d*\nformula. To calculate this, Cumming used *df* -- 1 where others have\nsuggested *df* -- 9. We retained Cumming's formula because *df* -- 1 can\naccommodate very small sample sizes, while *df* -- 9 does not work where\n*N* = 10 and actually increases effect size where *N* \\< 10.\n\n𝑑345 = 71 − :;\\<9=\\$\\> × 𝑑\n\n**Figure 5** Formula for calculating unbiased *d*.\n\nOnce effect sizes had been calculated, outliers could easily be observed\nthrough a funnel plot. Rather than excluding these, we adopted the\ncommon practice of winsorizing effect sizes at the 5^th^ and 95^th^\npercentiles to provide more robust results (cf. Li et al., 2012; Lipsey\n& Wilson, 2001). This turned out to be *d* = 3.0, within the range\nrecommended by Lipsey and Wilson.\n\nThe interpretation of effect sizes is also an issue. Cohen's (1988)\noriginal rule of thumb suggested that a *d* value of 0.2 could be\nconsidered a small effect, 0.5 medium and 0.8 large. For the field of\neducation, Hattie (2009) proposed levels of 0.2, 0.4, and 0.6, noting\nthat anything below 0.4 should be abandoned as effectively useless (p.\n18). Plonsky and Oswald (2014) argued convincingly for field-specific\nbenchmarks derived empirically from typical findings in that field.\nTaking the 25^th^, 50^th^, and 75^th^ percentiles as indicators for\nsmall, medium, and large effects, their study of 91 meta-analyses in SLA\nsuggested 0.6, 1.0, and 1.4, respectively, for within-groups designs and\n0.4, 0.6, and 0.9 for between-groups comparisons. We endorse this\napproach and adhered to these benchmarks in our study. Also typically\nincluded in reports of grouped effect sizes are the confidence intervals\n(CI), traditionally set at 95%---an arbitrary figure that parallels\nchoices for *p* values in the null hypothesis significance testing\n(NHST) statistical model (Oswald & Plonsky, 2010). A CI is a measure of\nheterogeneity within a collection of effect sizes, and thus a prediction\nof how likely it is that the same mean would be found for a different\nsample of studies from the same population. A large CI shows greater\nheterogeneity, suggesting that the same mean might not be found in a\ndifferent sampling from the same population. If the CI includes zero,\nthe mean is considered not to indicate a reliable effect. The procedure\nfor calculating CIs is provided in Appendix S3 in the Supporting\nInformation online.\n\n# Overall results \n\nApplication of the various inclusion/exclusion criteria reduced the\noriginal pool of 205 publications to 64, or just under one-third, for a\ntotal of over 3,000 participants. This might seem a low inclusion rate,\nbut N. Ellis (2006) noted that other meta-analyses have reported similar\nfigures, and Yun (2011) included only 10 from an original trawl of 200\npublications. Reassuringly, the rate of includable papers seems to be\nincreasing over time, a sign of growing rigor and better reporting, in\nline with Larson-Hall and Plonsky (2015). Our number of studies also\ncompared favorably with Oswald and Plonsky's (2010) survey of 27\nmetaanalyses in SLA, with a median of only 16 studies. In total, 88\nunique samples were ultimately harvested from our 64 studies, some\nyielding only a single effect size, others two or more. For any part of\nthe analysis, only a single effect size is reported for any given\nsample.\n\nFigure 6 shows the overall evolution of DDL research from the first\nempirical study in 1989, in which *DDL* refers to the entire pool of\nstudies collected for the present study (205), many of which could not\nbe included, *MA* to the number of empirical studies meta-analyzed here\n(64), some of which contained more than one unique sample, and *k* to\nthe number of unique samples (88). Following a typical pattern (Shintani\net al., 2013), empirical studies lagged behind early theoretical or\ndescriptive studies but have since taken off and were still increasing\nas of June, 2014.\n\n> ![](media/image4.png){width=\"5.696666666666666in\"\n> height=\"2.9366666666666665in\"}\n\n**Figure 6** Evolution of empirical data-driven learning studies (DDL)\nas a whole in relation to meta-analyzable studies (MA) and the number of\nunique samples (k).\n\nHaving selected the studies, and extracted and sorted the relevant data,\nwe put everything together to provide overall effect sizes for the two\nmain study types and then broke the whole back down again into subgroups\naccording to our coded variables (the potential moderators).\n\n## Overall effect sizes \n\nOf the 64 studies meta-analyzed, some had more than one experimental\ngroup, giving a total of 88 unique samples which we separated into C/E\nand P/P designs. As some studies compared the experimental group\nposttest to both a pretest and a control group, the results could be\ncounted in both categories, so that in the end we were able to work with\ndata from 50 C/E and 71 P/P samples.\n\nMain effect sizes are given in Table 2, where each row represents a\nunique sample, along with the number of participants in the control\n(where applicable) and experimental groups. Effect sizes are given for\nthe main comparisons: P/P (i.e., where the same participants were tested\nbefore and after a DDL intervention) and C/E (i.e., where control and\nexperimental groups were given the same posttest). More complete data\ncan be found in Appendix S4 and S5 in the Supporting Information online,\nwhich take the form of a standard spreadsheet. Though many statistical\npackages can help with meta-analyses, especially in producing visual\nrepresentations, all the essential information can be stored and\ncalculations performed transparently via a spreadsheet.\n\n## [**Table 2** Main effect sizes of all studies included in the met]{.underline}a-analysis \n\n<table>\n<colgroup>\n<col style=\"width: 6%\" />\n<col style=\"width: 0%\" />\n<col style=\"width: 40%\" />\n<col style=\"width: 0%\" />\n<col style=\"width: 4%\" />\n<col style=\"width: 2%\" />\n<col style=\"width: 6%\" />\n<col style=\"width: 6%\" />\n<col style=\"width: 13%\" />\n<col style=\"width: 2%\" />\n<col style=\"width: 13%\" />\n<col style=\"width: 1%\" />\n</colgroup>\n<thead>\n<tr class=\"header\">\n<th></th>\n<th colspan=\"3\"></th>\n<th></th>\n<th colspan=\"2\"><em>N</em></th>\n<th colspan=\"4\">Effect size (<em>d<sub>unb</sub></em>)</th>\n<th></th>\n</tr>\n</thead>\n<tbody>\n<tr class=\"odd\">\n<td><u>ID</u></td>\n<td colspan=\"3\"><u>Reference</u></td>\n<td><blockquote>\n<p><u>CG</u></p>\n</blockquote></td>\n<td colspan=\"2\"><u>EG</u></td>\n<td colspan=\"2\"><blockquote>\n<p><u>EG pre/EG post</u></p>\n</blockquote></td>\n<td colspan=\"2\"><u>CG post/EG post</u></td>\n<td></td>\n</tr>\n<tr class=\"even\">\n<td>1</td>\n<td colspan=\"3\">Abu Alshaar &amp; Abuseileek (2013)</td>\n<td>16</td>\n<td colspan=\"2\">16</td>\n<td colspan=\"2\"><blockquote>\n<p><sup>a</sup>3.00</p>\n</blockquote></td>\n<td colspan=\"2\"><blockquote>\n<p>0.87</p>\n</blockquote></td>\n<td></td>\n</tr>\n<tr class=\"odd\">\n<td>2</td>\n<td colspan=\"3\">Ashouri et al.
