Jo (2014)</td>\n<td colspan=\"3\"></td>\n<td colspan=\"2\"><blockquote>\n<p>4</p>\n</blockquote></td>\n<td colspan=\"2\"><blockquote>\n<p>1.08</p>\n</blockquote></td>\n<td colspan=\"2\"></td>\n</tr>\n<tr class=\"even\">\n<td colspan=\"2\"></td>\n<td><em>k</em></td>\n<td colspan=\"3\"></td>\n<td colspan=\"2\"></td>\n<td colspan=\"2\">71</td>\n<td colspan=\"2\">50</td>\n</tr>\n<tr class=\"odd\">\n<td colspan=\"2\"></td>\n<td><em>M</em></td>\n<td colspan=\"3\"><blockquote>\n<p>23.64</p>\n</blockquote></td>\n<td colspan=\"2\"><blockquote>\n<p>22.41</p>\n</blockquote></td>\n<td colspan=\"2\"><blockquote>\n<p>1.50</p>\n</blockquote></td>\n<td colspan=\"2\"><blockquote>\n<p>0.95</p>\n</blockquote></td>\n</tr>\n<tr class=\"even\">\n<td colspan=\"2\"></td>\n<td><em>SD</em></td>\n<td colspan=\"3\"><blockquote>\n<p>16.14</p>\n</blockquote></td>\n<td colspan=\"2\"><blockquote>\n<p>17.04</p>\n</blockquote></td>\n<td colspan=\"2\"><blockquote>\n<p>0.91</p>\n</blockquote></td>\n<td colspan=\"2\"><blockquote>\n<p>0.99</p>\n</blockquote></td>\n</tr>\n<tr class=\"odd\">\n<td colspan=\"2\"></td>\n<td>Upper 95% CI</td>\n<td colspan=\"3\"></td>\n<td colspan=\"2\"></td>\n<td colspan=\"2\"><blockquote>\n<p>1.71</p>\n</blockquote></td>\n<td colspan=\"2\"><blockquote>\n<p>1.22</p>\n</blockquote></td>\n</tr>\n<tr class=\"even\">\n<td colspan=\"2\"></td>\n<td>Lower 95% CI</td>\n<td colspan=\"3\"></td>\n<td colspan=\"2\"></td>\n<td colspan=\"2\"><blockquote>\n<p>1.28</p>\n</blockquote></td>\n<td colspan=\"2\"><blockquote>\n<p>0.67</p>\n</blockquote></td>\n</tr>\n</tbody>\n</table>\n\n*Note.* CG = control group; EG = experimental group. ^a^Effect sizes\nwinsorized to 3.0 standard deviations.\n\n### Within groups (P/P) and between groups (C/E) \n\nFor P/P designs, a total of 71 unique samples showed *d* ranging from\n--0.09 (the only negative score) to 3.0 following winsorizing in 10\ncases. The mean gain effect was *d* = 1.50 (*SD* = 0.91), higher than\nMizumoto and Chujo's (2015) *d* = 0.97 in Japan. This placed the result\nin the top quartile of Plonsky and Oswald's (2014) pooling of\nmeta-analyses in SLA outlined earlier and above their benchmark of 1.4\nfor a large effect. The 95% CI was between 1.28 and 1.71, well above\nzero and in a relatively narrow range that showed the comparatively low\nvariance in the studies.\n\nFor C/E designs (50 unique samples), the mean difference effect ranged\nfrom --0.39 (there were five negative scores) to 3.0 following\nwinsorizing for three studies. The mean difference effect was *d* = 0.95\n(*SD* = .99), where, as mentioned, Plonsky and Oswald found 0.6 for a\nmedium effect and 0.9 for a large effect.^3^ The CIs were slightly wider\nat 0.67 and 1.22, indicating a greater range in the results, but still\nwell above zero, suggesting confidence that the true mean for these\nstudies lay in this range.\n\nThe two sets of results can be visualized for dispersion in the funnel\nplots in Figure 7 and Figure 8. Apart from the obviously smaller sample\nsizes in the P/P design (because only one group was involved), the\nhorizontal spread also seemed rather different. P/P scores were spread\nfairly evenly across the scale, while C/E scores clustered around 0.5\nand tailed off above 1.0 (not counting the 10 winsorized scores). This\nsuggested that simply using unbiased *d* might not be sufficient to\nallow the two different designs to be satisfactorily combined.\n\n> ![](media/image5.png){width=\"4.41in\" height=\"3.69in\"}\n\n**Figure 7** Within-group (P/P) design (*M* = 1.51).\n\nIn addition to being a convenient way to visualise the results (cf.\nCumming, 2012), funnel plots also provide an indication of potential\npublication bias through any asymmetries (fewer studies to the left of\nthe mean suggesting that small samples with low effects go unpublished)\nor systematic small-sample effects (because the means are plotted\nagainst *k* size). Figure 7 shows that the P/P design mostly relied on\nquite small sample sizes, but these are relatively evenly distributed\neither side of the mean. Larger samples were used in C/E designs\n(involving two groups) and did indeed tend to reveal a funnel shape in\nFigure 8. Both are what we would expect and did not provide much\nevidence of publication bias (Norris & Ortega, 2000; Oswald & Plonsky,\n2010). However, it is clear that the means were pulled upwards by the\nstudies that were winsorized at 3.0; simply eliminating these as\noutliers would reduce the mean P/P effect size to 1.25 (*SD* = 0.72; CI\n= \\[1.07, 1.43\\]), and the mean C/E effect to 0.67 (*SD* = 0.67; CI =\n\\[0.47, 0.86\\]), which are still substantial results.\n\n> ![](media/image6.png){width=\"4.46in\" height=\"3.6866666666666665in\"}\n\n**Figure 8** Between-group (C/E) design (*M* = 0.95).\n\n# Results for moderator variables \n\nHaving pooled the results of these studies for the general picture, we\nthen broke them down again by moderator variables (MVs) to investigate\nvariation within the general picture (Lipsey & Wilson, 2001), with all\noriginal analyses presented in Appendix S6 and S7 in the Supporting\nInformation online. This assumed a random-effects model, which several\nresearchers have claimed should be the default setting for meta-analysis\n(Borenstein et al., 2009, Ch. 21; Cumming, 2012, p. 213; Oswald &\nPlonsky, 2010). On this basis, Q tests were not required because\nheterogeneity is implicit in this assumption. However, the choice of\nmodel is largely theoretical and unlikely to affect the values\nsubstantially (Oswald & Plonsky, 2010). In total, 84 variables in 25\ngroups were examined in the four coding categories (publication,\npopulation, treatment, and design).\n\n## Publication variables \n\nThere might be a tendency for effect sizes to increase over time as\nresearchers focus on the most promising questions (Lee, Jang, & Plonsky,\n2015) or conversely to decrease in a *Proteus effect* (Plonsky & Oswald,\n2014) whereby they regress toward the mean as research becomes more\nnuanced concerning specific features. The small number of early studies\nin particular made this difficult to assess here, whether looking at\nindividual years or grouping over different time periods. Figure 9 shows\nthe quartiles over three time periods for P/P and C/E designs. Both\nseemed to show an increase in effect size over time. Exact values for\nmeans and standard deviations are given in Table 3 along with CIs.\n\n![](media/image7.png){width=\"6.316667760279965in\"\nheight=\"5.243334426946632in\"}\n\n**Figure 9** Evolution in effect sizes over time.\n\nThe question of study quality is difficult to assess objectively, but\nthe publication source might provide some indication. The second section\nof Table 3 compares journal articles against PhD dissertations and other\npublication types (mainly book chapters). For P/P designs, it seems that\njournal articles gave the highest effect sizes, followed by PhD\ndissertations; this order changed for C/E comparisons, though few\nstudies were involved. As journals were the largest category, we\nseparated out those ranked in the top 50 of the SJR and JCR language and\nlinguistics categories: *Computer Assisted Language Learning*, *Language\nLearning*, *Language Learning & Technology*, *ReCALL*, and *System*.^4^\nThis gave a total of 25 studies in ranked journals, compared to 39 in\nunranked ones. The results showed higher effect sizes for ranked than\nunranked journals for both P/P and C/E designs, which may suggest\nsubmission bias (if researchers keep their best results for prestigious\njournals), or acceptance bias (if those journals only accept papers with\nsubstantial findings). Alternatively, studies that make it into the top\njournals could be carefully conducted to eliminate extraneous variables.\nA final indirect measure of quality may lie just in the number of pages.\nResearchers convinced that their study is important may go to more\ntrouble writing it up while those with doubts commit themselves only to\na short paper. Or, long papers might indicate tergiversation to\n\"contextualize\" small or ambiguous findings while short papers indicate\nconfidence in strong or clear findings. Our shorter papers produced\nhigher effect sizes than longer ones, again with minor differences for\nP/P and C/E designs.\n\n**Table 3** Breakdown of studies by publication date and type, M*(*d* ) *SD k M*(*d* ) *SD*\n\n## Design variables \n\nAn important component of study quality in DDL work appeared to be\npopulation. As shown in Table 4, more participants generally meant\nlarger effect sizes in P/P designs and the opposite in C/E designs. The\nsame patterns held for overall sample sizes. Only one study used an\napparently true control group, with most using comparison groups that\nfollowed a different treatment (such as explicit teaching or use of\ndictionaries) or on occasion providing the same students with different\ntreatments on different items so that they formed their own comparison\ngroup. The former seemed to provide slightly larger effect sizes, though\nboth were near or over the benchmark for large, and there were only\neight studies using the second design. Unfortunately, 42 of our 88\nunique samples gave no indication of how the groups were constituted.\nFor those that did, intact groups outnumbered random assignments, but\nthere was little difference in the resulting effect sizes (medium to\nlarge).\n\n> **4** Design variables found in the meta-analysis studies\n\nPretest/posttest studies Control/experimental studies\n\n95% CI 95% M*(*d* ) *SD k M*(*d* ) *SD*\n\n> In terms of data collection instruments, Table 4 indicates that\n> selected response tests (multiple choice) showed quite large effects\n> but featured in the fewest number of studies overall. Constrained\n> constructed responses (focusing on specific items with limited\n> response options) gave the largest effect sizes in P/P designs but the\n> lowest in C/E. The freest types, such as writing or translation,\n> showed a large effect in C/E studies and a medium effect in P/P. The\n> most common category of more than one type of instrument yielded large\n> (P/P) and medium (C/E) effects. But it should not be inferred that DDL\n> is more or less appropriate in line with this criterion. The\n> instruments used did not consistently or accurately reflect the\n> pedagogical or linguistic objectives of each study and were ultimately\n> a feature of the study design.\n>\n> Also of possible interest is the type of analysis conducted. Table 4\n> shows that this was usually in the form of NHST, especially with *t*\n> tests (in 47 of the 88 unique samples overall), followed by analysis\n> of variance (ANOVA or ANCOVA) in 35 cases. Effect sizes were provided\n> in some form for nine samples, though as mentioned earlier these were\n> recalculated here. In 13 cases descriptive statistics were provided\n> with no statistical analysis as such. It might be tempting to infer\n> that this group involved less sophisticated research overall---not\n> just in the analysis but also in the design. It was indeed this group\n> that produced the smallest effect sizes overall. In P/P studies, use\n> of more tests was associated with larger effect sizes, but in C/E\n> designs it seemed to complicate things---perhaps because several\n> derived from PhD dissertations which tended to produce lower mean\n> difference effect sizes. Finally, we looked at any tools used in these\n> studies other than those explicitly used to derive the effect sizes,\n> again on the assumption that the total number of instruments might\n> provide an indication of sophistication if not quality per se, but\n> effect sizes showed no discernible relationship to number or type of\n> instruments used (see Table 4).\n\n## Population variables \n\n> It is often objected that DDL may not be appropriate for all types of\n> learner, though few studies have addressed this question directly.\n> Individual differences are difficult to assess in meta-analyses,\n> though we did attempt to glean some studies including information\n> about age and sex. Average age was given explicitly in only a small\n> minority of cases and was not pursued because it overlapped with the\n> particular year in a program of study, where more information was\n> provided. Sex was not analyzed either, as the few studies that\n> provided the information did not separate their results by sex.\n>\n> There may however be larger cultural differences which can be analyzed\n> here. It is clear from Table 5 that DDL has been more widely\n> researched in Asia than in other parts of the world with large (P/P)\n> or medium (C/E) effect sizes, though the largest effects have been\n> achieved in the Middle East. It should be noted that a fifth of the\n> studies in Asia and nearly half of those in the Middle East produced\n> very large effects, winsorized down to 3.0, suggesting that design and\n> analysis may have a role to play. Taken at face value, these results\n> may seem counterintuitive because many Asian and Middle Eastern\n> cultures favor education that is teacher-fronted, deductive, and\n> strong on rote learning---the antithesis of DDL. This has been\n> observed by several researchers in Taiwan in particular (e.g., Yeh,\n> Liou, & Li, 2007) although Smith (2011, p. 294) noted that his\n> undergraduate students there \"expect to be taught in a way that is\n> markedly different from their high school experience\" and that \"the\n> last thing one would expect them to want is more gap-fills and error\n> correction exercises.\" Conversely, it was in Europe and North America\n> that effect sizes were rather lower (though still reasonably robust),\n> two regions where inductive, problem-solving approaches would seem\n> more in line with prevailing cultures. One obvious possibility is that\n> DDL was not different enough from traditional teaching in these parts\n> of the world, and this was somewhat borne out by C/E designs producing\n> the lowest effect sizes. Extending the analysis to individual first\n> language (L1) backgrounds, these correlated to a large extent with the\n> above findings, with speakers of Asian and Middle Eastern languages\n> showing larger effect sizes on P/P designs (with the exception of\n> Japanese), though the picture was again more mixed for C/E studies and\n> the number of unique samples for each language relatively small.\n>\n> Population samples used in the studies included in the meta-analysis\n\nPretest/posttest studies Control/experimental studies\n\n95% CI 95% CI\n\nSample type *k M*(*dunb*) *SD* lower upper *k M*(*dunb*) *SD* lower\nupper\n\n> Region Asia 36 1.55 0.89 1.26 1.85 18 0.84 0.91 0.42 1.26\n\nMiddle East 13 2.07 0.98 1.54 2.60 13 1.39 1.03 0.83 1.95\n\nEurope 12 1.15 0.75 0.73 1.58 13 0.95 1.13 0.34 1.57\n\nNorth America 10 0.95 0.61 0.58 1.33 6 0.31 0.36 0.02 0.60\n\nContext\n\nForeign language 57 1.56 0.95 1.32 1.81 44 1.03 1.02 0.73 1.33\n\nSecond language 10 0.95 0.61 0.58 1.33 6 0.31 0.36 0.02 0.60\n\nL1\n\nChinese 20 1.81 1.01 1.37 2.25 8 0.82 0.92 0.18 1.46\n\nRomance 5 0.69 0.32 0.41 .98 7 0.97 1.20 0.08 1.86\n\nJapanese 9 0.74 0.49 0.42 1.06 4 1.44 0.88 0.58 2.31\n\nPersian (Farsi) 7 2.18 1.07 1.39 2.97 6 1.88 0.98 1.10 2.67\n\nThai 7 1.68 0.51 1.30 2.05 6 0.33 0.71 --0.24 0.89\n\nArabic 4 1.74 1.14 0.62 2.86 6 1.08 0.97 0.31 1.85\n\nOther 8 1.38 0.84 0.80 1.96 9 0.75 1.04 0.07 1.43\n\nMixed 11 1.35 0.67 0.95 1.74 4 0.44 0.15 0.29 0.59\n\n## Sophistication variables \n\n> Target language was not a realistic variable because all but two\n> studies had English as the L2 (one Spanish, one mixed). Proficiency in\n> the L2 was particularly difficult to assess and involved a lot of\n> informed guesswork from the descriptions available with differing\n> terminology, sometimes derived from standardized tests, sometimes from\n> in-house tests, sometimes from the teachers'/researchers' individual\n> perceptions, which are likely to be culture bound. In their study of\n> \"advanced\" learners in major CALL journals, for example, Burston and\n> Arispe (2016) found that 50% were at B1 level and 34% at B2 levels\n> only on the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages. In\n> our case, the intermediate category in particular seemed to include\n> individuals who elsewhere would be ranked as lower- or\n> upper-intermediate, or even false beginner or advanced. Nonetheless,\n> Table 6 shows that we generally had moderately or even very large\n> effect sizes in most cases, the exception being lower-intermediate\n> learners in P/P studies. One might think that students specializing in\n> the L2 (including in linguistics, translation, or teacher training)\n> would have more sophisticated linguistic reflexes and thus do\n> relatively better with the techniques involved in DDL. This certainly\n> seemed to be the case for P/P designs, although the effect sizes for\n> students in nonlinguistic disciplines were also medium to large. C/E\n> studies produced the largest effect in the social sciences (but based\n> on few unique samples) and lower effect sizes in the hard sciences\n> (here engineering, maths, science, medicine, and architecture). Among\n> mixed groups, effect size was very low and the CI included zero.\n> Another possible indication of sophistication might be educational\n> level. Unfortunately, there is little research with high school\n> learners: six C/E samples (producing a large effect size) and only\n> four P/P samples (with a respectable mean effect size, though the CI\n> descended below zero indicating heterogeneity). At university level,\n> effect sizes were again mixed for different years (where this\n> information was available) and effect sizes for postgraduate students\n> seemed particularly promising, though again from few samples.\n\nBreakdown of studies by proficiency level of subjects, their degree\nspecialization and type of institution where they studied\n\nPretest/posttest studies M*(*d* ) *SD k M*(*d* ) *SD*\n\n## Treatment variables \n\nSome studies involved highly experimental treatments designed to limit\nvariables and isolate the DDL factor, and others were more ecological\nand integrated DDL into regular courses (see Table 7). To examine this,\nwe separated studies conducted under laboratory-like conditions from\nthose in regular classrooms; both contexts showed large effect sizes,\nexcept for C/E designs in lab conditions. Unfortunately, only two\nstudies were conducted in other contexts, so it was not as possible to\nsee how DDL resources might be used out of class or after a course has\nfinished. We also looked at the length of the intervention, though again\nthis involved a degree of informed guesswork because some measured\nduration in hours and minutes, others in class sessions, others in\nweeks, months, terms, semesters, or years. Those of two hours or less,\nusually in one class period, were considered short-term experimental\nstudies. Somewhat longer ones covering three to eight classes were\nconsidered medium duration (*M* = 10 hours 20 minutes). The remainder\nconsisting of at least 10 classes were considered long-term, typically\napproximating a semester's work for 25 to 30 hours, though some\nintroduced DDL for just a few minutes each class, others up to one year\n(three studies) or even two (one study). Again, differences depended on\ndesign. P/P studies yielded the largest effect sizes in medium- or\nshort-term contexts, and C/E studies gave the advantage to long-term\nwork---but always with medium to large effects.\n\n> Studies included M*(*d* ) *SD k M*(*d* ) *SD*\n\nDDL can be implemented in many different ways, notably in terms of the\ntype of interaction learners have with corpus data. It seems that those\nthat actually used technology, that is, where the learners used a\nconcordancer themselves or via some kind of CALL program, tended to show\nlarge effect sizes, but learners using concordance printouts or other\npaperbased materials did less well. Some studies used a combination of\nthe two, typically leading from work on paper to hands-on concordancing.\nThe results in these cases were mixed, with such designs producing large\neffects sizes in C/E studies, lower in P/P. Where learners had access to\ncorpus software, a few used small monolingual corpora (7,000 to 500,000\nwords), usually compiled with precise goals in mind from local sources\n(news websites, research articles, coursebooks, novels, learners' own\nproductions). These nonetheless provided respectable to strong effect\nsizes, particularly in C/E designs. Large monolingual corpora of 100 to\n500 million words or more also produced large effects. Intermediate size\ncorpora (1 to 29 million words) were more mixed---a large P/P effect\nsize and a small C/E one. However, not all studies provided information\nabout corpus size. In the case of parallel corpora, the L2 corpus tokens\nonly were taken into consideration. Reworking these calculations in\nterms of the corpus type rather than size, the most frequently used\npublicly available monolingual corpora were the Brown, BNC, and COCA.\nUsing calculations based on corpus type, the C/E designs produced more\nsubstantial effect sizes than P/P. The use of parallel corpora gave\nlarge effect sizes, most commonly where the L1 was Chinese or Japanese.\nUnfortunately, multimodal corpora cannot be considered here as they\nfeatured in only two studies, one of which was winsorized.\n\nAs for software, of the 51 studies that involved hands-on concordancing,\n15 used more than one software program. Among the remainder, only the\nBYU interface and LexTutor produced effect sizes based on five or more\nunique samples, three of which in each case derived from the same study.\nEven grouping the others by type (e.g., AntConc, WordSmith Tools, and\nthe Longman MiniConcordancer as instances of downloadable programs for\nuse with any monolingual corpus) only covered four studies. This made\nany interpretation delicate and difficult to explore in more detail from\nthe data available at the time of our study.\n\n## Objectives variables \n\nSurprisingly, perhaps, most DDL research to date has targeted language\nfor general purposes, resulting in reassuringly large effect sizes (see\nTable 8). Language for specific purposes also came out fairly well,\nthough the results were mixed in the case of language for academic\npurposes: a very small effect size for C/E designs with a lower\nconfidence limit approaching zero. Most research in this area has\nattempted to evaluate corpus use for learning rather than reference\npurposes, yielding large effect sizes. Where corpora were used as a\nreference resource (typically during the data collection phase of the\nstudy), effects were still large in P/P designs but medium in C/E.\n\n## [**Table 8** Objectives of M*(*d* ) *SD k M*(*d* ) *SD*\n\n*Note.* ^a^Language for general purposes. ^b^Language for specific\npurposes. ^c^Language for academic purposes.\n\nTwo final aspects for consideration were the language skills and\nlanguage forms targeted. These required more painstaking treatment,\nreturning to the individual subeffect sizes calculated for each study\nand the methodologies and instruments used to obtain them, ensuring that\nunique samples were not counted more than once for any MV. Language\nskills were counted when they constituted a genuine teaching focus in a\nstudy, as opposed to a spinoff of the data collection instrument. To the\ntraditional four skills (listening, speaking, reading, and writing), we\nadded translation as a third code. Further distinctions could be made\nfor subskills, especially using corpora for error correction or\nrevision, but this overlapped with the reference function discussed\nabove. The most revealing finding for skills (see Table 9) was the\npaucity of studies for speaking and listening. This did not mean that\nthe corpora used did not include (transcripts of) spoken language but\nthat the studies themselves did not directly teach or evaluate speaking\nor listening. Writing clearly dominated, though with mixed results---a\nmedium effect size for P/P designs, negligible in C/E. Translation might\nbe more promising, though it only featured in seven P/P studies, where\nit had a very large effect and has yet to be explored in C/E designs (at\nleast in terms of meta-analyzable data). The other skills similarly\nremain largely underresearched, making difficult any strong\npronouncement between productive and receptive skills.\n\n**9** Language s[kills and forms examined in the stu]{.underline}dies\nincluded in the meta-analysis\n\nPretest/posttest studies Control/experimental studies\n\n95% CI 95% CI\n\n*k M*(*d~unb~*) *SD k M*(*d~unb~*) *SD*\n\nLanguage target lower upper lower upper\n\nLanguage skill\n\nListening 4 0.42 0.11 0.31 0.53 4 0.59 0.87 --0.26 1.44\n\nSpeaking 0 -- -- -- -- 0 -- -- -- --\n\nReading 0 -- -- -- -- 3 1.80 1.47 0.14 3.47\n\nWriting 20 1.12 0.79 0.78 1.47 14 0.28 0.80 --0.14 0.70\n\nTranslation 7 2.04 0.79 1.46 2.63 0 -- -- -- --\n\nLanguage aspect\n\nVocabulary 29 1.54 0.95 1.19 1.88 22 0.68 0.96 0.28 1.08\n\nLexicogrammar 49 1.54 0.91 1.28 1.79 40 0.75 0.88 0.48 1.03\n\nGrammar 18 1.24 1.08 0.74 1.74 9 0.62 1.34 --0.25 1.50\n\nDiscourse 5 1.78 1.29 0.65 2.92 3 0.31 0.25 0.03 0.59\n\nLooking at language forms was even more complicated and involved\nrevisiting each study to see if it had a specific linguistic focus, even\nif this was not necessarily the stated aim. Vocabulary covered those\nstudies that mainly concentrated on learning quantities of new items\n(including phrasal verbs and other multiword units), often measured\nusing multiplechoice questions to test meaning in context. This\ninevitably segued into the second category of lexicogrammar, though here\nthe emphasis was less on meaning than on how the target word fits into\nits surroundings. The instruments often tested knowledge of collocations\nand colligations. This category in turn faded into grammar (e.g., tenses\nor articles), which itself gave way to discourse and textual awareness.\nOur distinctions undoubtedly reflect a substantial degree of subjective\njudgement, because language is itself fuzzy and notoriously resists\ndiscrete categorisation (Hunston, Francis, & Manning, 1997).\nNonetheless, we felt that some grouping could be useful for several\nreasons. First, learners were aware of vocabulary and grammar issues but\ntended to be less aware of usage and discourse. Related to this,\ndictionaries and grammar books are obvious resources, with usage manuals\nunderused, perhaps as they sit uncomfortably between the other tools,\nunable to provide as many entries as dictionaries or cover as much\ngeneralizable content as grammars. This means that even with an\nextensive command of vocabulary and grammar, learners may still have\ngreat difficulty in producing effective, natural-sounding language (cf.\nHoey, 2005). This is the gap where DDL can arguably make its greatest\ncontribution. Johns (2002, p. 109) claimed that it is \"on the\n'collocational border' between syntax and lexis... that DDL methods seem\nto be most effective,\" a claim supported by Mizumoto and Chujo's (2015)\nmetaanalytical finding of the largest effects for DDL in lexicogrammar.\nBut a border only derives meaning from its neighbours. DDL's focus on\ncontext may mean that it is difficult to acquire the large numbers of\nwords that spring to mind when thinking of vocabulary, while at the\nother end of the scale DDL may be \"difficult to reconcile with the 'big\nthemes' of language teaching\" such as grammar (Hunston, 2002, p. 184).\nMany further subcategorizations would be possible, but the distinctions\nare delicate enough as it is, and for the moment might be jeopardized by\nfiner granularity into, for example, collocation versus colligation.\nFrom the results obtained (see Table 9), it seems that DDL was a strong\nmethodology for learning language per se, including lexicogrammar,\nespecially in P/P comparisons. The differing effect sizes between the\ntwo designs for discourse again highlighted the need for caution when\ninterpreting data from small numbers of studies.\n\n# Discussion \n\nOur analysis uncovered a few weak results, but these were more than\noffset by many medium to strong ones. With a large dataset such as this,\nhowever, it would be easy not to see the wood for the trees. In this\nsection, we attempt to sketch an overall picture by returning to our\nthree research questions, looking at the most salient patterns derived\nfrom areas with the greatest number of samples.\n\n*How much DDL research is there?*\n\nIt is often claimed that there is little DDL research in the sense of\nempirical, results-oriented investigations, but this is clearly not\ntrue. To mid-2014, we identified 205 publications reporting empirical\nevaluation of DDL, with output generally increasing year after year.\nThis yielded 64 meta-analyzable studies over a 25-year period, with 88\nunique samples--- compare this to Norris and Ortega's (2000) 49 unique\nsamples over 18 years for effectiveness of L2 instruction as a whole.\nFurther, our meta-analysis did not include the many excellent\nqualitative DDL studies from the same period, the full extent of the\nfugitive literature, nor DDL studies published in languages other than\nEnglish. DDL research is a flourishing field.\n\n*How effective and efficient is DDL?*\n\nEffectiveness studies look at DDL's ability to increase learners' skills\nor knowledge through a pre/posttest design (P/P), efficiency studies\nthrough a control/experimental group comparison (C/E) of different ways\nof covering the same content. In our results, a focus on effectiveness\nyielded an average *d* of 1.5, efficiency 0.95. These figures both occur\nin the top quartile of meta-analyses in SLA covered by Plonsky and\nOswald (2014) and can thus be considered large in our field. It should\nalso be remembered that, unlike many of the metaanalyses reviewed by\nPlonsky and Oswald, our unbiased *d* was weighted for sample size and\nwinsorized to 3.0 in cases of higher values. Our results are\nparticularly strong in relation to CALL, where meta-analyses typically\nhave yielded small to medium effect sizes. For 12 direct C/E\ncomparisons, Plonsky and Ziegler (2016) reported a mean effect size of\n0.68. However, effect sizes in CALL correlated negatively with the\nnumber of studies sampled (--0.44), casting doubt on the robustness of\nthe findings overall. Our outcomes paint an optimistic picture of the\nvalue of big language data that can be entrusted to learners themselves.\n\n*How can we best account for any variation observed?*\n\nTempting though it may be (cf. Eysenck, 1978) to seize on a single\nstatistic in a meta-analysis and conclude that it works, it is more\ninteresting to look at \"what works for whom in what circumstances and in\nwhat respects, and how\" (Pawson & Tilley, 2004, p. 151), in other words,\nto look at which MVs contributed more or less to overall effects. Our\nintent here has been to present effect sizes for MVs as completely and\ntransparently as possible, with the supplementary materials (as part of\nthe Supporting Information online, available alongside this article, and\nthrough data and materials available through the Open Science Framework\nat [https://osf.io/jkktw]{.underline}) providing the raw data for others\nto analyse in their own way.\n\nThe resulting wealth of data can make it difficult to see patterns,\nhowever, especially as we have reported effects for both P/P and C/E\ndesigns, whereas most meta-analyses in SLA have concentrated only on a\nsingle design and may have presented a simplified picture. In particular\nhere, it is notable that the two designs did not systematically provide\nequivalent effect sizes, highlighting again the danger of fixating on a\nsingle value. From a possible 84 moderator variables in 25 different\ncategories similar to those commonly tested in other meta-analyses,\nwithin-groups designs yielded 49 large effect sizes, 20 medium, eight\nsmall, and only one lower than small. Between-groups designs yielded 47\nlarge, 19 medium, five small, and 11 lower than small. In total, this\nequates to 60% large effect sizes, 24.5% medium, with only 15.5% small\nor negligible.\n\nIn line with most meta-analyses in applied linguistics (a notable\nexception being\n\nGoldschneider & DeKeyser, 2001), we did not attempt a multiple\nregression analysis of our MVs. Such a procedure is mainly suited to\ncontinuous MVs rather than the categorical variables emerging from most\nmeta-analyses including ours, and where every cell is filled. One way to\nsimplify things is to concentrate only on the most robust findings,\nwhich we have done by including only those MVs where: (a) effect sizes\ncould be calculated for both P/P and C/E designs; (b) the CI did not\ninclude zero; and (c) the results were based on at least 10 samples\nsince, as we saw in the case of CALL, smaller samples may be less\nreliable.\n\nFor the 40 MVs where both designs produced an effect size under these\ncriteria, the correlation coefficient was .35. In 22 of the 40 cases,\nthe P/P and C/E *d* values ranked in the same band (19 large, three\nmedium). A further 15 differed by one level (14 large/medium, one\nmedium/small); only three pairs were out by more than this, supporting\nthe reliability of this approach. These values are given in Table 10,\nseparated into groups of MVs which tell us something about: (a) the\nquality of the studies involved; (b) the situations where DDL may be\nmore or less applicable; and (c) the effectiveness of different uses.\n\n**Table 10** Effect sizes for both within-group (P/P) and between-group\n(C/E) designs and moderator variables (MV)\n\n> MVs relating to quality\n\n## [Quality MV P/P C/E]{.underline} [Quality (cont.) Int+\n\nProficiency Int\n\n> Int--\n\nInstitution Uni 1\n\n> Languages\n\nSpeciality Other\n\n> Sciences\n\n*Note*. L = large (black), M = medium (dark grey), S = small (light\ngrey), 0 = negligible (white).\n\n-   Quality\n\nThe date of publication seemed to have little role to play in effect\nsize (see Table 10), though it is in recent years that the P/P and C/E\ndesigns both give large effect sizes. Although insufficient data were\navailable from other sources, journal articles gave large effect sizes,\nwhether from ranked or unranked journals. Most papers were between 11\nand 20 pages long, again giving large effects. Duration seemed not to be\na major factor either, giving one large and one medium effect size in\neach design, although ecological studies conducted in regular class\nconditions did both give large effect sizes. The remaining features all\ngave rise to medium or large results with two exceptions. It is unclear\nwhy large experimental group samples should give rise to such disparate\nresults, or why instruments requiring free responses should give smaller\neffect sizes in P/P than in C/E designs. These exceptions\nnotwithstanding, insofar as these features provided an indication of\nstudy quality, the large effect sizes obtained cannot be attributed to\nan abundance of poor quality research.\n\n-   Situations\n\nDDL has been more extensively explored in foreign than in second\nlanguage environments, achieving large effect sizes in the Middle East,\nand large to medium in Asia and Europe (see Table 10). This may\nindicate, again speculatively, that DDL is strongest where the\nlikelihood of native speaker (English) instructors is lowest, thus\noffering some measure of authenticity and learner independence, possibly\nmarried to the traditional focus on language form at the expense of\ncommunication (compared to North America, for example, where learners\nare surrounded by authentic input, independence is imposed,\ncommunication prevails, and DDL has not been as extensively trialled).\nContrary to popular opinion, it is not among postgraduates with advanced\nlevels of proficiency that DDL has been most widely researched, and\nlarge effect sizes have been found in first-year university courses for\nintermediate levels although, as noted earlier, definitions are loose in\nthis area. The reason for the difference between P/P and C/E designs at\nlower-intermediate level warrants further exploration. Although large\neffects have been found for learners specializing in languages, medium\neffects have also been reported in other sciences---remembering always\nthat medium still means in the top 50% of meta-analyses in SLA surveyed\nby Plonsky and Oswald (2014).\n\n-   Corpus use\n\nContrary to some claims, the DDL approach seems to be most effective\nwhen using a concordancer hands-on rather than through printed materials\n(large vs. medium/small effects) (see Table 10). Tailor-made local\ncorpora may be somewhat more effective than large public corpora, though\nin all cases the effect sizes were large or medium. This trend was not\nlimited to corpora for specific purposes because large effects for\ngeneral purposes were found as well, and large effects for learning as\nopposed to medium when corpora were used as a reference resource (e.g.,\nin writing, though insufficient studies could be included for different\nskills). When it comes to the language objectives themselves, we found\nlarge or medium effects for vocabulary and lexicogrammar, though there\nwere again insufficient studies to warrant strong claims for or against\ntheir use in grammar or discourse.\n\n# Summary and critical evaluation \n\nThe aim of this study was to quantify outcomes relating to the use of\nthe tools and techniques of corpus linguistics for L2 learning or use,\nwhich we labelled data-driven learning or DDL. The point of a\nmeta-analysis is not to promote or defend a given field but to provide a\nclearer overview, thus providing context for all. This is not\ndefinitive, as others may make different choices at any stage (defining\nthe field, selecting papers, coding, extracting effect sizes, pooling,\ninterpreting, etc.) and take a different perspective, even with\nidentical research questions in the exact same field. The entire dataset\nis available in the supporting information on line for just this reason\nand can be used to explore intriguing or counterintuitive results such\nas how proficiency interacts with other moderator variables.\n\nAn initial pool of 205 studies that had attempted empirical evaluation\nof some aspect of DDL showed output increasing over time. Of these, 64\nwere meta-analyzable giving 88 unique samples. This suggested that there\nis more empirical research than is sometimes claimed, and no evidence of\npublication bias was found. The average effect sizes (unbiased Cohen's\n*d*) were 1.50 for pre/posttest designs, 0.95 for control/experimental\ndesigns, both of which count as large inasmuch as they placed them in\nthe top quartile of meta-analyses in L2 research as a whole. Average\neffects seemed to be increasing somewhat over time, and large effects\ncannot be attributed to standard indicators of study quality. In\nparticular, journal articles gave higher effect sizes than other\npublications types, and ranked journals only slightly higher than\nunranked journals.\n\nIn terms of the 84 MVs analysed, 60% produced large and 24.5% medium\neffect sizes in the two designs---an encouraging finding overall.\nHowever, though the MVs we examined are typical of meta-analyses in\napplied linguistics, the current set is not exhaustive enough to account\nfor all variation across the studies, and it may well be that other\nfactors are responsible in the complex field that is language learning\n(e.g., Larsen-Freeman, 2006). Focusing only on the most robust results\n(i.e., MVs with at least 10 unique samples in both P/P and C/E), 70% had\nlarge effects, 25% medium, and only 5% small or negligible. The most\nconsistent large effects showed that DDL is perhaps most appropriate in\nforeign language contexts for undergraduates as much as graduates, for\nintermediate levels as much as advanced, for general as much as\nspecific/academic purposes, for local as much as large corpora, for\nhands-on concordancing as much as for paper-based exploration, for\nlearning as much as reference, and particularly for vocabulary and\nlexicogrammar. Many of these findings go against common perceptions, and\nthe elements missing from the list (e.g., skills or other language\nareas) are for the most part missing because there is as yet\ninsufficient research rather than because research evidence is against\nthem. There is nothing to suggest that they are inherently unamenable to\na DDL approach but are rather just difficult to operationalize. From\nthis we reach the somewhat surprising and possibly encouraging\nconclusion that DDL works pretty well in almost any context where it has\nbeen extensively tried.\n\nA meta-analysis cannot identify which theoretical underpinnings lead to\nthese results. However, once we know something of the effects, this may\nfeed back into theoretical and pedagogical discussions and inform future\nresearch. We are now in a position to respond to many of the\npractitioner misgivings we have heard over the years with what seems to\nbe pretty solid evidence. In no particular order, these are that\nlearners seem able to perceive language patterns despite the lines\nchopped off the concordance output and that DDL activities are not\nconfined to advanced learners, nor exclusively to simplified corpora or\nmediated data, nor to hands-off or paper-based activities, nor for\nlearning goals limited to vocabulary and collocation. The evidence on\nall these seems clear.\n\nAlthough meta-analysis has until recently remained a fairly marginal\nmethodology in applied linguistics, it has already generated some\ntraditions, and one of these leads us to a complaint about the quality\nof the work that we have reviewed. Our complaints about DDL work are not\nextensive, and the increasing effect sizes speak for themselves. Still,\nan initial count of 205 DDL studies was reduced to 64 partly due to our\ninclusion criteria but also because of missing data and incomplete\nreporting. Even for studies that were included, the coding sheet in the\nSupporting Information online shows blank cells for seemingly basic\ninformation such as corpora and software used, language objectives and\ntest instruments, materials and procedures, and participant information.\nFull meta-compliant recommendations for good reporting can be found in\nLarson-Hall and Plonsky (2015).\n\nSome of the weaker results in our collection reflect a plethora of\nresearch questions, especially in PhD dissertations. As in other areas\nof applied linguistics, unambiguous research questions, motivated and\ndoable experimental tasks, focused objectives, transparent study\ndesigns, and outcome measures clearly tied to learning tasks all led\nmore frequently to strong results than the alternatives did. Other weak\neffects are simply a factor of the limited number of studies focusing on\na given area, especially for languages other than English, in contexts\noutside higher education, for personalized use outside class, and with\nfocus on specific skills or language areas in addition to vocabulary or\nlexicogrammar. We cannot know if researchers are right to avoid DDL in\nthese cases until it has actually been studied there.\n\nAnother pressing need is for more longitudinal and delayed posttesting.\nIf a prime rationale for DDL is that it should be good for autonomy,\nlearning to learn, consciousness raising, and other forms of long-term\nchange in thought or action, then this should be evidenced in strong\nresults on delayed posttests. We have avoided this complex issue here\nfor reasons of space, but we should note that of the very few delayed\ntests reported, many are within PhD dissertations, and that PhD\ndissertations overall exhibit substantial differences in effects\naccording to design (large within-groups, small between-groups).\nNonetheless, the delayed effects are anomalously low, suggesting that it\nis not just the difficulty inherent in testing for one factor in the\ncomplexity of long-term studies and delayed tests, but that something\nelse is likely going on. Given the theoretical importance of delayed\ntesting in DDL, we hope that our exposure of this problem will encourage\nresearchers to give it greater attention in future, or to reexamine\nthese studies covered here with a view to clarifying this particular\nissue.\n\n# Conclusion \n\nAs far as we know, our meta-analysis represents the first time that DDL\nwork has been brought together for all to see and consider as a\nwhole---including for DDL researchers. For all of us, it should have\nbecome more apparent why this work is worth doing, what questions are\nmost worth asking, which designs worth pursuing, and what data must be\nincluded to assure one's work will be included in the next\nmeta-analysis---particularly information from the period between\nimmediate and delayed posttest. With the to-do list properly laid out,\nwe conclude that the future of DDL looks rather bright. There is a\ncorpus revolution under way in both applied linguistics and language\ninstruction (e.g., McCarthy, 2004), and what we have found here suggests\nthat even learners can participate. This would ideally be confirmed in a\nsubsequent remake of the present study in five years using some or all\nof the categories and variables that we have identified.\n\n# Notes \n\n1. Suxen stirred in his somewhat\ncomfortable straw bed, his senses immediately attuned to the myriad of\ncreature Ka signatures surrounding him. As an initiate, he had grown\naccustomed to the constant buzz of life energy, but today felt\ndifferent. There was an undercurrent of tension, a ripple in the usual\nebb and flow of the guild\\'s energy.\n\nGroaning softly, Suxen stretched and made his way to the small window.\nThe courtyard below was already bustling with activity, guild members\nhurrying about with purpose. His eyes fell on a familiar figure - Krik,\nthe kobold stable hand, darting between the legs of taller beings, his\nscales glinting in the morning light.\n\n\\\"Psst, Suxen!\\\" Krik\\'s voice carried up to the window. \\\"Big news!\nStrange folk arrived last night.\n\nOne of \\'em\\... one of \\'em feels like the forest itself!\\\"\n\nSuxen nodded, unsurprised. He\\'d sensed the newcomers\\' arrival, their\nunique Ka signatures impossible to miss. As he dressed and prepared for\nthe day, his mind raced with possibilities. The High Elven prince, whose\nmixed heritage sang a complex melody in Suxen\\'s senses. The woman whose\npresence seemed to flicker between different states of being, as if\noccupying multiple points in time simultaneously. And the druid, whose\nKa radiated with the primordial force of the fabled Quantum Forest.\n\nAs Suxen made his way down to the main hall, the air grew thick with\nanticipation. Guild members of all ranks gathered, their voices a low\nmurmur of speculation and concern. At the center of it all stood the\ngrizzled bardic hunter, a respected member known for his powerful\nconcoctions and deep understanding of creature behavior.\n\nThe debate raged as Suxen entered, words flying like arrows across the\nroom. The bohemeth crisis, it seemed, had reached a breaking point. Some\nargued for aggressive action, others for caution and diplomacy. Elyndor,\nthe High Elven prince, stood tall amidst the chaos, his voice ringing\nout in defense of the creatures.\n\nBut it was the sudden silence that fell over the room that caught\nSuxen\\'s attention. The Quantum Forest druid stepped forward, and with a\ngesture, caused a tree to sprout from the very stones of the hall. The\ndisplay of power was a stark reminder of the forces at play.\n\nSuxen, drawn by curiosity, edged closer to the center of the room. His\neyes fell upon a small cauldron the bardic hunter had been tending.\nWithin it bubbled a concoction that sent Suxen\\'s senses reeling - a\npotent mixture of pheromones and magic unlike anything he\\'d encountered\nbefore.\n\nWhat happened next would change the course of Suxen\\'s life forever. In\nhis eagerness to observe, he stumbled, knocking into the hunter. Time\nseemed to slow as the flask of concentrated pheromones arced through the\nair, its contents splashing across Suxen before the remainder fell into\nthe cauldron.\n\nThe reaction was instantaneous and chaotic. A wave of pheromones\nblanketed the hall, triggering primal instincts in everyone present. The\nBeastmasters, their animal natures awakened, began to shift and change.\nElyndor, caught in the wave, was struck by a quill from a transformed\nguild member.\n\nIn the midst of the chaos, Suxen felt a strange calmness wash over him.\nThe pheromones that had drenched him were not driving him to frenzy, but\ninstead awakening something deep within. With a clarity he\\'d never\nbefore experienced, Suxen understood the flows of Ka and pheromones\nswirling around him.\n\nActing on instinct, Suxen spoke a single word: \\\"Stop.\\\"\n\nThe effect was immediate. The raging Beastmasters froze, the chaos\nsubsiding like a receding tide. In the sudden quiet, all eyes turned to\nSuxen, a mix of awe and fear in their gazes.\n\nAs the dust settled, the true implications of what had occurred began to\ndawn on everyone present. The Quantum Forest druid spoke of far-reaching\nconsequences, of offspring that would shape the future. Taylinor, the\nwoman out of time, hinted at ripples spreading across the fabric of\nreality itself.\n\nSuxen stood at the center of it all, his mind reeling from his newfound\nabilities and the weight of responsibility that came with them. He knew,\nin that moment, that his journey was far from over. The Beastmaster\nGuild adventure was but a stepping stone, a crucible that had forged him\nanew.\n\nAs the guild leaders debated his fate, Suxen\\'s thoughts turned to the\nfuture. To the warrior guild that awaited him, to the monastery that\nwould one day be his home, and to his ultimate destiny as a herald.           "content": "State-of-the-Art Article\n\n**Conversation Analysis and language learning**\n\n**Paul Seedhouse** University of Newcastle upon Tyne, UK\n\nPaul.Seedhouse@newcastle.ac.uk\n\n> *Interest in Conversation Analysis (CA) and its possible applications\n> in the fields of language learning and language teaching has grown\n> considerably over the last five years. There are now a range of\n> publications which explore this area. The article therefore attempts\n> to synthesise the current state of the research and identify the\n> issues and problems that have arisen and those areas which are\n> suitable for further research. This article starts with a brief\n> introduction to CA methodology and then discusses the range of areas\n> within the broad field of language learning and teaching in which CA\n> has been applied: teaching languages for specific purposes; language\n> teaching materials design; language proficiency assessment; language\n> classroom interaction; NS--NNS (native/nonnative speaker) talk; and\n> code-switching. It then discusses the relationship between CA, Applied\n> Linguistics and Second Language Acquisition, and examines the complex\n> issue of what CA can contribute to the study of 'learning'. The issues\n> are illustrated by an example of a CA analysis of language learning\n> processes. The article proposes that there are now three distinct\n> approaches to the application of CA methodology to the field of\n> language learning and teaching. The article concludes by positioning\n> CA as a social science research methodology and considers possible\n> future directions for research.*\n\n# **1. Introduction**\n\n> Conversation Analysis (CA) is a methodology for the analysis of\n> naturally-occurring spoken interaction. It is a multi-disciplinary\n> methodology which is now applied in a very wide range of professional\n> and academic areas. There have been a number of different conceptions\n> of the relationship between CA and the broad field of language\n> learning and teaching, and CA has indeed been applied in research in\n> this field in many different ways. The recent and rapid growth in\n> interest and publications in this area means that the time is ripe for\n> a review of the current state of research.\n>\n> This article starts with a brief introduction to CA methodology and\n> then discusses the range of areas within the broad field of language\n> learning and teaching in which CA has been applied. I then discuss the\n> relationship between CA, Applied Linguistics and Second Language\n> Acquisition and examine the complex issue of what CA can contribute to\n> the study of 'learning'. I conclude by positioning CA as a social\n> science research methodology and consider possible future directions\n> for research.\n\n# **2. Conversation Analysis methodology**\n\n> This section provides a very brief introduction to CA methodology for\n> readers who are unfamiliar with it and stresses the very significant\n> differences between CA and descriptivist linguistic methodology. Space\n> precludes a full account here, but these are available in Levinson\n> 1983; Heritage 1984; Hutchby & Wooffitt 1998; ten Have 1999; Seedhouse\n> 2004. The discussion in this section is based on Seedhouse (2004).\n>\n> CA was started by sociologists Sacks and Schegloff as a sociological\n> 'naturalistic observational discipline that could deal with the\n> details of social action rigorously, empirically and formally'\n> (Schegloff & Sacks 1973: 289f.). This article will not discuss the\n> ethnomethodological principles which underpin CA due to space\n> constraints; such a discussion is available in Heritage (1984) and\n> Seedhouse (2004).\n>\n> At the start we should be clear that there is a fundamental difference\n> between the 'CA mentality' and the 'linguistic mentality' in relation\n> to the status of language. CA's primary interest is in the social act\n> whereas a linguist's primary interest is normally in language. CA,\n> therefore, does not treat language as an autonomous system independent\n> of its use; rather, it treats 'grammar and lexical choices as sets of\n> resources which participants deploy, monitor, interpret and\n> manipulate' (Schegloff et al. 2002: 15) in order to perform their\n> social acts.\n\n  -----------------------------------------------------------------------\n  Lang. Teach. 38, 165--187. doi:10.1017/S0261444805003010 Printed in the\n  United Kingdom ![](media/image1.png){width=\"7.666666666666666e-2in\"\n  height=\"7.333333333333333e-2in\"}2005 Cambridge University Press\n  -----------------------------------------------------------------------\n\n  -----------------------------------------------------------------------\n\n> *Dr Paul Seedhouse is Postgraduate Research Director in the School of\n> Education, Communication and Language Sciences at the University of\n> Newcastle upon Tyne, UK, and runs the Integrated Ph.D. programme in\n> Educational and Applied Linguistics. After teaching ESOL, German and\n> French in five different countries, he has published widely in\n> journals of applied linguistics, language teaching and pragmatics. His\n> monograph* The interactional architecture of the language classroom: a\n> CA perspective *was published by Blackwell in 2004, and he has edited\n> (with Keith Richards) the collection* Applying Conversation Analysis*,\n> published by Palgrave Macmillan in 2005.* Dr Paul Seedhouse, School of\n> Education, Communication and Language Sciences, University of\n> Newcastle upon Tyne, Newcastle NE1 7RU, UK.\n> Paul.Seedhouse@newcastle.ac.uk\n\n# 2.1AimsandprinciplesofCA\n\n> Talk-in-interaction has become the accepted superordinate term to\n> refer to the object of CA research (Drew & Heritage 1992b: 4).\n> According to Psathas (1995), CA studies the organisation and order of\n> social action in interaction. This organisation and order is one\n> produced by the interactants in situ and oriented to by them; it can\n> therefore only be understood from the participants' perspective. Since\n> the emic/etic distinction is vital to this article, we need to define\n> it at this point. According to Pike (1967: 37),\n>\n> \\[t\\]he etic viewpoint studies behaviour as from outside of a\n> particular system, and as an essential initial approach to an alien\n> system. The emic viewpoint results from studying behaviour as from\n> inside the system\\...Descriptions or analyses from the etic standpoint\n> are 'alien' in view, with criteria external to the system. Emic\n> descriptions provide an internal view, with criteria chosen from\n> within the system.\n>\n> What CA means by an emic perspective, however, is the participants'\n> perspective within the interactional environment in which the talk\n> occurs. This is the CA understanding of 'within the system' and this\n> explains why CA practitioners do not interview participants post-hoc\n> about their understanding of the interaction.\n>\n> The analyst's task is to develop an emic perspective, to uncover and\n> describe this organization and order; the main interest is in\n> uncovering the underlying machinery which enables interactants to\n> achieve this organisation and order. So one principal aim is to\n> characterise the organisation of the interaction by abstracting from\n> exemplars of specimens of interaction and to uncover the emic logic\n> underlying this organisation. Another principal aim of CA is to trace\n> the development of intersubjectivity in an action sequence. This does\n> not mean that CA provides access to participants' cognitive or\n> psychological states (see section 4.5 below for a discussion of the CA\n> perspective on socially distributed cognition). Rather, it means that\n> analysts trace how participants analyse and interpret each others'\n> actions and develop a shared understanding of the progress of the\n> interaction. Thus, CA practitioners aim 'to discover how participants\n> understand and respond to one another in their turns at talk, with a\n> central focus on how sequences of action are generated' (Hutchby &\n> Wooffitt 1998: 14).\n>\n> CA has developed its own subset of principles and procedures, which\n> will now be discussed. As with other forms of qualitative research,\n> the principles are not to be considered as a formula or to be applied\n> in a mechanistic fashion. It is essential to adopt a conversation\n> analytic mentality which 'involves more a cast of mind, or a way of\n> seeing, than a static and prescriptive set of instructions which\n> analysts bring to bear on the data' (Hutchby & Wooffitt 1998: 94).\n>\n> Sacks's most original idea, according to Hutchby & Wooffitt (1998), is\n> that there is order at all points in interaction. This was an\n> extremely radical idea in the 1960s as the dominant linguistic view\n> was that conversation was too disordered to be studied. This idea\n> leads to the concept of rational design in interaction: talk in\n> interaction is systematically organised, deeply ordered and methodic.\n> The principle of rational organisation is vital to an understanding of\n> institutional discourse. Different institutions have different\n> institutional aims and organisations of the interaction appropriate to\n> those aims. Seedhouse (2004) applies these principles to L2 classroom\n> interaction; see section 3.5 below.\n>\n> A second principle of CA is that contributions to interaction are\n> context-shaped and contextrenewing. Contributions are context-shaped\n> in that they cannot be adequately understood except by reference to\n> the sequential environment in which they occur and in which the\n> participants design them to occur. Contributions are context-renewing\n> in that they inevitably form part of the sequential environment in\n> which a next contribution will occur. As Heritage (1984b: 242) puts\n> it, '\\[t\\]he context of a next action is repeatedly renewed with every\n> current action', and is transformable at any moment. CA has a dynamic,\n> complex, highly empirical perspective on context; a broader discussion\n> is available in Schegloff (1987) and Seedhouse (2004). The basic aim\n> is to establish an emic perspective, i.e. to determine which elements\n> of context are relevant to the interactants at any point in the\n> interaction. The perspective is also an active one in which\n> participants talk a context into being.\n>\n> The third principle is that no order of detail can be dismissed, a\n> priori, as disorderly, accidental or irrelevant (Heritage 1984b: 241).\n> This principle follows from the first two and can be seen to underlie\n> the development of the highly detailed CA transcription system, its\n> minute analysis of the detail of naturally occurring data and its\n> highly empirical orientation. There is a great deal to be said on the\n> matter of transcription and there are inevitably some differences\n> between linguists (particularly phonologists) and CA practitioners\n> here. However, since these issues are not of central relevance to the\n> argument here, the reader is referred to the detailed discussions in\n> Hutchby & Wooffitt (1998), ten Have (1999) and Markee (2000). For\n> illustrations of the benefits of CA transcription, see Hutchby &\n> Wooffitt (1998) and Wei (2002). For present purposes we need only note\n> the following:\n\n  -----------------------------------------------------------------------\n       CA practitioners regard the recordings of naturally occurring\n       interaction as the primary data;\n  ---- ------------------------------------------------------------------\n       transcripts are designed to make the primary data available for\n       intensive analytic consideration by the analyst and other readers;\n\n       transcripts are inevitably incomplete, selective renderings of the\n       primary data which invariably involve a trade-off between\n       readability and comprehensiveness.\n  -----------------------------------------------------------------------\n\n> A data issue which is receiving increasing prominence is the question\n> of what constitutes adequate primary data for CA studies. At the start\n> of CA in the 1960s, the new technology of audio recording was the only\n> one available and telephone conversation data were easily accessible.\n> However, with the rise of video recording, it became possible to\n> include nonverbal communication and gaze in transcripts as well as\n> still photographs. Pioneering work in this area was undertaken by\n> Goodwin (e.g. Goodwin 1984) and Heath (e.g. Heath 1986). CA aims to\n> understand how social action is accomplished and claims that no detail\n> of the interaction can be dismissed as insignificant. It is therefore\n> argued (e.g. Ford, Fox & Thompson 1996; Zuengler, Ford & Fassnacht\n> 1998) that nonverbal communication and gaze are potentially important\n> features of face-to-face interaction and should therefore be detailed\n> in transcripts. Recent CA studies in the area of language learning\n> which demonstrate the significance of non-verbal communication and\n> gaze for our understanding of interaction include Zuengler, Ford &\n> Fassnacht 1998; Mori 2003; Carroll 2004; Lazaraton 2004; Olsher 2004.\n> The disadvantages of using extremely detailed non-verbal communication\n> and gaze information are that they increase transcription time\n> considerably and may render transcripts more difficult to read and\n> less accessible to a general readership. However, the nature of data\n> presented in CA studies has always been linked to technological\n> developments and no doubt further developments will have an impact in\n> this area.\n>\n> The fourth principle which follows from this is that analysis is\n> bottom-up and data driven; we should not approach the data with any\n> prior theoretical assumptions or assume that any background or\n> contextual detail are relevant. So in CA it is not relevant to invoke\n> power, gender, race or any other contextual factor unless and until\n> there is evidence in the details of the interaction that the\n> participants themselves are orienting to them. So it is incorrect to\n> say that CA does not consider background or contextual details; the\n> point is that it does so only if and when close analysis reveals\n> participants' orientation to such details.\n>\n> Another way of presenting the principles of CA is in relation to the\n> questions which it asks. The essential question which we must ask at\n> all stages of CA analysis of data is 'Why that, in that way, right\n> now?' This encapsulates the perspective of interaction as action (why\n> that) which is expressed by means of linguistic forms (in that way) in\n> a developing sequence (right now).\n\n# 2.2Typesofinteractionalorganisation\n\n> A number of interactional organisations which were uncovered by Sacks,\n> Schegloff & Jefferson (1974) and associates by grappling with their\n> data can now be employed in analysis by CA practitioners.\n>\n> First, we should clarify that these organisations are definitely not\n> the same as 'units of analysis' in the linguistic sense. Rather, they\n> should be understood as interactional organisations which interactants\n> use normatively and reflexively both as an action template for the\n> production of their social actions and as a point of reference for the\n> interpretation of their actions. We, as analysts, should use them in\n> the same way. The organisations are part of the context-free machinery\n> which people make use of to orientate themselves in indexical\n> interaction i.e. we employ them in a context-sensitive way. Similarly,\n> we are only able to interpret the context-sensitive social actions of\n> others because there is a context-free machinery by reference to which\n> we can make sense of them.\n>\n> **ADJACENCY PAIRS** are paired utterances such that on production of\n> the first part of the pair (e.g. question) the second part of the pair\n> (answer) becomes conditionally relevant. If, however, the second part\n> is not immediately produced, it may nonetheless remain relevant and\n> accountable and appear later, or its absence may be accounted for. The\n> adjacency pair concept does not claim that second parts are always\n> provided for first parts. Rather, it is a normative frame of reference\n> which provides a framework for understanding actions and providing\n> social accountability. So if we ask a question to someone who does not\n> then provide an answer, we may draw conclusions about that person.\n>\n> The notion of **PREFERENCE** issues from the organisation of the\n> adjacency pair. Preference is not related to the notion of liking or\n> wanting to do something, but rather involves issues of affiliation and\n> disaffiliation in relation to social actions. As Heritage (1984: 265)\n> puts it, 'there is a \"bias\" intrinsic to many aspects of the\n> organisation of talk which is generally favourable to the maintenance\n> of bonds of solidarity between actors and which promotes the avoidance\n> of conflict'. This structural bias manifests itself in preference\n> organisation. For many adjacency pairs there are alternative second\n> parts, so an invitation may be answered by an acceptance (preferred\n> action) or a rejection (dispreferred action). These two options are\n> performed in different ways. Preferred actions are normally delivered\n> without hesitation or delay at the start of the response turn.\n> Dispreferred responses are generally accompanied by hesitation and\n> delay and are often prefaced by markers such as *well* or *uh* as well\n> as by positive comments and appreciations. They are frequently\n> mitigated in some way and accounted for by an explanation or excuse of\n> some kind. As Heritage (1984: 269) demonstrates, the preferred\n> responses to actions are affiliative and conducive to social\n> solidarity, whereas dispreferred responses are disaffiliative.\n> However, if the dispreferred action is packaged so as to minimise the\n> degree of disaffiliation and conflict, e.g. by using accounts and\n> excuses, then the degree of disaffiliation is minimised.\n>\n> Sacks et al. (1974) provided the seminal account of the organisation\n> of **TURN TAKING** in ordinary conversation. This states a set of\n> norms with options which the participants can select. The basis of the\n> system is turn-constructional units (TCUs) and transition relevance\n> place (TRP). At a TRP the norms governing transition of speakers come\n> into play. Overlap occurs for a number of reasons and in a number of\n> ways. The system of turn-taking is normative, so speakers may choose\n> to perform specific social actions 'by reference to\n> one-partyat-a-time, even though they are realized through designedly\n> simultaneous talk' (Schegloff 2000a: 48). Overlap, then, may be\n> designedly used to intensify the affiliative or disaffiliative nature\n> of particular social actions. In institutional settings, the\n> organisation of turn-taking is constrained and related to the\n> institutional goal, and this is the case in language classroom\n> interaction (Markee 2000; Seedhouse 2004).\n>\n> **REPAIR** comes into play whenever there are problems in the\n> accomplishment of talk and may be defined as the treatment of trouble\n> occurring in interactive language use. Trouble is anything which the\n> participants judge is impeding their communication and a repairable\n> item is one which constitutes trouble for the participants. Schegloff,\n> Jefferson and Sacks (1977: 363) point out that 'nothing is, in\n> principle, excludable from the class \"repairable\"'. Repair is a vital\n> mechanism for the maintenance of intersubjectivity. It is of\n> particular importance for L2 learners and teachers to understand how\n> breakdowns in communication and misunderstandings are repaired, as\n> repair in the L2 classroom tends to carry a heavier load than in other\n> settings (Seedhouse 2004). It is important to distinguish\n> self-initiated repair (I prompt repair of my mistake) from\n> other-initiated repair (somebody else notices my mistake and initiates\n> repair). Self-repair (I correct myself) must also be distinguished\n> from other-repair (somebody corrects my mistake).\n>\n> Seedhouse (2004) suggests that interactional organisations of\n> turn-taking, adjacency pairs, preference organisation and repair are\n> often misunderstood by linguists to be a system of units and rules in\n> the descriptivist linguistic sense and to constitute the methodology\n> of CA. The interactional organisations themselves are stated in\n> context-free terms, but the vital point is that participants employ\n> these contextfree organisations in a context-sensitive way to display\n> their social actions. It is because the participants (and we as\n> analysts) are able to identify the gap between the context-free model\n> and its contextsensitive implementation that they (and we as analysts)\n> are able to understand the social significance of the\n> context-sensitive implementation. This is the basis of the CA claim to\n> be able to uncover the emic perspective.\n>\n> These interactional organisations were introduced in relation to\n> ordinary conversation by Schegloff, Sacks and Jefferson. A number of\n> studies (e.g. Drew & Heritage 1992a) describe how these interactional\n> organisations are adapted to institutional goals in different\n> institutional settings. Seedhouse (2004) describes how these\n> interactional organisations are adapted to and used in language\n> classrooms. For an extended illustration of how these organisations\n> can be applied in a CA analysis of language classroom interaction, see\n> Seedhouse (2004: 59--63).\n\n## 3. Applications of CA in relation to language learning and teaching\n\n> After introducing the relationship between CA and Applied Linguistics\n> (AL), I consider the latest CA and CA-informed research in the\n> following AL areas: teaching languages for specific purposes; language\n> teaching materials design; language proficiency assessment; language\n> classroom interaction; NS-NNS (native/non-native speaker) talk; and\n> code-switching. A common theme in the research is that competence is\n> co-constructed by the participants rather than being fixed and static.\n> As we will see in sections 4.2 and 4.3, there are several different\n> conceptions of CA and how it might be applied to language learning and\n> teaching. The studies reported in this section include a wide range of\n> conceptions of CA and CA-informed work.\n\n# 3.1ConversationAnalysisand AppliedLinguistics[^1]\n\n> Applied Linguistics (AL), by definition, has always focussed on\n> applications. CA, by contrast, has only relatively recently begun to\n> look closely at applications of CA (ten Have 1999, 2001; Heritage\n> 1999; Hester & Francis 2001; Drew 2005; Richards & Seedhouse 2005). In\n> his review of CA, Heritage argued that 'part of the claim of any\n> framework worth its salt is that it can sustain \"applied\" research of\n> various kinds' (Heritage 1999: 73), and he indicated that this aspect\n> might feature prominently in developments within the discipline.\n> However, the concept of application is by no means straightforward\n> (Heritage 1999). According to Richards (2005), the model of\n> application which is most consistent with the nature of CA is that of\n> description leading to informed action. Some of the studies cited\n> below (Packett 2005; Wong 2005) exemplify the use of this model.\n>\n> The development of an applied dimension in CA and its fundamental\n> concern with language as a form of social action suggest a natural\n> link with AL. There is currently growing interest within the field of\n> Applied Linguistics in CA methodology. This is evidenced by a growing\n> number of publications in Applied Linguistics journals which use a CA\n> methodology (Seedhouse 1994, 1997a, 1999a; Markee 1995; Jung 1999;\n> Boyle 2000b; Carroll 2000; Hosada 2000; Wong 2000a, 2002; Mori 2002;\n> Markee & Kasper 2004). Equally, there is growing interest in CA\n> circles in Applied Linguistics, as evidenced by recent publications by\n> Schegloff (2000b) in the journal *Applied Linguistics*, Schegloff,\n> Koshik, Jacoby & Olsher (2002) in the journal *Annual Review of\n> Applied Linguistics*, and Drew (2005). Schegloff et al. (2002: 14)\n> note that '\\[a\\] small but increasing amount of CA and CA-informed\n> research on talk in educational institutions directly addresses issues\n> of interest to applied linguists'. Applied linguistics, which has its\n> roots in language, finds its realisation through action, so a method\n> of inquiry that brings together these two aspects as part of a\n> coherent programme of investigation and description offers a\n> perspective to which applied linguists should be particularly\n> receptive.\n>\n> There is evidence that the two disciplines are moving closer together;\n> as Drew (2005: xx) puts it in his review of their relationship: 'A few\n> years ago, I would have said that AL and CA were wide apart; but now I\n> think\\...that there is an increasing convergence between the two'.\n\n# 3.2Teachinglanguagesforspecific purposes(LSPandESP)\n\n> The area of languages for specific purposes (LSP) can be informed by\n> CA research on institutional or professional discourse. As Jacoby\n> (1998a: 1) points out, LSP teachers have to prepare students to carry\n> out spoken professional communication in a second language. However,\n> the problem is that the LSP teacher sometimes has little idea of the\n> type of spoken interaction which takes place in the target\n> professional setting and the teaching coursebook often 'doesn't\n> reflect the communication reality in which (the students) actually\n> have to function'. If, then, the teacher wishes to provide students\n> with a curriculum based on the real-world target professional\n> communication norms, practices, and its own discourse 'culture', then\n> he/she may need to research the professional setting. In this case, CA\n> has much to offer in terms of the exploration of spoken interaction in\n> professional environments. Jacoby (1998a, b) provides a very\n> practical, step-by-step guide for LSP teachers in doing situated\n> discourse research, including collecting and analysing discoursal\n> data. Jacoby suggests (1998b: 9f.) several ways of exploiting\n> discoursal data in the classroom:\n>\n> extract pedagogical content and criteria for communicative success\n> from the data;\n>\n> bring in data samples to class for the students to observe, analyse\n> and appreciate;\n>\n> compare commercial LSP teaching materials with the reality observable\n> in the data;\n>\n> research findings may also feed into LSP curriculum, materials and\n> assessment design.\n>\n> CA methodology has spawned studies in a wide variety of professional\n> settings, as evidenced in collections such as Drew & Heritage (1992a),\n> Sarangi & Roberts (1999), Richards & Seedhouse (2005), and some papers\n> in McHoul & Rapley (2001) and Boden (1994). Settings covered by CA\n> studies include legal hearings, news interviews, visits by health\n> visitors, phone calls to emergency services and help lines,\n> psychiatric interviews, airplane cockpit talk, mediation and\n> counselling. In some professional settings, then, there is already a\n> body of CA research which can be exploited by LSP teachers, health\n> care being the most prominent. As Barnes (2005: 113) points out, CA\n> research covers not only the primary care medical interview (Heritage\n> & Maynard 2005) but also a wide range of contexts including\n> counselling (Perakyl¨ a¨ 1995) and health visitors (Heritage & Sefi\n> 1992). According to Koshik\n>\n> (2000: 8), 'CA research enables medical practitioners to understand\n> ways in which both their own and their patients' specific practices of\n> talk influence outcomes of medical interviews' and these insights can\n> be integrated into LSP teaching.\n>\n> Bowles (in press) suggests that CA research is an appropriate but\n> neglected resource for LSP research and applications. Bowles focusses\n> on openings of NS-NNS telephone interaction in service calls to\n> bookshops. He identifies a need for description of the differences in\n> sequencing conventions in different languages, the kind of language\n> used to implement these and a method for identifying, explaining and\n> practising sequencing difficulties. This would result in sequencing\n> information modified for speakers of specific languages which could\n> then feed into LSP materials and task design.\n>\n> CA methodology can offer a description of the organisation of an\n> institutional setting, for example, Atkinson & Drew (1979) and\n> Seedhouse (2004). CA can identify sequence organisations which may be\n> vital to the institutional business and which may need to be\n> understood or learnt by novices as part of their induction. An example\n> of a concrete and direct application of CA findings to the English for\n> specific purposes (ESP) classroom is provided by Packett (2005).\n> Packett works with students in Portugal who opt to study English as\n> part of their journalism degree course and who are required to record\n> a face-toface interview for potential radio broadcast as part of their\n> assessed course work. A key and problematic demand on these trainee\n> interviewers is that they should manage the interaction for the\n> benefit of the overhearing but absent audience.
