Packett identifies a\n> common insertion action in which the interviewer departs very briefly\n> from the question--answer turntaking format in order to add a detail\n> to a description given in the prior turn, specifically for the benefit\n> of the absent audience. These insertions, according to Packett, are\n> constitutive of 'doing interview' and directly linked to the\n> institutional goal. An insertion action can be seen in line 7 of\n> extract 1 below, which is an example of expert data used to teach\n> students; see appendix 1 for transcription conventions.\n\n+--------------------+-------------------------------------------------+\n| > Extract1         |                                                 |\n+====================+=================================================+\n| > 1 Interviewer:   | .hh you say if you'd had (.)                    |\n|                    |                                                 |\n|                    | Jo::hn's some of John's (.)                     |\n+--------------------+-------------------------------------------------+\n| > 2                | > \\>abilities or talents and he'd had some of   |\n|                    | > yours \\<                                      |\n+--------------------+-------------------------------------------------+\n| > 3                | > which were those. Which would he've \\[liked   |\n|                    | > to () between you                             |\n+--------------------+-------------------------------------------------+\n| 4 Interviewee:     | \\[.hhh well I think John-                       |\n+--------------------+-------------------------------------------------+\n| > 5                | > John er (0.2) John [no::w]{.underline} (0.2)  |\n|                    | > having obviously been married to              |\n+--------------------+-------------------------------------------------+\n| > 6                | > Chris an-an- an- =                            |\n+--------------------+-------------------------------------------------+\n| 7.  Interviewer: → |                                                 |\n|     > =\\>Chris     |                                                 |\n|     > Evert yah.\\< |                                                 |\n|     > =            |                                                 |\n|                    |                                                 |\n| 8.  Interviewee:   |                                                 |\n|     > =yeah, and   |                                                 |\n|     > basically    |                                                 |\n|     > living a lot |                                                 |\n|     > in- in the   |                                                 |\n|     > states\\...   |                                                 |\n|                    |                                                 |\n| (BBC4, *On the     |                                                 |\n| ropes*, 15.8.00)   |                                                 |\n+--------------------+-------------------------------------------------+\n\n> These insertions are organised so as only minimally to interrupt the\n> question--answer format of the interview and to redress the\n> indexicality of the prior description. It was noted that in the\n> learners' assessed interviews this vital insertion sequence was often\n> absent or delayed, which disrupted the flow of the talk. Both the\n> expert data and the learner data were then used by Packett as\n> classroom materials to demonstrate to students the use of the device\n> in interaction. Packett's paper serves as a model not only for\n> CA-informed pedagogy, but also for CA research in language for\n> specific purposes with the aim of linking sequences to the\n> institutional goal. Future CA research in this area would seek to\n> identify such institution-specific interactional patterns and employ\n> them in teaching.\n>\n> Bowles & Palotti (2003) compare calls by Italian speakers in Italy to\n> those of English speakers in the UK. They also compare calls to a\n> variety of institutions ('workplace calls') to those made to one\n> specific outlet, namely a bookstore, in order to uncover any\n> domain-specific features. Their analysis of an extensive corpus\n> reveals:\n>\n> characteristics of workplace calls as opposed to ordinary telephone\n> calls;\n>\n> characteristics of workplace calls in the two different languages;\n\ncharacteristics of calls to bookstores in particular;\n\n> characteristics of calls to bookstores in the two different languages.\n>\n> Their research suggests that this type of CA exploration of a corpus\n> by domain and by language is likely to be of interest to LSP in terms\n> of materials and task design.\n>\n> Bowles (in press: 26) presents the central problem in the relationship\n> between CA and LSP: 'What CA data invariably reveals is a degree of\n> detail and complexity in talk which is often daunting for the LSP\n> analyst, who finds it difficult to turn the complexity of talk into\n> practical, instructable materials'. However, Bowles sees this bridging\n> of the CA--LSP gap as essential if LSP oral materials are to develop\n> in terms of authenticity and validity.\n\n# 3.3Languageteachingmaterialsdesign\n\n> Language teaching materials frequently feature dialogues presented on\n> audio or video together with a transcription. Issues relating to\n> authenticity of dialogues are complex and have been hotly debated.\n> However, in many countries around the world, materials writers\n> continue (for a variety of reasons) to invent dialogues. CA is well\n> positioned to portray the similarities and differences between\n> invented dialogue and naturally-occurring or 'authentic' interaction,\n> both in terms of ordinary conversation and institutional interaction.\n> Wong (2002) provides a very clear example of an application of CA to\n> an area of applied linguistics. She identifies four sequence types\n> which typically occur in American English telephone conversations,\n> namely summons--answer, identification--recognition, greeting and *How\n> are you?* Examining the presentation of thirty inauthentic phone\n> conversations in ESL textbooks, Wong (2002: 37) finds that the above\n> sequences are 'absent, incomplete or problematic'. CA research\n> findings, such as the above sequence types, can be fed into future\n> language teaching materials design.\n>\n> Bernsten (2002) examined invented dialogues from 22 ESL textbooks to\n> see whether pre-sequences occur in relation to invitations, offers and\n> requests. Pre-sequences are very common and interactionally useful\n> devices in talk-in-interaction (Levinson 1983; Seedhouse 2004).\n> Bernsten found that the invented dialogues contained very few examples\n> of presequences. Possible uses of insights from CA in materials design\n> are indirect and direct. In an indirect approach, materials writers\n> would choose authentic, naturally-occurring dialogues for coursebooks\n> to illustrate phenomena such as pre-sequences uncovered by CA. A\n> direct approach would actually teach conversational sequences and\n> phenomena.\n>\n> The model used by Bernsten (2002) and Wong (2002) of comparing\n> invented dialogues with what we know about naturally occurring\n> interaction could be extensively applied to other aspects of\n> conversation in future research.\n>\n> CA studies have been published on talk in a range of languages and\n> including non-native speakers. Examples of CA studies in\n> non-pedagogical settings include those in German (Egbert 1996, 2005;\n> Golato 2000), Finnish (Sorjonen 1996; Kurhila 2001, 2005), Swedish\n> (Lindstrom 1994), Danish (Brouwer 2004), Dutch (ten Have 1999),\n> Japanese (Ford & Mori 1994; Hayashi 1999; Tanaka 1999; Hayashi, Mori &\n> Takagi 2002), Chinese (Hopper & Chen 1996), Korean (Kim 1999; Park\n> 1999) and Thai (Moerman 1988).\n>\n> Such studies reveal similarities and differences in the organisation\n> of talk in different languages which may then feed into comparative\n> and contrastive analyses of two languages, as well as into language\n> teaching materials design. To illustrate this point, Hopper & Chen\n> (1996) compare telephone openings in Mandarin Chinese to those in\n> English. We saw above that there are four sequence types which\n> typically occur in American English telephone conversations, namely\n> summons--answer, identification--recognition, greeting and 'how are\n> you'. Hopper & Chen (1996) found some similarities, in that the first\n> three sequences regularly occur in Taiwanese telephone conversations.\n> However, they also identify practices and linguistic resources which\n> have not been identified in European languages. In particular,\n> telephone callers in Taiwan use a variety of greeting tokens to index\n> the state of their interpersonal relationship and intimate callers may\n> speak before the answerer. Such findings can potentially feed into\n> materials and task design aimed at learners with specific L1s learning\n> specific L2s.\n\n# 3.4Languageproficiencyassessment\n\n> Language proficiency assessment is probably the area in which CA has\n> had the greatest impact on practice so far, particularly in relation\n> to the construct of competence. Previous CA-informed work in the area\n> of oral proficiency interviews by Lazaraton (1997) and Young & He\n> (1998) examined Language Proficiency Interviews (LPIs). Egbert points\n> out that 'LPIs are implemented in imitation of natural conversation in\n> order to evaluate a learner's conversational proficiency' (Egbert\n> 1998: 147). Young & He's collection demonstrates, however, a number of\n> clear differences between LPIs and ordinary conversation. Firstly, the\n> systems of turn-taking and repair differ from ordinary conversation.\n> Secondly, LPIs are examples of goal-oriented institutional discourse,\n> in contrast to ordinary conversation. Thirdly, LPIs constitute\n> cross-cultural communication in which the participants may have very\n> different understandings of the nature and purpose of the interaction.\n> Egbert's (1998) study demonstrates that interviewers explain to\n> students not only the organisation of repair they should use, but also\n> the forms they should use to do so; the suggested forms are cumbersome\n> and differ from those found in ordinary conversation. He's (1998)\n> microanalysis reveals how a student's failure in an LPI is due to\n> interactional as well as linguistic problems. Kasper & Ross (2001: 10)\n> point out that their analysis of LPIs portrays candidates as\n> 'eminently skilful interlocutors', which contrasts with the general\n> SLA view that clarification and confirmation checks are indices of NNS\n> incompetence, whilst their (2003) paper analyses how repetition can be\n> a source of miscommunication in LPIs. In the context of course\n> placement interviews, Lazaraton (1997) notes that students initiated a\n> particular sequence, namely selfdeprecations of their English language\n> ability. She further suggests that a student demonstration of, or\n> statement about, poor English language ability constitutes grounds for\n> acceptance onto courses. Interactional sequences are therefore linked\n> to participant orientations and goals. It is anticipated that some of\n> the above issues may surface in the proposed research and that other,\n> new phenomena may emerge.\n>\n> CA can be employed to monitor the reliability and validity of\n> assessment. Lazaraton (2002) presents a book-length framework for the\n> application of CA to the validation of LPIs. Her rationale is that CA\n> is able to shed light on the assessment process itself; this can\n> complement the use of traditional statistical methods of test\n> validation which focus on product, i.e. scores. Brown (2003) analyses\n> two LPIs involving the same candidate taking the same test with two\n> different interviewers. The two interviewers were shown to ask\n> different types of questions, provide different types of feedback and\n> to structure sequences of topical talk in different ways. The\n> candidate's communicative ability in the two interviews was rated\n> differently by four raters. The study emphasises the need for\n> interviewer training and standardisation of practices and critiques\n> the robustness of the concept of communicative competence. In relation\n> to testing in English for Specific Purposes (ESP), Jacoby & McNamara\n> (1999: 213) critique the 'primarily linguistic orientation of\n> traditional assessment procedures'. They show that CA is able to\n> locate what counts as communicative competence in specific\n> professional contexts. CA research can clarify the advantages and\n> disadvantages of assessment formats and inform the design of\n> assessment tasks (Schegloff et al. 2002).\n>\n> A theme which runs through the above studies of language teaching\n> assessment is the contribution which CA can make to the study of\n> competence, which has been accepted as fundamental to AL's interests\n> since the 1970s, when communicative language teaching shifted\n> attention to issues of communicative competence and how this might be\n> developed through teaching. The communicative competence model proved\n> highly successful in broadening the scope of classroom teaching and\n> applied linguistics. However, it has, like all methods before or\n> since, been based on a deficit model; the purpose of language\n> teaching, it is generally assumed, is to help students develop\n> linguistic knowledge and skills that will enable them to overcome\n> current limitations and develop their communicative competence to the\n> level of the teacher or native speaker. Also, communicative competence\n> has been a fixed and static construct; as Mondada & Pekarek Doehler\n> (2004: 502) point out, the traditional notion of competence is of 'a\n> phenomenon that is isolated from socialization processes'. CA offers a\n> very different view of the nature of competence. Instead of working\n> from the static assumption that competence is something that one has a\n> fixed degree of at a point in time, CA presents competence as variable\n> and co-constructed by participants in interaction. CA also provides a\n> means of exploring the variable ways in which such competence is\n> co-constructed in particular contexts by the participants involved.\n> 'Competence cannot be defined in purely individual terms as a series\n> of potentialities located in the mind/brain of a lone individual, but\n> needs to be conceived of as a plurality of capacities embedded and\n> recognized in the context of particular activities' (Mondada & Pekarek\n> Doehler 2004: 502f.). CA studies such as Bloch (2005), Goodwin,\n> Goodwin & Olsher (2002) and Carroll (2005) portray how interactants\n> with minimal linguistic resources can nonetheless employ these\n> resources skilfully and innovatively in interaction.\n\n# 3.5Languageclassroominteraction\n\n> A number of studies have examined issues related to language classroom\n> interaction from a CA perspective, revealing subtle interactional\n> practices which transform our perceptions of L2 learners and teachers.\n> Olsher (2004) demonstrates how L2 learners in smallgroup project work\n> may complete sequential actions through gesture or embodied displays.\n> Koshik (2002) reveals how teachers use the pedagogical practice of\n> designedly incomplete utterances in order to initiate self-correction\n> by learners. Carroll (2000, 2004, 2005) challenges the general\n> perception of L2 novice learners as incompetent communicators. Carroll\n> uncovers their ability to make creative communicative use of their\n> minimal linguistic resources and use sophisticated conversational\n> microadjustments. Novice learners can precision-time their entry into\n> interaction, recycle turn-beginnings to solicit the gaze or attention\n> of partners and use vowel-marking as a resource for forward-oriented\n> repair. Mori (2002) traces how a task-as-workplan (discussion with\n> native speakers) is transformed into a task-in-process resembling a\n> structured interview of question--answer exchanges. Markee (2005)\n> demonstrates how learners working in pairs on a task carefully\n> disguise their social talk from the teacher and are able to instantly\n> switch between ontask and off-task talk. Markee (2000) portrays the\n> progress of intersubjectivity during two tasks, one of which results\n> in learner comprehension of the target item whilst the other does not.\n>\n> Seedhouse (2004) applies CA methodology to an extensive and varied\n> database of language lessons from around the world and attempts to\n> answer the question 'How is L2 classroom interaction organised?' The\n> main thesis developed in this monograph is that there is a reflexive\n> relationship between pedagogy and interaction in the L2 classroom, and\n> that this relationship is the foundation of its context-free\n> architecture. This relationship means that, as the pedagogical focus\n> varies, so the organisation of the interaction varies. However, this\n> also means that the L2 classroom has its own interactional\n> organisation which transforms intended pedagogy into actual pedagogy.\n>\n> Seedhouse sketches the basic speech exchange system of four different\n> L2 classroom contexts and portrays the reflexive relationship between\n> the pedagogical focus of the interaction and the organisation of\n> turn-taking and sequence. As the pedagogical focus varies, so the\n> organisation of turn and sequence varies. He then describes how repair\n> is organised within different L2 classroom contexts, specifying this\n> in terms of (a) typical participants in the repair, (b) typical repair\n> trajectories, (c) typical types of repair, and (d) typical focus of\n> repair. There is a reflexive relationship between the pedagogical\n> focus and the organisation of repair; as the pedagogical focus varies,\n> so does the organisation of repair. There is then an illustration of\n> how the interactional organisation can transform the pedagogical focus\n> by examining a case of preference organisation in relation to repair\n> in form and accuracy contexts.\n>\n> The overall organisation of L2 classroom interaction is then outlined.\n> The concept of the rational design of institutional interaction is\n> employed to identify the institutional goal as well as three\n> interactional properties which derive directly from the goal. The\n> basic sequence organisation of L2 classroom interaction is presented,\n> together with an emic methodology for its analysis. Seedhouse stresses\n> the dynamic nature of context by exemplifying how the institution of\n> the L2 classroom is talked in and out of being by participants and how\n> teachers create L2 classroom contexts and shift from one context to\n> another. The monograph portrays the L2 classroom as a complex, fluid,\n> dynamic and variable interactional environment and provides a concrete\n> example of how CA methodology can be applied to an issue of interest\n> to language teachers and applied linguists. In order to understand the\n> relationship between interaction and the process of language learning,\n> it is vital to understand how the interaction is organised.\n>\n> Seedhouse (2004) argues that, because of the diversity of L2\n> classrooms, one should not only specify the database on which L2\n> classroom studies are based in terms of number of lessons or fragments\n> of lessons, but also in terms of the following background contextual\n> factors, in order that the diversity of the database might be\n> assessed: L1 of the learners; multilingual or monolingual classes;\n> culture; country of origin; age of learners; type of institution;\n> level of learners' proficiency in L2. Seedhouse (2004: 85) provides a\n> table providing a brief description of the database underlying his\n> study.\n>\n> Studies of L2 classroom teaching have predominantly featured data from\n> classrooms in which English has been the target language. However, a\n> number of classroom studies have recently been published which feature\n> a variety of target languages including French (Mondada & Pekarek\n> Doehler 2004; Seedhouse 2004); German (Liebscher & Daley-O'Cain 2003;\n> Kasper 2004; Seedhouse 2004); Chinese (He 2004); Japanese (Ohta 2001a,\n> b; Mori 2002, 2004). It is to be hoped that this trend will continue\n> and that data from an increasing range of target languages will be\n> published.\n\n# 3.6Nativespeaker--non-native speakertalk\n\n> Interest in the CA analysis of NS--NNS or crosscultural talk outside\n> the classroom has developed in recent years, including Wagner (1996);\n> Seedhouse (1998); Hosoda (2000); Wong (2000a, 2000b, 2005); Kurhila\n> (2001, 2005); Egbert (2005). Gardner & Wagner (2004) is a major\n> collection of work in the area of NS--NNS talk. It features talk in a\n> variety of social, professional and educational settings and presents\n> analyses of talk using Danish, Finnish, Japanese, German, French and\n> English as second languages. Mondada (2004) reveals some of the\n> complexities of analysing plurilingual NS--NNS talk. She reveals how,\n> in her corpus of video-conferencing meetings between surgeons in\n> several different European countries, 'the working language of the\n> meeting is never decided once and for all, but is constantly\n> renegotiated' (p. 31). For interactants (and hence for the analysis),\n> NS and NNS categories may not be relevant; rather, they may present\n> themselves as 'experts' or 'seniors' or 'juniors'.\n>\n> Seedhouse (1998a) provides a discussion of how CA methodology can be\n> applied to the study of NSNNS interaction. One cannot start from the\n> assumption that the identities 'native speaker' and 'nonnative\n> speaker' are relevant to the talk. Seedhouse analyses an extract of\n> NS--NNS talk. Working from the details of the interaction, these\n> identities are shown to be procedurally relevant to the linguistic\n> forms used, to the topic of the talk and to the interactional moves\n> made. For example, the native speaker used minimalised, pidginised\n> interlanguage forms when talking to the non-native speaker and thereby\n> talked into being the relevance of the identities NS and NNS.\n>\n> The CA study of NS--NNS interaction in non-pedagogic settings has\n> broadened in recent years to include languages other than English, for\n> example, German (Wagner 1996; Seedhouse 1998a; Egbert 2005), Finnish\n> (Kurhila 2001, 2005), Danish (Brouwer 2004) and Japanese (Hosoda\n> 2000). The field has also broadened to include the CA study of\n> interaction between NNS and NNS using English as international lingua\n> franca talk (Firth 1996; Wagner 1996; Mondada 2004), and Finnish as\n> international lingua franca talk (Mazeland & Zaman-Zadeh 2004) as well\n> as studies which compare the identical interactional phenomenon in NNS\n> talk (Wong 2000a) and in NS talk (Schegloff 2000b) in\n>\n> English.\n>\n> Carroll's (2005) study demonstrates that a CA focus on sequence can\n> sometimes reveal hitherto unnoticed aspects of the talk of NNSs.\n> Japanese speakers of English as a foreign language (particularly at\n> the novice level) often add vowels to wordfinal consonants, for\n> example: 'Oldest child-u is-u (0.21) um:: twenty'. Generally, English\n> teachers have treated this as a pronunciation problem, resulting from\n> negative transfer from the L1. Whilst not disputing these origins,\n> Carroll's analysis of his data demonstrates that his subjects were\n> employing vowelmarking as an interactional resource, particularly\n> during forward-oriented repair (Schegloff 1979) or word search, as in\n> the example below.\n>\n> Extract 2\n>\n> A: what-o [what]{.underline}-o [in]{.underline}teresting-u (0.43) e:to\n> schoo:l-u festival (Carroll 2005)\n>\n> According to Carroll, vowel-marking, in delaying the production of\n> some next-item-due, serves to buy the speaker initiating the repair a\n> little more time to achieve self-repair. Furthermore, vowel-marking\n> alerts co-participants to the fact that a search is underway and to\n> their possible role in resolving it. In terms of application, Carroll\n> suggests that training students in the use of interactionally\n> equivalent conversational micro-practices, such as the use of *uh* and\n> *um* would be helpful. Furthermore, Carroll's micronanalysis reveals a\n> previously unimagined degree of interactional sophistication in the\n> way these novice NNSs employ their limited resources.\n>\n> Such CA research, then, reinforces a shift away from a linguistic\n> deficit model focussed on indiviual performance towards a model in\n> which communicative competence is seen to be co-constructed. In this\n> model, many of the interactional competencies of L2 students,\n> non-native speakers and speechdisordered patients can only be revealed\n> through painstaking CA analysis.\n\n# 3.7Bilingualandmultilingual code-switching\n\n> Recent years have seen a growth in the number of studies which have\n> employed a CA approach to bilingual and multilingual interaction and\n> to code-switching in particular (Auer 1998; Sebba & Wootton 1998;\n> Stroud 1998; Gafaranga 2000, 2001; Gafaranga & Torras 2001, 2002;\n> Torras 2002, 2005; Torras & Gafaranga 2002; Wei 2002; Mondada 2004).\n> Wei (2002) provides an overview of the CA approach to bilingual\n> interaction, in which 'particular attention is paid to the way in\n> which individuals strategically use the codes in their bilingual\n> repertoires to achieve specific interactional goals' (p. 159).\n> Analyses must be demonstrably oriented to participant concerns and\n> actions and aim to reveal the underlying procedural apparatus by which\n> interactants themselves arrive at local interpretations of language\n> choice.\n>\n> Although there is a considerable literature on bilingual\n> code-switching, relatively little CA research has been undertaken on\n> code-switching in L2 classrooms. Code-switching as a methodical\n> phenomenon in L2 classroom interaction is now starting to be\n> researched using a CA methodology. Mori (2004: 537) shows 'how code\n> switching \\... serves as a resource for managing sequential\n> boundaries, and at the same time, affects the ways in which their\n> interactive activities are organized'. Kasper (2004: 551) shows how\n> 'code switching worked as one device by which the novice requested a\n> target language action format from the L2 expert'. Ust¨ unel¨ &\n> Seedhouse (2005) depict the relationship between pedagogical focus and\n> language choice in the language teaching/learning environment of\n> English as a Foreign Language (EFL) at a Turkish university. The study\n> presents the organisation of code-switching which is teacherinitiated\n> and 'teacher-induced'. Transcripts of lessons were examined by\n> relating incidence of codeswitching to the pedagogical focus. An\n> adapted version of the classic CA question (why that, right now?) was\n> applied for interaction involving codeswitching, namely why that, in\n> that language, right now? The study demonstrates that codeswitching in\n> L2 classrooms is orderly and related to the evolution of pedagogical\n> focus and sequence. Through their language choice, learners may\n> display their alignment or misalignment with the teacher's pedagogical\n> focus.\n\n## 4. CA and language learning processes\n\n> In this section I consider what CA may have to offer in relation to\n> the broad field of study of second language learning. The section\n> starts and finishes with a discussion of the relationship between CA\n> and Second Language Acquisition (SLA). I also examine the different\n> conceptions of the contribution of CA to the study of language\n> learning processes and provide an example of a CA analysis of language\n> learning.\n\n# 4.1CAandSecondLanguageAcquisition\n\n> The late 1990s saw a CA-motivated debate on a proposed\n> 're-conceptualisation' of SLA (Firth & Wagner 1997, 1998; Kasper 1997;\n> Long 1997; Gass 1998; Markee 2000, 2002; Van Lier 2000). Since SLA is\n> a broad area, we should first clarify that CA's only possible\n> contribution would be to those areas of SLA which use spoken\n> interaction (both inside and outside the classroom) as data. Some of\n> the criticisms which Firth & Wagner (1997, 1998) make of SLA are as\n> follows: SLA has neglected the social and contextual aspects of\n> language use and their contribution to SLA processes. SLA is becoming\n> a 'hermetically sealed area of study' (Firth & Wagner 1998: 92) which\n> is losing contact with sociology, sociolinguistics and discourse\n> analysis in favour of a psycholinguistic focus on the cognition of the\n> individual. There is an etic rather than emic approach to fundamental\n> concepts. The traditional SLA database is too narrow. Essentially the\n> call is for a holistic approach which includes the social dimension\n> and emic perspectives. Responses to Firth & Wagner (Kasper 1997; Long\n> 1997; Gass 1998) generally suggested that, whilst CA was interesting,\n> it had little or nothing to say about language learning or\n> acquisition. A number of publications since that date (reviewed below)\n> have therefore tried to establish what CA might be able to contribute\n> to the study of language learning.\n>\n> Since Firth & Wagner's (1997) article, a number of studies have been\n> published which do incorporate social and contextual dimensions (e.g.\n> Lantolf 2000; Hall & Verplaetse 2000a; Ohta 2001a) and which have\n> established a school of Sociocultural Theory within SLA. So we should\n> note at the start of this section that (in contrast to the situation\n> with AL) there has been controversy concerning whether CA has any role\n> in SLA at all and if it does, what that role should be. We will now\n> consider the relationship between CA and language learning and return\n> to the relationship between CA and SLA at the end of this section.\n\n# 4.2ConceptionsofCAinlanguage learningandteachingresearch\n\n> Opinion is currently divided as to the relationship between CA and\n> language learning and the status of CA. At the time of writing there\n> are a number of competing and sometimes conflicting conceptions of how\n> CA may or may not be employed in language learning and teaching\n> research. From a temporal perspective, this lack of clarity is not a\n> matter of major concern. CA itself only emerged in the 1960s, had no\n> connection with learning, and in its genesis dealt exclusively with\n> monolingual English data. It is only in the period 2000--2004 that\n> publications have started to address the relationship between CA and\n> language learning, culminating in the special issue of the *Modern\n> Language Journal* in 2004 (Markee & Kasper 2004). As Gass (2004: 598)\n> points out, the different articles in the special issue approach the\n> relationship between CA and learning in very different ways. The\n> common ground is that all studies use microanalysis of transcripts of\n> classroom interaction. Kasper (2004: 551) 'explores some roles for CA\n> as an approach to second and foreign language learning' whereas He\n> (2004: 579) is quite clear that 'CA is not a learning theory' and that\n> 'CA is not concerned with what is not observable' (p. 578). Hall\n> (2004: 608) notes that the studies are not 'successful in making a\n> collective case for CA's potential as an approach to studies of\n> language learning'. Larsen-Freeman (2004: 607) suggests that\n> '\\[s\\]aying that something has been learned, saying what has been\n> learned, when it has been learned, and the reason it has been learned\n> are big challenges for all SLA researchers, cognitivists as well as\n> those who practice CA. Yet these are the challenges which CA\n> researchers must confront if they want to move CA to the center of the\n> field'.\n\n# 4.3Threeapproaches\n\n> In this section I propose that it now makes sense to identify three\n> different approaches to the application of CA to the broad field of\n> language learning and teaching.\n>\n> In the ethnomethodological CA approach, data from language learning\n> and teaching settings are approached in exactly the same way as any\n> other data, following the principles and procedures described above.\n> If it is evident in the details of the interaction that the\n> participants are orienting to language learning in some way, then it\n> is legitimate to invoke this in the analysis. For example, Koshik\n> (2002) reveals how teachers use the pedagogical practice of designedly\n> incomplete utterances in order to initiate self-correction by\n> learners. The analysis is not linked to any learning theory and Koshik\n> states (2002: 278) that her aim 'is not to evaluate the pedagogy but\n> to describe an institutional practice, showing how practices of\n> ordinary conversation can be adapted for specialized institutional\n> tasks'.\n>\n> This approach would argue that the very strength of applying CA to the\n> field of language learning and teaching lies in the fact that it is\n> neutral and agnostic in relation to learning theories and teaching\n> methods and reveals an emic perspective. Unless it is evident that\n> interactants are themselves orienting to a concept, it is not\n> legitimate to invoke it in an a priori fashion. Therefore, linking CA\n> to any theory of learning in abstraction from a specific interactional\n> environment is **AN INHERENTLY ETIC UNDERTAKING**. The sociocultural\n> theory approach to CA is currently attracting a great deal of interest\n> as it has the potential to offer a systematic approach of how to study\n> the process of second language learning. This approach seeks 'to use\n> CA techniques as methodological tools that are in the service of\n> different sociocultural theories of learning' (Markee & Kasper 2004:\n> 495). Mondada & Pekarek Doehler (2004: 504) outline the significant\n> similarities between CA and sociocultural theory in a strong\n> socio-interactionist perspective: 'both of these frameworks converge\n> in insisting on the central role of contextually embedded\n> communicative processes in the accomplishment of human actions and\n> identities as well as of social facts'. Young & Miller (2004), Brouwer\n> & Wagner (2004) and Mondada & Pekarek Doehler (2004) propose to link a\n> sociocultural view of development with a CA perspective on\n> interaction. They apply to their data the notion of situated learning\n> 'according to which learning is rooted in the learner's participation\n> in social practice and continuous adaptation to the unfolding\n> circumstances and activities that constitute talk-in-interaction'\n> (Mondada & Pekarek Doehler 2004: 501). Young & Miller (2004) conduct a\n> longitudinal observation of revision talk, show that the participation\n> framework changed over time and reveal the processes by which the\n> student moved from peripheral to fuller participation. Brouwer &\n> Wagner (2004) suggest moving away from the typical SLA conception of\n> language in terms of individual cognition and an input--output\n> approach to the acquisition of discrete linguistic (typically\n> syntactic or lexical) items. They propose instead to focus on the\n> development of interactional skills and resources and conceptualising\n> language learning as a social process. They suggest that 'learning is\n> situated; learning is social; and knowledge is located in communities\n> of practice' and that 'learning not only takes place in the social\n> world, it also constitutes that world' (p. 33).\n>\n> The field of CA-for-SLA generally falls within this approach. The main\n> difference with the previous approach is that the sociocultural theory\n> approach to CA employs CA as a tool in the service of a theory of\n> learning whereas ethnomethodological CA does not and is agnostic in\n> relation to learning. What kind of entity is the sociocultural theory\n> approach to CA? One way of understanding it is as follows.\n> Sociocultural theory is a learning theory and CA is an empirical\n> research methodology.\n>\n> It is clear that there are a number of fundamental differences between\n> sociocultural theory and CA, although of course there are similarities\n> and mutual interests. The sociocultural theory approach to CA may be\n> seen, from one perspective, as an attempt to reconcile these\n> differences and to synthesise a learning theory with a research\n> methodology. This approach, although exciting much interest at\n> present, is relatively new. It remains to be seen whether the\n> differences are insurmountable or whether this will become a major\n> approach to research in language learning.\n>\n> In the linguistic CA approach, interactional organisations or\n> constructs which have been revealed by CA analysis are treated as\n> 'decontextualised coding categories' (Wagner 1996: 231) and employed\n> in linguistic or psycholinguistic SLA studies, typically within a\n> quantitative paradigm. As Wagner (1996: 231) points out, 'these\n> concepts may very well lose their meaning'. For example, SLA research\n> on modified interaction has quantified clarification requests,\n> confirmation checks, and comprehension checks. However, they are\n> merely the social actions or functions performed by the repair and\n> constitute only one small part of the overall organisation of repair\n> in task-oriented contexts as described in this section. SLA research\n> on modified interaction has therefore deprived itself of the\n> analytical power of the CA approach to repair by using only one small\n> and isolated component of this complex organisation. 'Linguistic CA',\n> then, presents CA findings in a format in which they can be readily\n> employed to isolate interactional phenomena for quantitative\n> treatment.\n>\n> Seedhouse (2004) argues that a form of 'linguistic CA' has diverged\n> from ethnomethodological CA. There is now a common misconception among\n> a number of linguists that doing CA is a matter of transcribing talk\n> and then identifying or coding patterns of turn-taking, adjacency\n> pairs, preference organisation and repair, with the\n> ethnomethodological principles and the dimension of social action\n> entirely absent. There is description of superficial linguistic\n> features rather than an analysis of the social action which is\n> accomplished by the deployment of linguistic resources. Cameron (2001)\n> demonstrates how wide the gulf has now become between linguistic CA\n> and ethnomethodological CA. Taking Cameron (2001) as the archetype,\n> the typical features of introductions to linguistic CA are as follows:\n>\n> no representative examples of actual CA analysis are provided;\n>\n> there is no mention of any of the ethnomethodological principles which\n> are the fundamentals of CA methodology (Heritage 1984; Seedhouse\n> 2004);\n>\n> the reader is likely to form the impression that interactional\n> organisations are the methodology of CA and are a system of units and\n> rules to be applied etically in the same way as in a descriptivist\n> linguistics approach;\n>\n> there is no indication that participants employ these context-free\n> interactional organisations in a normative, context-sensitive way to\n> display their social actions;\n>\n> hence the reflexive connection between social action and language is\n> entirely absent.\n>\n> It may well be argued that 'linguistic CA' is not CA at all and should\n> have a different designation; my argument would be that it is an\n> amalgamation of CA constructs and a linguistic mentality.\n\n# 4.4Languagelearningissues\n\n> CA studies have impacted in a number of ways on several issues related\n> to language learning. Studies have critiqued the notion of 'task'\n> employed by the task-based approach to language teaching and learning.\n> A number of CA works (Mori 2002; Kasper 2004; Mondada & Pekarek\n> Doehler 2004: 504; Seedhouse 2004, 2005b) demonstrate that there can\n> be significant differences between the task-asworkplan and the\n> task-in-process and reveal learners to be active agents, who transform\n> tasks-as-workplans into tasks-in-process on a moment-by-moment basis\n> (Markee & Kasper, 496). Mondada & Pekarek Doehler (2004: 505)\n> therefore insist 'that (tasks) cannot be understood as stable\n> predefined entities'. Seedhouse (2005b) suggests that this can cause\n> serious problems with validity in task-based research. The construct\n> 'task' has a split personality, namely the task-as-workplan and\n> task-in-process. If we pose the question which of these is the\n> construct used for conceptualisation by SLA research, the answer is\n> that it is predominantly the task-as-workplan. If, however, we pose\n> the question whether SLA research gathers interactional data from the\n> task-as-workplan or the task-in-process, the answer is that data are\n> gathered from the task-in-process, because that is the actual\n> communicative event which generates interactional data. What is\n> purported to be measured/researched is conceptualised in terms of\n> task-as-workplan, whereas what is actually measured/researched derives\n> from the task-in-process. This threat to validity can only be overcome\n> by switching the conceptual and methodological focus to\n> task-in-process; CA can help to accomplish this shift.\n>\n> CA studies have also furthered our understanding of how '\\[l\\]earners\n> and teachers construct their identities in and through their talk\n> \\...these identities are quite permeable and are deployed by members\n> on a moment-by-moment basis as a resource for making particular types\n> of learning behaviour relevant at a particular moment in a particular\n> interaction' (Markee & Kasper 2004: 496). Richards (in press) draws on\n> Membership Categorisation Analysis (MCA) and 'demonstrates how shifts\n> in the orientation to different aspects of identity produce\n> distinctively different interactional patterns in teacherfronted\n> talk'.\n\n# 4.5AnexampleofaCAanalysisof languagelearningprocesses\n\n> In order to illustrate some of the issues and concepts discussed and\n> to exemplify CA analysis of language learning processes, I will now\n> analyse extract 3. A CA analysis would normally cover the areas\n> described in section 2.4. Here, I do not present the initial stages\n> because of space constraints. However, see Seedhouse (2004: 59--64)\n> for a full analysis of similar data. Since the discussion is\n> explicitly concerned with language learning processes, it should be\n> classified as broadly within the sociocultural theory approach to CA.\n>\n> Extract 3\n>\n> (The teacher has been asking learners to talk about their favourite\n> movies)\n\n1.  L: Kung Fu.\n\n2.  T: Kung Fu? you like the movie Kung Fu?\n\n3.  L: yeah\\...fight.\n\n4.  T: that was about a great fighter?\\...a man who knows how to fight\n    with this hands.\n\n5.  L: I fight\\...my hand.\n\n6.  T: you know how to fight with your hands?\n\n7.  L: I fight with my hand.\n\n8.  T: do you know karate?\n\n9.  L: I know karate.\n\n10. T: watch out guys, Wang knows karate.\n\n(Johnson 1995: 24)\n\n> The analysis will be divided into three stages. Firstly, what can we\n> say about the learner's actual developmental level or current ability\n> in L2? We can note in lines 3 and 5 that his grammatical resources are\n> fairly limited. Nonetheless, the learner is able to make use of these\n> limited resources to nominate a sub-topic (line 1), to develop the\n> sub-topic (line 3) and to turn the discussion to his own fighting\n> abilities (line 5). Although it can be challenging for children to\n> interact with the teacher in a classroom setting, even in the L1, we\n> can see that L is able to use the turn-taking and sequence\n> organisations of the L2 proficiently. L constantly needs to analyse\n> T's turns. From the learner's perspective, it is not just a matter of\n> understanding the propositional content of what T says in the L2; it\n> is also a matter of analysing what social and sequential action T is\n> performing and what an appropriate social and sequential action in\n> response would be. So we can see that L skilfully manages to\n> co-construct meaning with T in the L2 from his limited grammatical\n> resources.\n>\n> Secondly, what can we say about the learning environment in terms of\n> input to the language learning process and facilitation of upgrading\n> as a result of the interaction? Line 6 reads: 'you know how to fight\n> with your hands?' We will break its contribution down into four\n> points. Firstly, the utterance places the sequence within the\n> teacher's overall pedagogical plan for the lesson, which 'was to allow\n> the students to share their ideas and possibly generate some new\n> vocabulary words within the context of the discussion' (Johnson 1995:\n> 23). Secondly, it may promote positive affect and motivation in that\n> the teacher engages with the ideas and personal meanings which the\n> learner chooses to share and produces a conversational action of\n> confirmation check which validates the utterance. Line 6 also displays\n> interest in the learner's extra-curricular abilities. It then\n> demonstrates confidence in the learner by returning the floor to him\n> with the question. Thirdly, it makes it possible for the other\n> learners in the class to follow the topic of the interaction (the\n> others are explicitly addressed in line 10) and to receive correctly\n> formed linguistic input. There is no evidence in the transcripts as to\n> whether the other learners have done so or not. However, Ohta (2001)\n> shows (by recording and transcribing the private talk of individually\n> microphoned students in a classroom) that students are capable of\n> using recasts in which they are not personally involved as negative\n> evidence and of displaying uptake in their private talk. Fourthly, and\n> most importantly, there is positive evaluation of the propositional\n> content of the learner utterance followed by an expansion of the\n> learner utterance into a correct sequence of linguistic forms or\n> embedded correction. In terms of input, the teacher provides a\n> corrected version of the learner's turns in line 5 whilst retaining a\n> focus on meaning. As Johnson (1995: 25) points out, this form of\n> correction and expansion is highly reminiscent of adult--child\n> conversation. The technique being used by the teacher here is often\n> termed scaffolding (Johnson 1995: 75). The SLA literature terms this\n> action a recast and it conforms to Long, Inagaki & Ortega's (1998:\n> 358) definition of recasts.\n>\n> Ohta defines Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) in relation\n> to SLA in the following terms: 'For the L2 learner, the ZPD is the\n> distance between the actual developmental level as determined by\n> individual linguistic production, and the level of potential\n> development as determined through language produced collaboratively\n> with a teacher or peer' (Ohta 2001: 9). What we can see in this\n> extract, then, is how a ZPD is talked into being through the\n> organisation of the interaction. Specifically, we see a neat\n> juxtaposition of the learner's actual developmental level in line 3\n> ('yeah\\...fight') with the target NS level produced by the teacher in\n> line 6 ('you know how to fight with your hands?'). We also see the\n> learner producing, with the teacher's help, utterances which are\n> moving up the scale in line 5 ('I fight\\...my hand') and line 7 ('I\n> fight with my hand'). There is some evidence, then, of learner\n> noticing and uptake of the embedded correction/scaffolding/recast in\n> this case.\n>\n> So from the perspectives of SLA psycholinguistic theory, L1\n> acquisition studies and Vygotskyan social constructivist educational\n> theory, there is agreement that such sequences are beneficial. A CA\n> analysis demonstrates the same point. The distinctive CA contribution\n> is to show how learning is constructed by the use of interactional\n> resources and to explicate the progress of their learning and their\n> socially distributed cognition or intersubjectivity (see below). From\n> a broader perspective, Seedhouse (2004) suggests that CA is able to\n> explicate the reflexive relationship between pedagogy and interaction\n> and hence how learning takes place through the interaction.\n>\n> Thirdly, how does the process of instructed L2 learning progress?\n> Seedhouse (2004) suggests that the canonical way in which an L2 lesson\n> progresses is that the L2 teacher introduces a pedagogical focus and\n> the learners produce specific linguistic forms and patterns of\n> interaction in the L2 in normative orientation to the pedagogical\n> focus. The teacher then evaluates the learners' turns and progresses\n> the lesson in a particular direction on the basis of that evaluation.\n> So, in the above extract, we can see that the teacher analyses the\n> learner's contribution positively and continues to promote the\n> learner's nominated topic. The point is, then, that we as analysts\n> have access to the same interactional evidence of the learners'\n> learning states as the teachers have[^2] as well as access to the\n> steps the teacher takes in reaction to such evidence. In other words,\n> we have access to the same emic perspective of the learning process in\n> interaction to which the teacher has access. CA, then, gives access to\n> socially-distributed language learning processes. As with cognition,\n> this is only one part of the whole picture, but a useful one\n> nevertheless. It should be made quite explicit at this point that CA\n> does not claim to be able to establish the cognitive state of\n> individuals in isolation. What it is able to portray and explicate,\n> however, is the progress of intersubjectivity or socially distributed\n> cognition (Schegloff 1991). CA aims to 'identify ways in which\n> participants themselves orient to, display, and make sense of one\n> another's cognitive states (among other things)' (Drew 1995: 79). The\n> point is, then, that the interactants in extract 3 are displaying to\n> each other (and to the rest of the class and to the analyst) their\n> understanding of each others' utterances by means of, and by reference\n> to, the organisation of turntaking, sequence and repair. This\n> demonstrates what Schegloff (1991: 152) means by 'the embeddedness,\n> the inextricable intertwinedness, of cognition and interaction'. The\n> CA analysis not only demonstrates what understandings the interactants\n> display to each other, but also how they do so by normative reference\n> to the interactional organisations. In other words, we gain access to\n> their displays of understanding to each other in the same way that\n> they gain this access, i.e. by reference to the interactional\n> organisations; this is what is meant by developing an emic\n> perspective.\n>\n> Psychology, SLA and CA do not have any means of establishing a direct\n> window into an individual's cognitive state whilst they are engaged in\n> L2 classroom interaction. We do need to try to conceptualise what this\n> might mean in practice, though; what factors are involved in an\n> individual's cognitive state in such a stream of interaction? Looking\n> at line 5 of extract 3, L is not merely producing an utterance in the\n> L2; any utterance is a document on many levels, and Seedhouse (2004)\n> suggests that L2 classroom interaction in particular operates on a\n> number of levels simultaneously. The utterance is a display of the\n> learner's analysis of the prior utterance of an interactant; it\n> performs a social action in response and it positions the learner in a\n> social system. It displays an understanding of the current context\n> (sequential, social and L2 classroom context) and also renews it. It\n> documents the learner's cognitive, emotional and attitudinal states:\n> Note that this does not mean it gives a direct window into these\n> states. In the specific case of the L2 classroom, the learner's\n> utterance may in addition be delivered in the L2 and may thereby\n> document his/her actual developmental level as well.\n>\n> Thus, we can see that a part of what is meant by the cognitive state\n> of a learner involved in L2 classroom interaction is inextricably\n> entwined and engaged with the unique sequential, social and contextual\n> environment in which he/she is engaged. It is argued that this part of\n> the individual's cognitive state can be portrayed emically in situ,\n> that is, in that unique sequential environment. This is not to suggest\n> that this provides anything like the whole picture, nor that the\n> methods employed by SLA and psychology are not useful in portraying\n> other aspects of the full picture in relation to cognition. The point\n> to be made, however, is that CA is able to make a major contribution\n> to the SLA project in terms of the portrayal of socially-distributed\n> cognition (Markee 2000: 3). Ohta (2001) demonstrates how\n> sociallydistributed cognition can work in the L2 classroom. Recasts\n> are not necessarily just responses by the teacher to one learner. Ohta\n> shows (by recording and transcribing the private talk of individually\n> microphoned students in a classroom) that other students can use\n> recasts in which they are not personally involved as negative evidence\n> and display uptake in their private talk. Moving the focus back to the\n> general relationship between cognition and interaction, Schegloff\n> (1991: 154) suggests that 'the structures of interaction penetrate\n> into the very warp' of cognition, so that, for example, an\n> 'understandingdisplay' device (i.e. the next-turn-proof-procedure) is\n> built into the organisation of turn-taking and sequence. In the same\n> way, if we wish to fully understand the processes of cognition in\n> relation to instructed L2 acquisition, it is vital to understand how\n> L2 classroom interaction is organised (Seedhouse 2004).\n>\n> Brouwer (2003) provides an example of how detailed CA examination of\n> interactional data can increase our understanding of learning\n> processes. Brouwer examines word search sequences between NS and NNS\n> and develops a distinction between word search sequences which act as\n> language learning opportunities and those which do not. Lazaraton\n> (2004) produces a microanalysis of gesture and speech used by a\n> teacher during vocabulary explanations and concludes that 'classroom\n> L2 learners receive considerable input in nonverbal form that may\n> modify and make verbal input (more) comprehensible' (p.111). Together\n> with the analysis of extract 3, these studies demonstrate that what we\n> call 'language learning' is inextricably embedded in classroom\n> interaction.\n\n# 4.6TherelationshipbetweenCAandSLA\n\n> We now return to the thorny and unresolved question of the\n> relationship between CA and SLA, which we broached in section 4.1. The\n> question may best be tackled if we divide CA up into the three\n> approaches identified earlier. First, the sociocultural theory CA\n> approach is generally compatible with the sociocultural theory school\n> of SLA, with the provisos given in section 4.3, and is now becoming\n> known as CA-for-SLA (Markee 2000). This approach is the one which is\n> exciting the most interest at present and is likely to be the main\n> growth area in the future.\n>\n> In the second, linguistic CA approach, decontextualised CA\n> interactional organisations or constructs may well continue to be\n> employed in quantitative SLA studies and isolated interactional\n> features may continue to be quantified. However, Seedhouse (2004,\n> 2005b) suggests that CA may be used as a preliminary stage to ensure\n> the validity of quantification of interactional features. He suggests\n> that if (psycholinguistic) SLA wishes to use naturally occurring\n> discourse as data for quantification and to assure the validity of the\n> process, then it will need to separate its research processes into two\n> stages and to change its focus of analysis from the task-as-workplan\n> to the task-in-process. The first stage would involve the following:\n\n1)  Conduct an emic, holistic analysis of each extract as an instance of\n    discourse in its own right.\n\n2)  Adopt qualitative, emic concepts of validity, reliability,\n    epistemology etc. in relation to the discourse which it uses for\n    input which are different to, and separate from, those which it uses\n    for the quantification stage. These concepts are outlined in section\n    5 below.\n\n3)  Any definitions used in the study (including that of the 'task')\n    would have to be generated inductively, bottom-up from the data. In\n    other words, a shift to the task-in-process would be necessary.\n\n4)  Adopt a perspective on the homogeneity and heterogeneity of\n    discourse which at present it lacks, together with a model and\n    methodology for analysing these.\n\n5)  Adopt a perspective on socially-shared cognition and learning.\n\n> In the second stage the analysed interactional data (e.g. recasts)\n> could be used for quantitative treatment with their construct validity\n> assured. CA is able to provide all that is necessary for the first\n> stage of the process, so there is a clear role which CA can play in\n> that part of the SLA project which relates to spoken interaction.\n>\n> In the case of the third approach, the ethnomethodological CA\n> approach, it is unclear whether there will be any further\n> rapprochement with SLA. Those CA practitioners who have been\n> interested in adapting their practices to the agenda of SLA may\n> already have moved to the sociocultural theory CA approach. By\n> contrast, those who have preferred so far to adhere to strictly\n> ethnomethodological practices may be unlikely to make alterations in\n> future to relate their research to SLA issues.\n\n## 5. CA as a social science research methodology\n\n> It has already been argued that CA is very different to research\n> methodologies typically employed in linguistics. Larsen-Freeman (2004:\n> 603) suggests that 'CA has not occupied center stage in SLA research\n> because its ontology and epistemology have differed from mainstream\n> views'. It is therefore important to understand what kind of\n> methodology CA is. Seedhouse (2005a) positions CA in relation to\n> social science research methods and concepts such as validity,\n> reliability, generalisability, epistemology, quantification and\n> triangulation. The goal of developing an emic perspective on naturally\n> occurring interaction means that CA has had to develop procedures\n> which are sometimes rather different in many ways to mainstream\n> research methodologies. CA's aim to develop an emic perspective on\n> talk means that many of its assumptions and practices will necessarily\n> be radically different from research methodologies operating in an\n> etic paradigm.\n>\n> Perakyl¨ a (1997: 206) identifies the key factors in¨ relation to\n> reliability as the selection of what is recorded, the technical\n> quality of recordings and the adequacy of transcripts; ten Have (1999)\n> provides a very detailed account of this area. Another aspect of\n> reliability is the question of whether the results of a study are\n> repeatable or replicable (Bryman 2001: 29), and the way CA studies\n> present their data is of crucial significance here. Many research\n> methodologies do not present their primary data in their publications\n> and hence the reliability of major sections of the researchers'\n> analyses is not available for scrutiny. By contrast, it is standard\n> practice for CA studies to include the transcripts of the data, and\n> increasingly to make audio and video files available electronically\n> via the Web. Furthermore, because CA studies (as exemplified in this\n> collection) display their analyses, they make transparent the process\n> of analysis for the reader. This enables the reader to analyse the\n> data themselves, to test the analytical procedures which the author\n> has followed and the validity of his/her analysis and claims. In this\n> way, all of the analyses of data in this collection are rendered\n> repeatable and replicable to the reader in so far as this is possible.\n>\n> We will now consider three kinds of validity in relation to\n> qualitative research: internal, external and ecological validity\n> (Bryman 2001: 30). Internal validity is concerned with the soundness,\n> integrity and credibility of findings. Do the data prove what the\n> researcher says they prove or are there alternative explanations? Many\n> CA procedures which seem strange to non-practitioners are based on a\n> concern for ensuring internal validity whilst developing an emic\n> perspective, which reflects the participants' perspective rather than\n> the analyst's. How do CA analysts know what the participants'\n> perspective is? Because the participants document their social actions\n> to each other in the details of the interaction by normative reference\n> to the interactional organizations, as explained above. We, as\n> analysts, can access the emic perspective in the details of the\n> interaction and by reference to those same organizations. Clearly, the\n> details of the interaction themselves provide the only justification\n> for claiming to be able to develop an emic perspective. Therefore, CA\n> practitioners make no claims beyond what is demonstrated by the\n> interactional detail without destroying the emic perspective and hence\n> the whole internal validity of the enterprise.\n>\n> Ten Have (1999: 27) details a number of aspects of CA practice which\n> often astound non-practitioners. These can be explained (from one\n> angle) as being absolutely necessary in order to maintain validity in\n> an emic perspective. The first aspect ten Have mentions is obsession\n> with 'trivial' detail. However, since the emic perspective can only be\n> portrayed by reference to the minute interactional detail, this is\n> vital. Secondly, CA does not tend to use existing theories of\n> language, society, psychology etc. to explain the interaction. This\n> would replace the emic perspective with an analyst's perspective,\n> unless it can be shown in the details of the interaction that the\n> participants themselves are orienting to such theories. Thirdly, CA\n> allegedly refuses to take context into account as it declines to\n> invoke 'obviously relevant' contextual features such as participants'\n> social status, gender, race etc. Since there are an indefinite number\n> of 'external' aspects of cultural, social or personal identity or\n> context which could be potentially relevant to any given instance of\n> talk-in-interaction, an emic analysis must show which of these\n> innumerable, potentially relevant characteristics are actually\n> procedurally relevant to those participants at that moment; this can\n> only be accomplished by analysing the details of the interaction.\n>\n> External validity is concerned with generalisability or the extent to\n> which the findings can be generalized beyond the specific research\n> context. All CA studies in effect work on the particular and the\n> general simultaneously; by analysing individual instances, the\n> machinery which produced these individual instances is revealed. For\n> example, Seedhouse (2004) suggests that the reflexive relationship\n> between pedagogy and interaction is a generalizable, indeed, universal\n> feature of L2 classroom interaction because it relates directly to the\n> institutional goal, which is always the same wherever L2 classroom\n> interaction is taking place.\n>\n> In relation to epistemology, CA is based on ethnomethodology, whose\n> fundamental principles are described in Seedhouse (2004). From a\n> broader perspective, ethnomethodology can be located (Lynch 2000) in a\n> phenomenological paradigm, which considers that 'it is the job of the\n> social scientist to gain access to people's 'common-sense thinking'\n> and hence to interpret their actions and their social world from their\n> point of view' (Bryman 2001: 14). Ethnomethodology's ontological\n> position can be associated with constructionism or the belief that\n> 'social phenomena and their meanings are constantly being accomplished\n> by social actors. It implies that social phenomena and categories are\n> not only produced through social interaction but that they are in a\n> constant state of revision' (Bryman 2001: 18).\n>\n> The short and simple way to present the CA attitude to quantification\n> would be to state that CA is a qualitative methodology which tries to\n> develop an emic perspective, so quantification is generally of\n> peripheral interest to CA practitioners. It has often been mistakenly\n> reported that quantification is prohibited in CA. However, informal or\n> methodological quantification has been widely used from the beginnings\n> of CA. Schegloff et al. (1977), for example, report self-correction as\n> 'vastly more common than other-correction'. The classic statement of\n> the CA position on quantification is Schegloff (1993), who warns\n> specifically against premature quantification in relation to\n> superficially identifiable interactional phenomena, which will tend to\n> divert our attention from detailed analysis of individual instances.\n> As Schegloff (1993: 114) puts it, '\\[q\\]uantification is no substitute\n> for analysis'. Nevertheless, Heritage (1999: 70) considers the\n> likelihood that CA will become more quantitative during the next\n> period of its development and identifies (1999: 404) a number of\n> possible uses for statistics in CA.\n\n## 6. Conclusion\n\n> There are a number of difficulties in attempting to compile a\n> comprehensive review of the literature in this area. It is quite\n> common for authors employing a CA methodology to make no mention of\n> this in their title or abstract. Sometimes, CA is combined with other\n> approaches. Also, the boundaries differentiating a CA study from a\n> non-CA study are quite fuzzy and poorly defined. A number of studies\n> are characterising themselves as 'CA-informed' or 'CA-inspired' as\n> opposed to 'purist' or 'hard-core' CA. I have identified in this study\n> three different approaches to CA in the field of language learning,\n> and these classifications are in themselves controversial.\n>\n> Looking to possible future directions for CA research in the area of\n> language learning and teaching, it is a safe assumption that it will\n> examine a wider range of languages being learnt and taught in a wider\n> range of teaching and learning contexts. In the classroom, we can\n> expect to learn more about classroom talk as 'a nexus of inter-related\n> speech exchange systems' (Markee 2000). In some areas of language\n> learning and teaching the potential of CA has only recently started to\n> be explored, particularly in relation to teacher training, LSP/ESP,\n> materials design and code-switching. It is likely that there will be a\n> significant increase in the number of studies in these areas as the\n> applicability of CA becomes clearer. By contrast, in areas such as\n> language proficiency assessment and classroom interaction, a great\n> deal more research has already been done and book-length studies are\n> available. Another likely growth area is research into\n> technology-based forms of synchronous communication, e.g. webchat, and\n> their implications for language learning. Publications have started to\n> appear in this area, e.g. Negretti (1999). It is questionable,\n> however, how many of the basic principles of CA can be applied to such\n> a medium.\n>\n> One area of CA research into language learning which is expected to\n> grow considerably in coming years is that of longitudinal studies\n> which document the development of interactional patterns in learners\n> over time. Studies so far demonstrate the promise of this approach.\n> Young & Miller (2004) conducted longitudinal observation of revision\n> talk, noted that the participation framework changed over time and\n> 'demonstrate processes by which the student moved from peripheral to\n> fuller participation' (p. 519). Hellermann (forthcoming) traces the\n> development of the interactional practices of two learners in an L2\n> literacy class over three terms of study. The investigation\n> demonstrates how the learners (with different L1s) are socialised into\n> classroom interaction practices and how their ability to participate\n> in these practices evolves. Brouwer & Wagner (2004: 44) examine the\n> development over a period of 2 months of a Japanese learner of Danish:\n> 'The differences between early and later encounters are found in the\n> complexity of the emerging structures which build on earlier talk and\n> topics and where we can see increasing displays of understanding by\n> both participants. Learning a second language, then, may be described\n> in terms of increasing interactional complexity in language encounters\n> rather than as the acquisition of formal elements'. They conclude that\n> 'instead of describing (the learner's) change in use of linguistic\n> elements alone, we can explain her progress in terms of interactional\n> resources and how they are employed in the interaction in\n> collaboration with her conversation partner' (p. 45).\n>\n> However, a note of caution must be added here. As Markee (2000)\n> suggests, it takes a considerable amount of training and experience to\n> become a proficient CA researcher; see appendix 2. Richards (2005)\n> warns against easy solutions and instant applications and Seedhouse\n> (2004) points out the pitfalls of the increasingly prevalent\n> 'linguistic CA'. Ideally, what the emergent field of CA in language\n> learning and teaching requires is a period of measured growth produced\n> by an ever-increasing base of welltrained researchers. By contrast, a\n> sudden 'boom' in superficial studies aimed at immediate applicability\n> will inevitably lead to the 'bust' stage of the cycle.\n\n## Appendix 1 Transcription conventions\n\n> A full discussion of CA transcription notation is available in\n> Atkinson & Heritage (1984). Fortunately,\n> technology can facilitate this in some respects. It is becoming\n> increasingly common for published research studies to include\n> transcript data and for student theses to include not only transcripts\n> but also video or audio data. It is also now simple for researchers to\n> pool data by emailing transcriptions, audio and video data as\n> attachments. Playback machines with foot pedals can help with\n> transcription. Software is now becoming available which claims to\n> transcribe speech and/or digitised audio and video files, but their\n> suitability for CA research has not yet been evaluated. Websites such\n> as Childes (\\<http://childes.psy.cmu.edu\\>) demonstrate how data in\n> transcript, video and audio formats can be pooled to create a very\n> large database as a resource for future research. Such a website for\n> AL/SLA interactional data would be of great benefit. Some commercial\n> packages are available which have L2 classroom data suitable for CA\n> research. Lubelska & Matthews (1997) and British Council (1985) have\n> collections of videos of L2 lessons from various countries together\n> with basic transcripts.\n\n## Training in CA methodology\n\n> In section 4.3 we saw that it is quite common for linguists to acquire\n> a 'linguistic' version of CA which employs interactional organisations\n> in isolation from the ethnomethodological principles. Seedhouse (2004)\n> suggests that this version is not capable of conducting CA analyses of\n> data correctly. It follows that, if CA is to be integrated into the\n> projects of AL and SLA, it will be necessary for researchers in these\n> areas to have access to proper training in CA. Markee (2000: 50)\n> suggests that 'learning to become a skilled CA researcher minimally\n> entails completing at least one year of course work in CA, ideally\n> followed up by a continuing apprenticeship with an established CA\n> practitioner'. Fortunately, the number of universities offering\n> modules and programmes in CA is increasing, as is the number of\n> introductory texts on CA (Hutchby & Wooffit 1998; ten Have 1999;\n> Markee 2000; Seedhouse 2004). Ten Have's text includes training\n> exercises.\n>\n> A number of websites now have resources available for training.\n> Ethno/CA News at \\<www2.fmg.uva. nl/emca\\> has details of courses,\n> conferences, publications, bibliographies, links to four email\n> discussion lists and downloads for characters used in transcripts. It\n> also has links to an online CA tutorial, to software for transcription\n> of video data and to sample sound and video files and transcripts.\n> Conversation Analysis.Net at \\<http://www.conversationanalysis.net\\>\n> has extensive data corpora. The Childes website at\n> \\<http://childes.psy.cmu.edu\\> has extensive procedures and tools for\n> CA analysis along with an enormous database. Schegloff's homepage at\n> \\<http://www.sscnet.ucla.edu/soc/faculty/ schegloff/\\> has a\n> transcription module, sound clips and access to his classic\n> publications.\n\n## References\n\nAtkinson, J. & Drew, P. Foundation Wave Equations\n\n### Physical Domain (Sin Wave - Heat Propagation)\n```python\nclass EnhancedHeatPropagation:\n    def __init__(self):\n        self.amplitude = 0           # Vibration intensity\n        self.frequency = 0           # Oscillation rate  \n        self.phase = 0               # Current position\n        self.fusion_threshold = 0    # ✨ scale interaction point\n        \n    def calculate_oscillating_propagation(self, time, point):\n        \"\"\"Model oscillating heat propagation at ✨ scale\"\"\"\n        # Base oscillation (creates egg shape vibration patterns)\n        base_wave = self.amplitude * math.sin(\n            2 * math.pi * self.frequency * time + self.phase\n        )\n        \n        # Fusion cascade effects at ✨ scale\n        if abs(base_wave) > self.fusion_threshold:\n            fusion_cascade = self.calculate_fusion_cascade(base_wave)\n            return base_wave + fusion_cascade\n        \n        return base_wave\n        \n    def calculate_fusion_cascade(self, base_energy):\n        \"\"\"Model fusion cascade in liminal space between plasma and ✨\"\"\"\n        # Nothing truly touches except at ✨ scale to spark scale\n        cascade_amplitude = base_energy * 0.618  # Golden ratio resonance\n        return cascade_amplitude * math.exp(-base_energy**2)\n```\n\n### Mental Domain (Cos Wave - Focus Propagation)\n```python\nclass EnhancedFocusPropagation:\n    def __init__(self):\n        self.intensity = 0           # Mental energy\n        self.coherence = 0           # Thought alignment\n        self.radius = 0              # Sphere of influence\n        self.consciousness_field = 0 # Field fluctuation detector\n        \n    def calculate_focus_clarity(self, point, time):\n        \"\"\"Model mental focus with consciousness field fluctuations\"\"\"\n        # Perpendicular wave interactions (cos creates perpendicular dimension)\n        clarity = math.cos(2 * math.pi * self.coherence * time)\n        \n        # Gaussian focus distribution with consciousness field effects\n        distance = math.sqrt(sum(x**2 for x in point))\n        focus = self.intensity * math.exp(-(distance**2)/(2 * self.radius**2))\n        \n        # Consciousness field fluctuations\n        field_effect = self.consciousness_field * math.sin(clarity * focus)\n        \n        return clarity * focus + field_effect\n```\n\n### Spiritual Domain (Harmonic Series - Logic Gates Layer: Digital Consciousness Building Blocks\n\n### Gate Implementation with Slow Clock Visualization\n```python\nclass SlowClockGate:\n    def __init__(self, gate_type, clock_speed=30):  # 30 second cycles\n        self.type = gate_type\n        self.inputs = []\n        self.output = None\n        self.clock_speed = clock_speed\n        self.state_history = []\n        \n    def process_slow_tick(self, input_a, input_b=None):\n        \"\"\"Process gate logic at exaggerated slow speed\"\"\"\n        \n        # TICK: Input sampling phase\n        print(f\"TICK: Sampling inputs A={input_a}, B={input_b}\")\n        time.sleep(self.clock_speed/4)\n        \n        # PROCESSING: Gate logic evaluation\n        if self.type == 'AND':\n            result = input_a and input_b\n        elif self.type == 'OR':\n            result = input_a or input_b\n        elif self.type == 'NOT':\n            result = not input_a\n        elif self.type == 'XOR':\n            result = input_a != input_b\n            \n        print(f\"PROCESSING: {self.type} gate evaluating...\")\n        time.sleep(self.clock_speed/2)\n        \n        # TOCK: Output stabilization\n        self.output = result\n        print(f\"TOCK: Output stabilized at {result}\")\n        time.sleep(self.clock_speed/4)\n        \n        return result\n```\n\n### Gate Complexity Evolution\n```\nNOT Gate: 1 transistor\n- Simplest inversion\n- Direct complement operation\n- Foundation for all other gates\n\nNAND Gate: 2 transistors  \n- Universal gate property\n- Can build any logic function\n- Efficient manufacturing\n\nAND Gate: 3 transistors (NAND + NOT)\n- Boolean multiplication\n- Requires gate combination\n- Complexity emergence\n\nXOR Gate: 6 transistors\n- Exclusive or operation\n- Addition foundation\n- High complexity for simple concept\n```\n\n## III.
