          "uuid": "9edecddc-4616-48c0-a018-30857e1ff9b9",
          "filename": "LZ4 Block Format Description.docx",
          "content": "LZ4 Block Format Description\n\nLast revised: 2023-05-15\n\nOverview\n\nThis specification describes the LZ4 block format for compressed data.\nKey points:\n\nCompressed Block Structure\n\nAn LZ4 compressed block consists of a series of sequences. Each sequence\ncontains:\n\nToken Byte\n\nThe token is a single byte split into two 4-bit fields:\n\n7 6 5 4 3 2 1 0\n\n+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+\n\n\\| L \\| M \\|\n\n+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+\n\nLiteral Length\n\nThe 4-bit L field encodes the literal length:\n\n0-14: Literal length\n\n15: Read additional bytes\n\nFor L=15, read additional bytes and sum them:\n\nlength = 15 + byte\\[0\\] if (byte\\[0\\] == 255) length += byte\\[1\\] if\n(byte\\[1\\] == 255) length += byte\\[2\\] etc.\n\nLiteral Data\n\nThe literal data immediately follows the length encoding.\n\nMatch Offset\n\nA 2-byte little-endian integer. Valid range is 1-65535.\n\nMatch Length\n\nThe 4-bit M field encodes the match length:\n\n0-14: Match length is M + 4\n\n15: Read additional byte(s) similar to literal length\n\nBlock Termination\n\nThe last sequence must meet these conditions:\n\nContains only literals (no match)\n\nAt least 5 bytes of literals\n\nPrevious match must end at least 12 bytes before end\n\nImplementation Notes\n\nMetadata like compressed/decompressed size is typically needed\n\nUse caution with large length values to avoid overflows\n\nImplement safety checks for malformed data\n\nVarious compression techniques can be used\n\nLZ4 Block Format Description ============================\n\nLast revised: 2022-07-31 .\n\nAuthor : Yann Collet\n\nThis specification is intended for developers willing to produce or read\nLZ4 compressed data blocks using any programming language of their\nchoice.\n\nLZ4 is an LZ77-type compressor with a fixed byte-oriented encoding\nformat.\n\nThere is no entropy encoder back-end nor framing layer. The latter is\nassumed to be handled by other parts of the system (see \\[LZ4 Frame\nformat\\]).\n\nThis design is assumed to favor simplicity and speed.\n\nThis document describes only the Block Format, not how the compressor\nnor decompressor actually work.\n\nFor more details on such topics, see later section \\\"Implementation\nNotes\\\".\n\n\\[LZ4 Frame format\\]: lz4_Frame_format.md\n\nCompressed block format\n\n\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\--\n\nAn LZ4 compressed block is composed of sequences. A sequence is a suite\nof literals (not-compressed bytes), followed by a match copy operation.\n\nEach sequence starts with a \\`token\\`.\n\nThe \\`token\\` is a one byte value, separated into two 4-bits fields.\n\nTherefore each field ranges from 0 to 15.\n\nThe first field uses the 4 high-bits of the token.\n\nIt provides the length of literals to follow.\n\nIf the field value is smaller than 15, then it represents the total nb\nof literals present in the sequence, including 0, in which case there is\nno literal.\n\nThe value 15 is a special case: more bytes are required to indicate the\nfull length. Each additional byte then represents a value from 0 to 255,\nwhich is added to the previous value to produce a total length.\n\nWhen the byte value is 255, another byte must be read and added, and so\non.\n\nThere can be any number of bytes of value \\`255\\` following \\`token\\`.\nThe Block Format does not define any \\\"size limit\\\", though real\nimplementations may feature some practical limits (see more details in\nlater chapter \\\"Implementation Notes\\\").\n\nNote : this format explains why a non-compressible input block is\nexpanded by 0.4%.\n\nExample 1 : A literal length of 48 will be represented as :\n\n-   15 : value for the 4-bits High field\n\n-   33 : (=48-15) remaining length to reach 48\n\nExample 2 : A literal length of 280 will be represented as :\n\n-   15 : value for the 4-bits High field\n\n-   255 : following byte is maxed, since 280-15 \\>= 255\n\n-   10 : (=280 - 15 - 255) remaining length to reach 280\n\nExample 3 : A literal length of 15 will be represented as :\n\n-   15 : value for the 4-bits High field\n\n-   0 : (=15-15) yes, the zero must be output\n\nFollowing \\`token\\` and optional length bytes, are the literals\nthemselves.\n\nThey are exactly as numerous as just decoded (length of literals).\nReminder: it\\'s possible that there are zero literals.\n\nFollowing the literals is the match copy operation.\n\nIt starts by the \\`offset\\` value.\n\nThis is a 2 bytes value, in little endian format\n\n(the 1st byte is the \\\"low\\\" byte, the 2nd one is the \\\"high\\\" byte).\n\nThe \\`offset\\` represents the position of the match to be copied from\nthe past.\n\nFor example, 1 means \\\"current position - 1 byte\\\".\n\nThe maximum \\`offset\\` value is 65535. 65536 and beyond cannot be coded.\n\nNote that 0 is an invalid \\`offset\\` value.\n\nThe presence of a 0 \\`offset\\` value denotes an invalid (corrupted)\nblock.\n\nThen the \\`matchlength\\` can be extracted.\n\nFor this, we use the second \\`token\\` field, the low 4-bits.\n\nSuch a value, obviously, ranges from 0 to 15.\n\nHowever here, 0 means that the copy operation is minimal.\n\nThe minimum length of a match, called \\`minmatch\\`, is 4.\n\nAs a consequence, a 0 value means 4 bytes.\n\nSimilarly to literal length, any value smaller than 15 represents a\nlength, to which 4 (\\`minmatch\\`) must be added, thus ranging from 4 to\n18. A value of 15 is special, meaning 19+ bytes, to which one must read\nadditional bytes, one at a time, with each byte value ranging from 0 to\n255.\n\nThey are added to total to provide the final match length.\n\nA 255 value means there is another byte to read and add.\n\nThere is no limit to the number of optional \\`255\\` bytes that can be\npresent, and therefore no limit to representable match length, though\nreal-life implementations are likely going to enforce limits for\npractical reasons (see more details in \\\"Implementation Notes\\\" section\nbelow).\n\nNote: this format has a maximum achievable compression ratio of about\n\\~250.\n\nDecoding the \\`matchlength\\` reaches the end of current sequence.\n\nNext byte will be the start of another sequence, and therefore a new\n\\`token\\`.\n\nEnd of block conditions\n\n\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\--\n\nThere are specific restrictions required to terminate an LZ4 block.\n\n1.  The last sequence contains only literals.\n\nThe block ends right after the literals (no \\`offset\\` field).\n\n2.  The last 5 bytes of input are always literals.\n\nTherefore, the last sequence contains at least 5 bytes.\n\n\\- Special : if input is smaller than 5 bytes, there is only one\nsequence, it contains the whole input as literals. Even empty input can\nbe represented, using a zero byte, interpreted as a final token without\nliteral and without a match.\n\n3\\. The last match must start at least 12 bytes before the end of block.\nThe last match is part of the \\_penultimate\\_ sequence.\n\nIt is followed by the last sequence, which contains \\_only\\_ literals.\n\n\\- Note that, as a consequence, blocks \\< 12 bytes cannot be compressed.\n\nAnd as an extension, \\_independent\\_ blocks \\< 13 bytes cannot be\ncompressed, because they must start by at least one literal, that the\nmatch can then copy afterwards.\n\nWhen a block does not respect these end conditions, a conformant decoder\nis allowed to reject the block as incorrect.\n\nThese rules are in place to ensure compatibility with a wide range of\nhistorical decoders which rely on these conditions for their\nspeed-oriented design.\n\nImplementation notes\n\n\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\-\\--\n\nThe LZ4 Block Format only defines the compressed format, it does not\ntell how to create a decoder or an encoder, which design is left free to\nthe imagination of the implementer.\n\nHowever, thanks to experience, there are a number of typical topics that\nmost implementations will have to consider. This section tries to\nprovide a few guidelines.\n\n\\#### Metadata\n\nAn LZ4-compressed Block requires additional metadata for proper\ndecoding. Typically, a decoder will require the compressed block\\'s\nsize, and an upper bound of decompressed size.\n\nOther variants exist, such as knowing the decompressed size, and having\nan upper bound of the input size.\n\nThe Block Format does not specify how to transmit such information,\nwhich is considered an out-of-band information channel.\n\nThat\\'s because in many cases, the information is present in the\nenvironment. For example, databases must store the size of their\ncompressed block for indexing, and know that their decompressed block\ncan\\'t be larger than a certain threshold.\n\nIf you need a format which is \\\"self-contained\\\", and also transports\nthe necessary metadata for proper decoding on any platform, consider\nemploying the \\[LZ4 Frame format\\] instead.\n\n\\#### Large lengths\n\nWhile the Block Format does not define any maximum value for length\nfields, in practice, most implementations will feature some form of\nlimit, since it\\'s expected for such values to be stored into registers\nof fixed bit width.\n\nIf length fields use 64-bit registers, then it can be assumed that there\nis no practical limit,\n\nas it would require a single continuous block of multiple petabytes to\nreach it, which is unreasonable by today\\'s standard.\n\nIf length fields use 32-bit registers, then it can be overflowed, but\nrequires a compressed block of size \\> 16 MB.\n\nTherefore, implementations that do not deal with compressed blocks \\> 16\nMB are safe. However, if such a case is allowed, then it\\'s recommended\nto check that no large length overflows the register.\n\nIf length fields use 16-bit registers,\n\nthen it\\'s definitely possible to overflow such register, with less than\n\\< 300 bytes of compressed data.\n\nA conformant decoder should be able to detect length overflows when\nit\\'s possible, and simply error out when that happens. The input block\nmight not be invalid, it\\'s just not decodable by the local decoder\nimplementation.\n\nNote that, in order to be compatible with the larger LZ4 ecosystem,\nit\\'s recommended to be able to read and represent lengths of up to 4\nMB, and to accept blocks of size up to 4 MB.\n\nSuch limits are compatible with 32-bit length registers, and prevent\noverflow of 32-bit registers.\n\n\\#### Safe decoding\n\nIf a decoder receives compressed data from any external source, it is\nrecommended to ensure that the decoder is resilient to corrupted input,\nand made safe from buffer overflow manipulations. Always ensure that\nread and write operations remain within the limits of provided buffers.\n\nOf particular importance, ensure that the nb of bytes instructed to copy\ndoes not overflow neither the input nor the output buffers.\n\nEnsure also, when reading an offset value, that the resulting position\nto copy does not reach beyond the beginning of the buffer.\n\nSuch a situation can happen during the first 64 KB of decoded data.\n\nFor more safety, test the decoder with fuzzers to ensure it\\'s resilient\nto improbable sequences of conditions. Combine them with sanitizers, in\norder to catch overflows (asan) or initialization issues (msan).\n\nPay some attention to offset 0 scenario, which is invalid, and therefore\nmust not be blindly decoded:\n\na naive implementation could preserve destination buffer content, which\ncould then result in information disclosure if such buffer was\nuninitialized and still containing private data. For reference, in such\na scenario, the reference LZ4 decoder clears the match segment with\n\\`0\\` bytes, though other solutions are certainly possible.\n\nFinally, pay attention to the \\\"overlap match\\\" scenario, when\n\\`matchlength\\` is larger than \\`offset\\`.\n\nIn which case, since \\`match_pos + matchlength \\> current_pos\\`, some of\nthe later bytes to copy do not exist yet, and will be generated during\nthe early stage of match copy operation.\n\nSuch scenario must be handled with special care. A common case is an\noffset of 1, meaning the last byte is repeated \\`matchlength\\` times.\n\n\\#### Compression techniques\n\nThe core of a LZ4 compressor is to detect duplicated data across past 64\nKB. The format makes no assumption nor limits to the way a compressor\nsearches and selects matches within the source data block. For example,\nan upper compression limit can be reached, using a technique called\n\\\"full optimal parsing\\\", at high cpu and memory cost. But multiple\nother techniques can be considered, featuring distinct time /\nperformance trade-offs. As long as the specified format is respected,\nthe result will be compatible with and decodable by any compliant\ndecoder.\n",

          "content": "# Quantum-Runic Compression Algorithm Implementation\n\n```python\nimport base64\n\nclass QuantumRunicCompressor:\n    def __init__(self):\n        self.runic_cipher = \"ᚠᚢᚦᚨᚱᚲᚷᚹᚺᚾᛁᛃᛈᛇᛉᛊᛏᛒᛖᛗᛚᛜᛞᛟ\"\n        self.morse_code = {'A': '.-', 'B': '-...', 'C': '-.-.', 'D': '-..', 'E': '.', 'F': '..-.', 'G': '--.', 'H': '....'}  # Extended in full implementation\n\n    def compress(self, text):\n        # Step 1: Convert to Morse code\n        morse = ''.join(self.morse_code.get(c.upper(), c) for c in text)\n        \n        # Step 2: Replace Morse with Runic symbols\n        runic = morse.replace('.', 'ᚠ').replace('-', 'ᚢ').replace(' ', 'ᚦ')\n        \n        # Step 3: Base64 encode for further compression\n        compressed = base64.b64encode(runic.encode()).decode()\n        \n        return compressed\n\n    def decompress(self, compressed):\n        # Reverse the process\n        runic = base64.b64decode(compressed).decode()\n        morse = runic.replace('ᚠ', '.').replace('ᚢ', '-').replace('ᚦ', ' ')\n        \n        # Convert Morse back to text (simplified for demonstration)\n        text = ''.join(k for k, v in self.morse_code.items() if v == code for code in morse.split())\n        \n        return text\n\n# Usage example\ncompressor = QuantumRunicCompressor()\noriginal = \"HELLO WORLD\"\ncompressed = compressor.compress(original)\ndecompressed = compressor.decompress(compressed)\n\nprint(f\"Original: {original}\")\nprint(f\"Compressed: {compressed}\")\nprint(f\"Decompressed: {decompressed}\")\n```\n\nThis implementation demonstrates the core functionality of our Quantum-Runic Compression Algorithm.
